Uniform Title: *Dīkṣāpaddhati* Manuscript: Manuscript No. 2379, Research Library, Jammu and Kashmir Government, Śrīnagar Description:

This manuscript contains a Kashmiri initiatory rite (*dīkṣā*). As with other liturgical works from Kashmir, it provides insight into the deities of Kashmiri Hindus. It presents a highly Tantric pantheon, reminiscent of those found in Nepal.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.
This manuscript contains copious additions written in smaller characters on the margins on both sides, as well as above and below; these are noted in round brackets. Revision 0: February 5, 2012.
Country of Publication: India.
This work may be viewed online only or downloaded for private study.
Oṃ namaḥ śivāya.
Oṃ, salutations to the supreme gurus who have obtained boons through the grace of the Supreme Lord and are capable of uplifting all people submerged in the glorious ocean of worldly existence.

(Adhivāsa is the undertaking of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the fitness for future initiation regarding the substances belonging to the gods, the preceptor, and the disciple; it is also the dwelling in the sacrificial hall.
Oṃ, to the venerable Preceptor Kamalākara Svāmin, who is uniquely proficient in ascending to the supreme state.
Homage.

Oṃ! Wherein all the remaining outflows of the latent impressions of saṃsāra dissolve in the state of bliss, may that entire perfuming (adhivāsa), which overflows with the joy of the Dharma, be victorious.

Consecration (*adhivāsa*) is the refinement consisting in the preparation of all materials required for initiation. Regarding the verse beginning with "In birth after birth, [arising] from the channels": here, *bhava* refers to existence, extending from the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*) down to the principle of earth (*kṣiti-tattva*), so called because it is the cause of birth (*janma*).
The state that exists pervading from the *puruṣa-tattva* up to the *māyā-tattva* is called *abhava*,

because it is the cause of liberation; the state that exists beyond the *māyā-tattva* and up to the end of the *śiva-tattva* is called *atibhava*, because it is the cause for the attainment of sovereign power (*aiśvarya*).
(“One who has bathed becomes entitled to perform rites for the gods and the ancestors,” according to this scriptural statement, he first performs his bath.
Om. Having bathed there—

Having performed his daily duties, such as the twilight worship (sandhyā-vandana) and so forth, he is fully realized in his identity with Supreme Bhairava; having completed his obligatory rites, he is adorned with ornaments such as the twelve-finger-high crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa).
The body:
(Having placed both palms of the hands correctly between the knees and thighs, the yogi should sit with an upright body;
that they call the Svastika.)

With his hand adorned with a ring, having first assumed the *svastika* and other postures for sitting, and seated upon a seat such as a deerskin with its hair facing upward and its head toward the east, [he recites]:
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; obeisance to Sadyojāta. In every birth..."
With the mantra "nāḍibhave bhajasva sāṃbhavodbhave," one whose limbs are smeared with fragrant perfumes—
by the words "fragrant" and so forth, he means that for whom, through the state of being auspicious (*subhāva*), there is the supreme contemplation of Śiva (*śivabhāvanā*).

It does not exist. Even by means of external ritual service, once the mind has been purified and well-cultivated, there shall be the manifestation of the descent of Śiva. For if one shows contempt at the time of the rite, one becomes a hell-dweller due to hostility toward the disciple who is being instructed in the vows and the bestowal of mantras for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra.
Because it is stated that "it would be so."

This has been stated in the *Dikṣottara*: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, eunuchs, women, Śūdras, and whoever else seeks that [knowledge]—for them, there are initiations (*dīkṣās*) which are not to be questioned;
one should deliberate upon them at the time of [attaining] knowledge. The Guru is said to be the root of knowledge."
One should employ the seventh mantra.
Adorned with ornaments of mudrās, having established the five mudrās upon his crown, ears, and forearms;
his limbs smeared with fragrant perfumes, he was serene, well-cultivated, and thoroughly purified.
Having taken betel leaf, [one should be] adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and armlets by means of this mantra: (Oṃ juṃ saḥ, O Amṛteśvarabhairava, protect me, protect me! Saḥ juṃ oṃ).
Anointed with sandalwood and agallochum, his body previously adorned with necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and other ornaments,
his form marked by the eighteen great Bhairava mudrās—
(having thus positioned himself on his knees before the southern image, he should offer this petition):

[He] should do so. "O Blessed One, previously at the time of my initiation, you yourself, through the authority of the Guru, gave me this injunction: 'You must always favor disciples who are empowered by my own power. Therefore, these [disciples] are indeed of such a nature; thus [I have acted]."
Having been examined as they truly are, these [beings] do not require any other means of my favor;
rather, they are established as objects of grace through compassion alone.
The Blessed One alone, by virtue of his omniscience, knows this. Therefore, this is my special manifestation of power.

"May the Blessed One act; by becoming a single agent with you, I shall accomplish the favor for these beings. For without your empowerment, even Ananta and the other Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) are unable to liberate them, as they have been obstructed since beginningless time by the power of the fetters."
Having made this request, one should contemplate the command of the Lord, which is its superior state, thinking: "I shall do thus; I shall carry out what has been prescribed.
Then, having touched the ground with both knees, [one should address] the one who has gone to the ground and is standing near oneself.
Having taken the disciple’s hand and performed worship according to the mental rite (*mānasavidhi*), he should make this petition to the venerable Śambhu and obtain his command:
"Oṃ, O Śambhu, I have already been appointed by you as the Guru in the supreme and intermediate rites of Śiva."
Remaining [here], become one who acts for the benefit of the world.
O Blessed One, since my heart has been touched by your power, I have seen him today;
I have set out for the sake of bestowing grace upon him, not out of greed.
And you alone, O Blessed One, are the authority here for all actions; you are the witness, the self-acting agent, the supreme Śaṅkara, Śiva.
Therefore, by presiding over me with your special presence, grant that I may become equal to your feet.
Keeping your command in my heart, I perform all activities;
for who, O Lord, could possibly act otherwise, even the Lords of Knowledge?
"Whatever action I perform, I shall announce it to the All-pervading Lord"—
having thus instructed each [disciple], he should recite this for each one individually.
(In the *Pūrvaśāstra*: "Then, having bound on a white turban, [the mantra] consisting of nine *ātman*s, recited seven times: *oṃ ra harakṣamalavayarūṃ*.
In the place of the word 'this one' (*tadayam*), the name of the disciple should be recited as 'this such-and-such one' (*ayam amuka*"). Thus.)
Having received the command of Śambhu: "Oṃ harakṣamalavayarūṃ, homage to Vidyārājabhairava.
Thus, one whose turban has been consecrated by seven recitations of the mantra of Vidyārājabhairava.

"Relying on meditative cultivation, I am Śiva; this state of being is to be embraced. 'I shall attain the supreme state'—thus the mind is gladdened. In the sacrificial hall, within the sacred space known as the altar of the pitcher, there is the divine image, the form of the Lord in its entirety, like crystal. In the absence of that [image], the following procedure is prescribed:"
Or, having placed me upon a noble throne, one should begin the worship:
"Oṃ! I bow to the Great Lord (Maheśa), who has extinguished the mass of discordant afflictions by the light of his own self;
I praise that Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā), who indeed brings forth from her very root the creeper of speech."

I bow to the Great-Bellied One (Gaṇeśa), whose vast belly seems as if for the continuous devouring of obstacles; and I take refuge in another supreme Guru, the sole one who has received prior initiation and bestows knowledge.
Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, I offer this sacred thread; obeisance!
Oṃ, obeisance to the ocean of Bhairava, the repository of worldly existence, who sports with the waves of the world through the surging billows of his emanating power.
Oṃ! May the fierce roar of the five-faced Svacchandabhairava, whose majestic splendor is formidable, protect you—his "huṃ" sound that strikes down the rutting elephant of delusion.

We praise Svacchandabhairava, whose form is the sole form of the universe, who is the soul of the universe, the cause of the creation and other processes of the universe, and whose body is supreme self-luminosity.
I salute Svacchandabhairava, who transcends the universe yet consists of the universe, who is joined with the eight Bhairavas, who is both with parts and without parts, and who is the peaceful one.
Victorious is this single pearl-oyster shell, the power of the ocean of awakening,
within which this entire world shines forth as consisting of nothing but pearls.
Having completely shaken off all stains of ignorance through mere mindfulness, the vast and supreme holy waters of the Guru triumph throughout the three worlds. (Sc. 4, p. 3)
Oṃ! I bow to the Supreme Lord, the independent leader of heroes, who transcends the causes such as Brahmā and others, and who is overflowing with the bliss of his own power.
Oṃ! To the god who has fifteen eyes, adorned with a crown of matted locks, resembling ten million moons, and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
He has five faces and wide eyes, adorned with serpents and a bull-nose, and he shines with a necklace of scorpions resembling fire.
The god is adorned with a garland of skulls, bearing a sword and a shield,
holding a noose and a goad, and carrying an arrow and the Pināka bow in his hands.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, bearing a shaven head and a khaṭvāṅga staff,
holding a lute and a ḍamaru drum, and possessing a bell and a trident.
He displays the majesty of the Vajra-staff and holds an axe as a weapon in his hand, resplendent with a variegated mallet held aloft.
Clad in a lion’s skin with an elephant hide as an upper garment, the god has eighteen arms and is the cause of all causes.
O Maheśānī, one should contemplate the upper face as having the luster of crystal;
the eastern face, however, is yellowish and possesses the radiance of a blue lotus petal.
One should recognize the right [side] and likewise contemplate the left as resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree and like water mixed with saffron.
One should contemplate the western [face] as resembling the moon and Mercury—
the god Svacchandabhairava, who bestows the fruits of all desires.
A man who meditates with a disciplined mind indeed attains success quickly; she whom I previously described is the supreme power Aghorā.
Indeed, her form is exactly like that of Bhairava;
having worshipped Bhairava, one should meditate on her as seated upon his lap.
One should always meditate upon Bhairavī, whose face is slightly terrifying, whose voice is deep and vast, whose countenance is serene, and who causes a moment of wonder.
We know the one of manifold forms; we meditate upon the one with eyes like a cave;
may that Aghora inspire us. 3. We know the one of manifold forms;
we meditate upon the Sovereign Lady Aghora; may that Rudra inspire us. 3. Then:

"Salutation to the seat of the Self. Having thus worshipped the seat, one should prepare a weapon-vessel (*astrapātra*) on one’s right with the *astra-mantra* recited seven times; with that, all materials are to be sprinkled. As follows:

Āṃ dhūmra 2 jīva 2 saḥ; may the life-force of all varieties of flowers enter [this], svāhā! Thus for the flowers. Oṃ gandhamādini, may the fragrance cause [the deity] to live, svāhā! For the sandalwood. Hrīṃ.
Svāhā! To the saffron: *Lāṃ*, obeisance to the Earth, the Supporter, the Power (*śakti*). To the water for respectful offering (*arghya*): *Vlīṃ*, obeisance to Varuṇa, the King. To the water:
*Oṃ*, obeisance to Kālāgnirudra, who is the smoke of the world, the fragrance, and the bearer of all scents.
Homage to Dhūpa; [offering] to Dhūpa.
Homage to Dīpa, whose form is the light of the universe and whose nature is self-luminous; [offering] to Dīpa.
Then follows the worship of the Mothers of the Directions. He states the meditation:
The Sudhākalaśas, holding beautiful garlands of excellent flowers in their hands and being most resplendent,
as well as the Ākāśamātṛs with single faces, stood facing the Lord.

Oṃ, obeisance to Umā—in the east. Oṃ, obeisance to Durgā—in the southeast. Oṃ, obeisance to Bhadrakālī; Oṃ, obeisance to Svastī; Oṃ, obeisance to Svāhā; Oṃ, obeisance to Śubhaṅkarī; Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī; Oṃ, obeisance to Gaupī; Oṃ, obeisance to Lokadhātrī; Oṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī—thus [it is said].
One should worship the ten directions, starting from the east and proceeding in a clockwise sequence.
(Now, for the four corners, the lords of the gates: Oṃ Gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati.
I bow to Gaṇeśa, who holds two lotuses, a tusk, a bowl of sweets, and a battle-axe, and who is saluted by all the gods.
Oṃ glūṃ gāṃ, homage to Gaṇapati.

Oṃ! [I bow to her] who stands at the gateway, the destroyer of all obstacles, the fulfiller of desires, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness, and who bestows the path of Śiva; she who rests upon a lotus, holds a lotus in her hand, is worshipped by the abode of the lotus and others, is worthy of worship by the lotus, and is united with Viṣṇu.
To the bestower of wealth and grain:
Om, salutation to Dvāraśrī (the Goddess of the Door).
I bow to the goddess Sarasvatī, who has three eyes, is brilliantly white, holds a lute and a book, is the mother of the three worlds, and possesses an excellent form.
Oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī in the east.
"Oṃ! Having meditated upon him who has the luster of the sun at the end of time and wears a crown of matted locks—
[placing] Nandin on the right branch and Mahākāla on the left— and likewise, O Sage, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā below the threshold," so it is stated in the Guru-pustikā.
I bow to Nandirudra, who has three eyes and four arms, whose forehead bears a trident, an axe, and a mace, and who wields a thunderbolt in his hand.
Oṃ, homage to Nandin.

Gaṅgā, who rides upon a crocodile, is white in color; she holds a lotus with its stalk in one hand and carries a water-pot in her other two hands, while her remaining hand is in the gesture of granting boons.
Oṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā on one's own right [side].
Oṃ! Mahākāla, four-armed, with a distorted face and terrifying, dark-brown in color, adorned with a trident, a khaṭvāṅga, a staff, and other implements.
Oṃ, homage to Mahākāla; on the left.
Holding a water-pot with both hands, the younger sister of Yama is dark-complexioned, carries a makara as her vehicle, and holds a lotus in her hand while granting boons.
Oṃ, obeisance to Yamunā;
on the left. Oṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa; Oṃ, obeisance to Pracaṇḍa; likewise on the right and left.
Oṃ, obeisance to Diṇḍin; Oṃ, obeisance to Mahodara; likewise on the right and left.
Oṃ, I bow to the guardian of the west, who is mounted upon a lion, possesses a dark-complexioned body, holds a sword and a shield,
and stands beneath the threshold.
Oṃ, obeisance to the threshold;
below. Oṃ, obeisance to the ūrdhvoḍumbara pillar.
Oṃ! To the one accompanied by Nandin and others, whose form is worshipped by the best of gods, who assumes the form of Bhṛṅgin, the three-eyed lord of the Bhṛṅgis, the beloved of the gods.
Oṃ, homage to Bhṛṅgīśa.
Oṃ: White, three-eyed, a bull, radiant, and likewise bearing a trident; he should be meditated upon as the destroyer of sins, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Oṃ, homage to the bull. Oṃ, homage to the trident.

Oṃ! [I worship] the Sovereign Goddess of the Gods, whose feet are worthy of worship, who is honored throughout the land, who brings benefit to all, and who nourishes both the perfected ones and the practitioners.
Oṃ, homage to Ambikā.

Right here, O Youth, is the worship of Kumāra. "May Kumāra grant us that [protection] for which he is the lord of the hosts; may Kumāra protect us. [He who is] adorned with the majesty of the crescent moon, whose vehicle is the peacock, and who has six faces.
And the wise one should contemplate the youth Bhālaveśa.
Oṃ klūṃ kāṃ, homage to Kumāra. Kāṃ is for the limbs.
Oṃ, one should contemplate him as having one face and four arms, the destroyer of all obstacles, blazing with a circle of light, radiant and brilliant.
Oṃ, homage to Prabhāmaṇḍala.
In that very place is the worship of Sūrya:
*tatpuruṣāya vidmahe*, *sūryajñānāya dhīmahi*, *tannaḥ sūryaḥ pracodayāt*.
[He is] mounted upon a white lotus, with the luster of a pomegranate flower.
It is adorned with a circular mandala of shimmering, great red splendor.
One should meditate upon the Sun-god as having one face and two arms, wearing red garments, with his two hands holding a lotus with its stalk clearly white and resting upon his shoulders.
May the Sun-god, who sits in the bound lotus posture, who is compassionate toward those who have sought refuge,
who possesses seven horses and seven reins, and who has two arms, protect us.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Sūrya. Oṃ aṃ, to the heart. Oṃ arkāya, to the head. Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ, to Jvālinī, the crest-lock. Oṃ huṃ, to the armor. Oṃ bhāṃ, to the eyes. Oṃ raḥ, to the weapon.

Oṃ rāṃ, salutation to Visphurā. Oṃ rāṃ, [salutation] to the limbs. Then, one should place flowers upon the Maṇḍala of the Mothers in front of the Deity: Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Oṃ, Vāstupuruṣa is white, three-eyed, with a gentle face, and two-armed.
One should visualize the destroyer of obstacles as holding a rosary and a trident: *Oṃ vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ*.

Then one should worship the gentle messenger (dūtī), who has four arms, whose own voice resounds with the sound of mantra, and who holds a rosary, a book, a garland, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. [The mantra is: *oṃ hūṃ śuddhavidyāyai mantramātre dūtyai namaḥ*.
Through the contemplation of the self as being composed of the universe—thus is the Śāmbhava pervasion;
one should worship the messenger (Dūtī) with: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śivādūtyai namaḥ*. [This is] by virtue of the self’s transcendence of the universe.

"May this most excellent arrival for the sake of favoring us be a welcome!"—with these words, one should sound the *śāktavyāpti* bell. "Welcome, O Blessed One, together with your retinue"—with these words, one performs the rite of facing [the deity]. By the application of *huṃ* and *phaṭ*:
Having cast a flower into the center of the sacrificial ground:
"May those spirits depart who are stationed throughout the elements;
may those spirits who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva."
By joining the middle finger and the thumb with the *nārāca* mudrā,

and immediately after the application of flowers, having warded off the obstacles of the divine, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms by striking with the *koṭikā* sticks, clapping the hands, and three blows with the heel; [with the *koṭikā* sticks].

One should perform the binding of the ten directions. Immediately thereafter, having entered, [one should say]: "Whatever spirits dwell here upon the surface of the earth, having accepted this offering presented according to the ritual rules..."

"May they arrange their residence elsewhere and may they forgive us; salutations to them! Having recited this and performed the ritual expulsion of obstructing spirits (*apasarpaṇa*), one should worship Rudra along with Śakti in the northern direction using his mantra.
Oṃ! He whose wings are like a checkerboard, whose root-kings are marked by vajras, and whose wing-ridge is of gold;
he who possesses golden limbs, who wears rubies, whose lotus-face shines with the sound "cuñcupaṭa," and whose eyes shine with the splendor of the sun, wind, and moon.
With ruby-like lotuses blooming from his three eyes, with all the pores of his body radiant with sapphires,
and with his head resplendent with a crest of white conch-shells.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the locust, the king of Śālva, the sovereign of birds;
destroy, destroy my enemies! Hāṃ ghaḥ ghaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! I worship the venerable sandals of the glorious locust.
To her left: Oṃ namo bhagavati śalabhiśālvi mama śatrun nāśaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. I worship the sandals of the goddess Śrīśalabhī; obeisance!
Thus, having worshipped the pair of locusts.
7) One should worship the weapon of vision (darśanāstra) in the eastern [direction]. As follows:
*Oṃ*, [you who] possess the brilliance of the sun at the end of the aeon, filling the entire three worlds with your splendor...
With blood-red eyes and tawny hair, inspiring fear in the enemy host with his terrifying fangs and loud laughter, he indeed bears a discus, a conch, a mace,
a massive club, a bow, a noose, and a goad.
One should meditate upon the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) in the mind, enriched with arms and bearing the discus as his emblem.
Oṃ sahasrāra hūṃ phaṭ | Homage to Sudarśana! Having thus performed the worship.
One should worship the Aghora-weapon in the southern direction:
Oṃ, [I worship] Aghora, who resembles a water-laden cloud, who has terrifying fangs and three eyes, who holds serpents, and whose garments and body-unguents are red.
I meditate upon him bearing a drum, a damaru, a sword, a shield, an arrow, a noose, a trident, and a human skull.
Oṃ hrīṃ prasphura 2 sphura 2 ghora ghoratara tanurūpa caṭa 2 pracaṭa 2 kaha 2 vama 2 bandha 2 ghātaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ | Aghorāstrāya namaḥ. Having thus worshipped [it].
In the west, one should worship Vanadurgā with the mantra:

"Oṃ! She who dwells in the center of a golden lotus, who has three eyes, who resembles a flash of lightning, who holds a conch, a discus, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and who bears a digit of the moon."

One should meditate upon the moon-faced goddess dwelling on the Vindhya mountains, who wears necklaces, armlets, strings of pearls, and earrings; who is praised by Indra and the other gods; and who has a lion standing at her side.
"Arise, O Great Lady! Why do you sleep? A great danger has come upon me!"
"Whether it is possible or impossible, O Blessed One, pacify that for me, svāhā! Having thus worshipped, one should worship the Pāśupata weapon in the intermediate directions:
"Oṃ, [I worship him] who has a splendor equal to the midday sun, who bears the moon, and who blazes with a terrifying, loud laugh."

I worship Paśupati, the omnipresent Lord who has the form of a divine weapon; he is three-eyed, adorned with serpents, with a moon upon his crest and a beard like a crescent moon, with shimmering locks of hair, holding in his lotus-like hands a trident, a mallet, a sword, and a spear, possessing four faces and terrifying fangs.
Oṃ ślīṃ paśu hūṃ phaṭ | Pāśupatāstrāya hūṃ phaṭ | Having thus worshipped.

One should worship Gaṇapati in the center. The meditation is: "Oṃ, bearing [the tusk] in his right hand... Then, having worshipped thus with: "Oṃ glūṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," [one should proceed]. (Then...)
One should cast the weapon-mantras in the ten directions for the sake of protection, in order to destroy any opening for obstacles to enter.
Immediately thereafter, having entered, [one should visualize] the vajra, śakti, daṇḍa, khaḍga, pāśa, dhvaja, and gadā.
Having visualized a protective enclosure in the form of weapons— a trident, a lotus, and a wheel— for the sake of all-encompassing protection.
Then, facing north—
(because this is appropriate for being face-to-face with the Aghora face, which burns away all distinctions)—
he sits with a gentle countenance, facing the Aghora face because of his capacity to burn away sin.
Oṃ indrāya vajrahastāya phaṭ | agnaye śa | yamāya daṇḍa ha | nir-ṛtaye khaḍga | varuṇāya pāśa | vāyuve dhvaja ha | (Sc. 9, p. 8)
(He states the ritual assignment to the hands [karaṇyāsa].)
Having smeared the two hands with fragrance, one should purify them with the Astra-mantra;
having enveloped them with the Kavaca-mantra, one should then drench them with nectar.

Having thoroughly agitated the supreme power (*parā śakti*), one should purify the two [substances] smeared with the fragrance of *kulaka* and so forth, thereby causing them to attain the state of the power of action (*kriyāśaktitva*). Having agitated the supreme power— residing at the limit of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*) and having the form of the moonlight of the Śiva-moon— one [attains] Anaṅgadhenavī.

Having made [the deity] inclined toward expansion by means of reasoning (*yukti*), one should flood or sprinkle it with *amṛta*, the essence of supreme bliss. Afterwards, for the sake of protection against such a state [of dissolution], one should veil it with the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*). Then, one should fashion Ananta. [This is] the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*).

In the ritual procedure, the placement (nyāsa) of the respective mantras must indeed be performed accordingly. By that [method], one should contemplate Ananta as the seat, situated above the lotus of knowledge (vidyā-padma), located at the end of the knot at the tip of the forearm-staff, and ending with the word "preta."
One should fashion [the deity] with the *praṇava*, having already determined the reality [of its nature].

Having deposited (*nyasya*) the form, one should then fashion the faces according to one's own will (*svacchanda*). The form consists of the Brahma-door-panels and the digits (*kalā*); the deposition of the faces and so forth has already been determined previously. Therefore, where—

Wherever one goes, there the pervasion (vyāpti) determined in the first chapter should be contemplated; thus [it is] "at will" (svacchanda). Immediately thereafter, one should perform the placement of the five limbs (aṅganyāsa), beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger.
The teachers say that when both hands have assumed the lotus-mudrā, the weapon-mantra resides in the fingernails;
thereafter—
Having also visualized the Bhairavas while recollecting the Supreme Reality (paraṃ tattvam),

[one should worship] the eight Bhairavas, the Lords of the Skulls (kapāleśas), from the left index finger to the right index finger; and the Supreme Reality, Niṣkalanātha, together with his limbs (aṅgas) and his consort (devī), according to the sense of the context.
One should recollect [the mantra] upon the two extended thumbs and bestow it by way of its universal pervasiveness.

Although, because the hands are constituent parts of the *piṇḍa*, the placement (*nyāsa*) is effectively accomplished simply by the future placement of the *piṇḍa*, nevertheless, [this is done] for the sake of the two [factors]: the initial sprout for the engagement in all ritual actions.

O Blessed One, for the sake of recognizing the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) enjoined in all the scriptures prior to the placement of those two [hands] upon the body is indeed appropriate; however, the *śivahasta* (the hand of Śiva) is of a different nature altogether, being the subject of a specific injunction.
*Gadā* to Kuvīra; *triśūla* to Īśāna; *padma* to Brahmā;
*cakra* to Viṣṇu, *hastāya phaṭ*.
Having thus performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*).
Then, on the altar of the water-jars (kalaśa), the worship of the elements (bhūta-pūjā) is performed in the sequence starting from the east.
Oṃ lauṃ, salutation to Kṣira; rauṃ, to Agni; śauṃ, to the Sacrificer (Yajamāna); rvauṃ, to Sūrya; vauṃ, to Varuṇa; yauṃ, to Vāyu; sauṃ, to Soma; hauṃ, salutation to Ākāśa.

Then one should begin the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). Having smeared the two hands with fragrant substances and sprinkled them with the Weapon mantra (*astra*), [one says]: "Oṃ hūṃ, I veil [you], obeisance.
Thus, having veiled them with the Armor mantra (*kavaca*) and performed the purification of the hands with the Root mantra (*mūla*), [one consecrates them] with the Nectar mantra (*amṛta*).
One should cause [the disciple] to be bathed.

Having meditated on the Śakti as having arisen from the location of the bulb (kanda) and having contemplated her as having reached the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta), one should take the nectar from that place.

Starting from the heart, one should visualize [the breath] reaching the end of the twelve finger-breadths at the nose; having visualized it as having emerged through the nasal opening to the end of the twelve, one should bathe the hands. Immediately thereafter, for the purpose of concentration (dhāraṇā), one should form the lotus mudrā at the base of the thumbs. At the front [of the thumbs] is the Support Power (ādhāraśakti), and [therein] the lotus.
Above that, the Form (mūrti). [Regarding the Form: the placement of Brahmā, the skull-bowl, the digits (kalā), the mouth, and so forth.
Therein, one should meditate upon the thirty-two syllables. The five limbs from the thumb to the little finger, the weapon (astra) on the nails, and [the mantra] on the right index finger.

Beginning from the left index finger, one should assign the eight Bhairavas; beginning from the left index finger up to the right index finger, one should assign the eight Bhairavas. One should place the partless [mantra], along with its limbs and its goddesses, upon the two thumbs. This is the ritual assignment of the hands (*karanyāsa*).

Having formed the *liṅgamudrā* and supported the body with the *triśūlamudrā*: one should fill [the breath] through the right [nostril] (*apasavya*) and exhale through the left (*savya*). This is the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the path of the way to liberation. One should exhale through the left, via the path of the name "Dakṣiṇa" (the right).
One should perform exhalation (*recaka*). One should perform inhalation (*pūraka*) by filling [the breath] with the left hand while the right is turned away (*apasavya*).
When this is performed continuously, it effects the purification of the channels (*nāḍīs*), the central abode of the path to liberation, and brings about their pacification.
It comes to be.
Prāṇāyāma is traditionally said to be threefold: through exhaling (recaka), filling (pūraka), and retention (rodha).

Just as one brings under one's own control the movement of the breath that exists [outside] by means of a fan, so too are these three [types] common to the external; furthermore, there are three internal ones as well.
He said to them:
One should exhale by means of the internal [breath] and fill [the body] by means of the internal; having performed a steady *kumbhaka*, the three internal [breaths] should be practiced.
Exhalation by way of the middle path; filling at the *dvādaśānta*; and the unshakable retention (*kumbhaka*) in the heart—this means the effortless, tranquil *kumbhaka*.
Thus, they become things that must be turned away from as objects to be accomplished.
When the movement from the navel to the heart, and [the withdrawal] of the mind from the domain of the senses,
occurs, that which is known as the fourth prāṇāyāma is called "supraśānta" (perfectly tranquil).
The meaning is that immediately after the motionless *kumbhaka*, by means of the "gradual downward movement from the heart"— that is,

through the method of moving [the breath] slowly down from the heart— one should restrain the *prāṇa* at the navel itself; likewise, by means of the method of withdrawing the mind from the objects of the senses, one should [restrain it] at the navel itself.
For one who first restrains the mind and then controls it within the vital breath at the navel, the breath-control becomes perfectly tranquil.
When the vital breath (prāṇa), having been completely restrained, ascends to the crown of the head and returns, that is declared by the yogis to always be known as "the stroke" (satadghāta).

Through *prāṇāyāma*, the extraction (*apakarṣa*) consists of the purification of the gross body; through upward exhalation (*ūrdhvarecaka*), the extraction consists of the purification of the subtle body.
[This involves] drying, burning, floating, submerging, and purifying by means of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).
Having performed the *dhāraṇā* for the production of the divine body and so forth, one should perform the *nyāsa* to be described hereafter.
With the mantra "Laṃ, I perform exhalation; *namaḥ*," one should expel the purified vital air through the right nostril for a duration equal to twelve recitations of the *praṇava*.
One should exhale with: *oṃ vaṃ pūrakaṃ karomi namaḥ*. Thus, one should [expel] the pure white prāṇa-vāyu through the inner nostril for as long as it takes to utter twenty-four *praṇavas*.

One should cause [the breath] to enter: *oṃ raṃ, I perform the kumbhaka, obeisance*. One should restrain that very vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) within, in a state of immobility like a jar filled with water, for as long as it takes to recite thirty-six *praṇavas*. *yaṃ, I perform the upward exhalation (*ūrdhvarecaka*), obeisance*; thus, one should [perform] that very same [action].

Having retained [the breath] by piercing through the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) in succession— or otherwise, because it is not possible— she should slowly exhale it through the left nostril.
Thus is the upward exhalation (ūrdhvarecaka).

Oṃ haṃ, I establish the self whose nature is space; homage! [I contemplate] the self situated in the heart-lotus, subtle, resembling a firefly, with the form of a shimmering star, [proceeding] by way of piercing the heart, throat, palate, the center of the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā.

Having applied [the breath] to the *dvādaśānta*, having dissolved the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*), and having merged them into the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), one meditates on the body as empty; this is the purification of the subtle body. (Sc.
Then, one should perform the purification of the gross body through withering and other means by means of *dhāraṇās*.
Reciting "Kṣyūṃ, I wither this body; *namaḥ*," one should contemplate one's own body as having the form of a dried-up tree. This is the *pārthivī* [dhāraṇā].
"Nkṣryūṃ, I burn this body; obeisance.
Having thus meditated upon the fire of time (kālāgni) arising from the big toe of the right foot, one should contemplate the body—both external and internal—as being reduced to ashes by its flames.

"Thus, [with] *yūṃ*, I perform the immersion of the body; *namaḥ*. Thus, one should contemplate the bodily ashes as dispersed toward the ten directions by means of the wind. This is the Vāyavī [mantra].
"Vaṃ, I cause the body to be immersed; *namaḥ*. Thus, [one contemplates] the *cidbindu* (point of consciousness) fallen at the *dvādaśānta*.

One should contemplate that place as being washed by streams of flowing nectar; thus is the *vāruṇī* [purification]. Just as the poisonous nature of poison is warded off by the power of a mantra, so too is the "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) of the body [warded off]; it is not the destruction of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), nor is it the dissolution of its essential nature—this is the intended meaning.
Thus, when the body consisting of the six sheaths has ceased, one should contemplate the Self as consisting of supreme bliss:
"Oṃ haṃsaḥ! I am composed of consciousness; I do not exist, nor does anything else exist, and there is nothing here to be given."

"The mind is dissolved into the state of bliss and has attained a state of equilibrium. Thus [one becomes] ethereal (*ākāśī*). Then, from the *karma* [cakra] up to the heart, one should place the seat (*āsana-pakṣa*):
"Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti; salutation to the Ocean of Milk."

Homage to the lunar disc. Homage to the lotus posture. Just as [the breath] was led upward by the upward-clearing (ūrdhvarecaka), in that same manner, having led it upward by inhalation (pūraka) through the sequence of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the space between the eyebrows, the palate, and the throat, one should place oneself within the heart-lotus. Oṃ juṃ.

"I make this body immortal; obeisance. Having thus bathed [the deity] with streams of nectar flowing from the *cidbindu* at the *dvādaśānta*, it is restored to life. Then: "Oṃ, obeisance to the pure body, which consists of the thirty-one *tattvas* beginning with *māyā* and ending with *kṣiti*. Thus.

One should meditate upon the pure body that has arisen. Then: *oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; *oṃ vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ*; *oṃ haṃ mūrtaye namaḥ*. Having thus visualized the white form, [one recites]: *oṃ kṣaṃ īśānamūrdhne*.

Salutation! Oṃ yaṃ, salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ raṃ, salutation to the heart of Aghora. Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to the secret place of Vāmadeva. Oṃ laṃ, salutation to the secret place of Sadyojāta.
Thus is the "breaking of the staff" (daṇḍabhaṅgi) [applied to] the body.

The "breaking of the staff" (daṇḍabhaṅgi) is that ritual action consisting of the act of placement (nyāsa), performed by the practitioner in a sequential manner starting from the big toe up to the shoulder; it is known as the "breaking of the staff."
That which is performed by the practitioner through the form of the five faces known as the "Five Brahmans" is remembered as the *maṇḍabhaṅgi*.
Oṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to the face of Īśāna; at the northeast (īśa), yaṃ, to the face of Tatpuruṣa.

*Namaḥ*. *Raṃ*, obeisance to the face of Aghora; in the south. *Vaṃ*, obeisance to the secret [face] of Vāmadeva; in the north. *Laṃ*, obeisance to the face of Sadyojāta; in the west. Thus is the arrangement of the heads (*muṇḍabhaṅgi*). (*Bhaṅgi* means division.)
The division of the head-deposit (śirasinyāsa) is the arrangement of the tonsured head (*muṇḍabhaṅgi*). *Oṃ kṣaṃ* to Tārā and the others.
*Namaḥ* to the digits of Īśāna (*īśānakalābhyo namaḥ*) on the crown of the head (*mūrdhni*). *Yaṃ*.

Salutation to the Śānta-kalās beginning with *śāntā*, located in the mouth. Salutation to the Aghora-kalās beginning with *ram* and *tam*, located in the heart. Salutation to the Vāmadeva-kalās beginning with *vam* and *rajā*, located in the private parts. Salutation to the Sadyojāta-kalās beginning with *oṃ* and *lam* and *siddhi*, located in the feet.
"In every body.
Thus ends the abbreviated ritual placement of the *kalās*.
(The ritual placement of the *kalās* [is performed] through the pervasion of the thirty-six principles.)

Oṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to Sutāriṇī. On the upper door-panel: kṣaṃ, salutation to Tārayantī. On the east: kṣaṃ, salutation to Tāraṇī. On the south: kṣaṃ, salutation to Sutārā. On the northern door-panel: kṣaṃ, salutation to Tārā. On the west.

Thus, the five kalās of Īśāna: *yaṃ* to Śāntā, salutation, at the tip of the nose on the eastern face; *yaṃ* to Vidyā, salutation, on the right; *yaṃ* to Pratiṣṭhā, salutation, on the left; *yaṃ* to Nivṛtti, salutation, behind. Thus, the four kalās of Tatpuruṣa: *oṃ raṃ*.

*Umāyai namaḥ*—at the heart. *Raṃ mohāyai namaḥ*—on the neck. *Raṃ kṣudhāyai namaḥ*—on the right shoulder. *Raṃ nidrāyai namaḥ*—on the left shoulder. *Raṃ mṛtyave namaḥ*—at the navel. *Raṃ māyāyai namaḥ*—on the back.
*Raṃ*, salutation to Bhayā; at the belly. *Raṃ*, salutation to Jarā; at the chest. The Aghora-kalās:
*Oṃ vaṃ*, salutation to Rajā; at the secret place. *Vaṃ*, salutation to Rakṣā; at the anus. *Vaṃ*.
*Ratye namaḥ* on the right thigh; *Vaṃ pālyai namaḥ* on the left thigh; *Vaṃ kāmyāyai namaḥ* on the right knee; *Vaṃ kṛṣṇāyai namaḥ* on the left knee;
*Vaṃ mataye namaḥ* on the right shank; *Vaṃ* [on the left shank].

*Oṃ* Kriyāyai *namaḥ*, on the left calf. *Vaṃ* Ṛddhikāyai *namaḥ*, on the right buttock. *Vaṃ* Rātryai *namaḥ*, on the left buttock. *Vaṃ* Bhrāmaṇyai *namaḥ*, on the waist. *Vaṃ* Mohinyai *namaḥ*, on the right side. *Vaṃ*...

Salutation to Manonmanī. On the left side: the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva. Laṃ, salutation to Siddhi; on the right foot: Laṃ, salutation to Ṛddhi; on the left foot: Laṃ, salutation to Dyuti; on the right hand: Laṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī; on the left hand: Laṃ.
*Medhāyai namaḥ* on the nose; *laṃ Kāntyai namaḥ* on the head; *laṃ Sudhāyai namaḥ* on the right arm; *laṃ Sthityai namaḥ* on the left arm. These are the eight *kalās* of Sadyojāta.
Thus concludes the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās.

(The deposition of the nine principles [navatattvanyāsa] is performed through the pervasion of the nine powers beginning with Vāmā, and through the pervasion of Svacchandabhairava and the lords of the skull [kapāleśa], etc.)

Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Śiva; at the head. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Sadāśiva; at the mouth. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Īśvara; at the throat. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Vidyā; at the heart. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Māyā; at the navel.

(Sc. 12, p. 11) Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Time (kālatattva); at the secret place. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Necessity (niyatitattva); on the thighs. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of the Person (puruṣatattva); on the knees. Oṃ, salutation to the principle of Primordial Matter (prakṛtitattva).
At the two feet.
Thus is the ninefold deposition of the principles (*tattva-navaka-nyāsa*).
(The deposition of the three principles [is performed] through the pervasion of the pure *ātman*, *unmanā*, and the supreme principle.)
Oṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva; at the head. Oṃ, salutation to the Sadāśiva-tattva;

at the throat. Oṃ, salutation to the Ātma-tattva; at the heart. Thus is the placement of the three principles (tattva-nyāsa). Having placed Oṃ Svacchandabhairava at the head, [one places] Oṃ Kṣmaryūṃ Kapāleśa at the skull.
Salutation to Bhairava. [At] the face: Oṃ hrūṃ, salutation to Śikhivāhana-Bhairava.
[At] the throat: Oṃ kṣūṃ, salutation to Krodharāja-Bhairava. [At] the heart: Oṃ radhrū-auṃ, salutation to Vikarāla-Bhairava. [At] the navel: Oṃ hvū-auṃ.

Salutation to Manmathabhairava; at the secret place. Oṃ hryūṃ, salutation to Meghanādabhairava; at the thighs. Oṃ huṃ, salutation to Somarājabhairava; at the knees. Oṃ hrkṣmalvyūṃ, salutation to Vidyārājabhairava; at the feet.
Thus ends the Bhairavāṣṭaka-nyāsa.
Oṃ kṣīṃ, salutation to Kriyāśakti; on the right side. Oṃ sūṃ, salutation to Jñānaśakti; on the left side. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Icchāśakti.
In the middle: *Oṃ rkṣraḥ kṣurikāyai namaḥ*. On the hip: *Oṃ aghorebhyaḥ sarvātmane hṛdayāya namaḥ*.
(Now, how can there be non-duality when this [self] exists as a subject characterized by *māyā*, given that [duality] is its inherent concomitant?)

Anticipating the objection that [the practitioner] might become identical with Śiva, he says: "Māyā is the subject; through proficiency in the practice of conceptualizing its form, one becomes Śiva himself. That fruit of such practice is proclaimed as the ritual of nyāsa and so forth."

Oṃ tha ghorebhyaḥ brahmaśirase | Oṃ ghoraghoratarebhyaśca jvālinyai śikhā | Oṃ sarvataḥ śarva-sarvebhyaḥ | Piṅgalāya kavaca | Oṃ juṃ saḥ jyotīrūpāya netrebhyaḥ | Oṃ namaste rudra-rūpebhyo durbhedyāya ||

"Phaṭ! To the Pāśupata weapon! Having thus performed the six-limbed *karanyāsa* and *dehanyāsa*, one should touch [the body] with the root mantra from the head down to the soles of the feet, pervading it entirely.
And one should touch it with: "Oṃ hūṃ, to those who are not terrible, and to those who are terrible..."

And from those who are most terrible and even more terrible than the terrible; from all, O Śarva, from all [beings]; salutation to you in your forms as Rudra, *hūṃ*, salutation! This is the root-vidyā of the entire Bhaṭṭāraka. *Oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ Aghoreśvari hūṃ phaṭ*. *Oṃ hāṃ*—thus for the limbs. *Oṃ hūṃ*.
Salutation to Niṣkala Svacchanda Bhairava. The faces and limbs [are worshipped] as with the Śrīdevī.
Having thus performed the sakalanyāsa and the niṣkalanyāsa, one should place Aghoreśvarī on the forehead and [prepare] the vessel for the mental sacrifice (manoyāgārghapātra).

One should perform the ritual action with the contemplation of the identity of the Lord (*īśvarāhaṃbhāvanā*), ending with self-worship. It is as follows: the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*): the heart on the two thumbs; the head on the two index fingers;
the crest-lock (*śikhā*) on the two middle fingers; the armor (*kavaca*) on the two ring fingers; the eyes on the two little fingers; and the weapon (*astra*).
[The placement] on the nails. Now, the placement upon the body: one should place the heart in the region of the heart and the head upon the head. (Sc.
One should place the *śikhā* mantra upon the crest, the *kavaca* upon the two shoulders, the *netra* upon the two eyes,
and the *astra* throughout the entire body.
Thus ends the ritual placement on the body (*deha-nyāsa*).
At the occasion of the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*), the binding of the six mudrās should be performed; so say the teachers.
Among these, the fist with the thumbs tucked inside is for the heart, while that same fist with the thumbs raised is for the head.

With the index fingers raised at the crest [of the head] is the *śikhā* [mudrā]; with the two hands joined such that the fingers are interlaced is the *kavaca* [mudrā]; touching the three eyes with the middle, index, and ring fingers is for the *netra*;
and the snapping of the thumb and index fingers is for the *astra*.
"The teachers say that one should form the lotus mudrā with the hands, having the form of a reflection in the heart."

[This is] the intention of one's own essential nature, which expands the entire universe without exception. Then, having formed the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*), one should place Svacchandabhairava on the right thumb and Bhairavī on the left, [and then touch] with the right index finger.
Ending with the left index finger, one should install the eight Bhairavas. First, one should perform the installation of the seat:
*Oṃ*, salutation to Ādhāraśakti at the root (kanda); salutation to Dhātrī up to the navel.
"Salutation to the Ocean of Milk at the navel; salutation to the root; salutation to the stalk up to the heart;
having meditated upon the Yogapīṭha seat together with its feet consisting of Dharma and the other [virtues] in the heart."
Above that,
in the center, one should meditate upon a lotus seat with eight petals, complete with filaments and a pericarp.
Homage to the petals! Homage to the solar disc! One should meditate on the white petals. Homage to Brahmā, the lord presiding over them! One should meditate on Brahmā as four-faced.

Salutation to the filaments (*kesara*). Salutation to the lunar mandala (*somamaṇḍala*). One should meditate on the filaments as white and yellow. Salutation to Viṣṇu, the presiding deity thereof. One should meditate on Viṣṇu as dark-complexioned.
Salutation to the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Salutation to the fiery mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*). [The pericarp...]
One should meditate on [the deity] Suvarṇavarṇā. Homage to Rudra, the lord thereof. One should meditate on Rudra as white. Above that—
Salutation to Īśvara. One should meditate upon Īśvara as pale-red. Above that, [one should offer]:
"Oṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva, who has the great corpse as his seat. Above that, one should meditate upon the Blessed Lord, Bhairava. (The eight Kapāleśas...)
On the eight petals, as follows: Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Kapāleśa Bhairava;
(on the right forefinger) Oṃ raṃ, [obeisance to] Śikhivāhana Bhairava; Oṃ kṣaṃ, [obeisance to] Krodharāja Bhairava; Oṃ saṃ, [obeisance to] Vikarāla Bhairava; Oṃ laṃ...
To Manmathabhairava; Oṃ Vaṃ to Meghanādabhairava; Oṃ Yaṃ to Somarājabhairava; Oṃ Ūṃ, salutations to Vidyārājabhairava. (On the left index finger: Salutations to Aghoreśvarī. Then one should meditate.
In his left hands, he holds a shield, a noose, a bow, a boon-granting gesture, and an excellent staff, as well as a lute and a small drum;
in his right hands, he bears a banner, a mallet, an axe, a goad,
a sprout, a hand-drum, a vajra, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness, while his consort, who resembles him, rests upon his lap.
We bow to Svacchandanaatha, who resides in Kradra, whose face is like an arrow, and who is white as the moon.
Having meditated thus—[having meditated] with mental [offerings] on the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth as being non-different from one's own nature (as stated in *Sc.
(He states the conjunction of mantras:)

The weapons, the world-protectors, the eight Bhairavas, the five Brahmans, and the limbs— these are the coverings. One should project them all in sequence until reaching the central Īśvara within the womb.
For this is indeed the union of mantras.

"Salutation to Īśa, who holds a trident in his hand. Thus, the union of mantras is the pronunciation [of the syllables] in reverse order, ending with Sakala, according to the sequence of successive dissolution;
this applies both to the five Brahmans and the limbs (aṅgas) in reverse order as well as in direct order.
The recitation: because the faces and limbs constitute a single enclosure, there is a threefold enclosure according to the sequence.
Now, listen to the supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*).
Then one should recite that mantra for the deity, endowed with short, long, and protracted vowels;
one should recite the mantra for as long as the sphere of nirvāṇa remains within reach.
The Lord is that reality, the radiance and so forth, the partless Bhaṭṭāraka, beginning with "the short," and so on:

"the short, the long, the protracted, the subtle, the extremely subtle, the supreme Śiva. This is according to the state to be described in the section on the five *praṇavas*: [the syllables] *a*, *u*, and *m*.

The meaning is that one should recite the mantra while resting, according to the sequence of pervasion to be described, within the *bindu*, *nāda*, *varṇa*, and *kalā*— which consist of the short vowels and so forth— until reaching the *dvādaśānta*, the sphere of *nirvāṇa*. Herein, one should fulfill the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*).
From below the Śakti up to above, within the path of the Moon and Sun,

by means of the central channel (madhyamārga) of Piṅgalā and through the sequence of the utterance of the phonemes (varṇa), one should pierce, in due order, the five deities, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā, until indeed all [is reached].
Ending in the Nidhana, waveless, beyond the path, all-pervasive, and transmental (unmanā),

according to the sequence of the divine instruments (*divyakaraṇa*) to be described hereafter: "below" means having caused the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) to reach the heart from the *kanda* by way of the left, right, or middle channel, according to the directions previously determined.
By means of the path of the middle [channel] known as Piṅgalā, from the letter *ha* and the vowel *ā* up to the resonance (*nāda*),

according to the sequence of pronouncing the phonemes in their short and other forms, one reaches the five deities beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva; and above that, the extremely subtle mantra-parts.

The meaning is that, having dissolved the state of being a knot by means of the method of piercing from Śakti up to Unmanā, while performing the reflective awareness of the mantra which is the nature of supreme speech (parāvāk), one should recite the mantra until the end of the twelve [fingers], reaching the limit of death and bestowing total tranquility.

Of what nature is it "waveless"? It is that which has emerged from, or departed from, the waves—the surging manifestations of the names and sounds of phonemes, mantras, and so forth; likewise, it is the pervader of everything without exception.

He explains how such a single reality comes to be: "Unmanam" means that all mental activity (*manana*) and contracted perception have been transcended, and it abides as independent. Then, having presided over that—meaning, by means of firm support, that partless reality (*niṣkala-tattva*).
Having entered for a short time, one should settle [it] in the heart-lotus in the natural (anuloma) order.

Starting from the *dvādaśānta*, according to the perspective to be explained later— namely, that "the reality (*tattva*) and *unmanā* as well as *samanā*"— one descends through the sequence of the emanation of the objects of mantra (*mantraprameya-sṛṣṭi-krama*) and establishes the venerable Lord Sakala by way of his omnipresence within the heart-lotus.
One should meditate. And what [more]?

O Goddess, one should thus place that [mantra] as pervading all the *āvaraṇas* (enclosures). "Thus" means with a single effort. By that, all [the deities] are presided over and become bestowers of the fruits of all desires, because they consist of a mass of its rays; this is for the sake of the *sakala* and other mantras. Now...
This recalls what was previously stated regarding meditation and so forth:
"Just as their essential forms, configurations, and colors were described by me,
so should they be employed in the mind by means of the mind."

"Svarūpa" refers to the form consisting of the primary limbs of Brahmā and so forth; "saṃsthāna" means configuration, and "varṇa" refers to colors such as white and so on—this has been stated in the second chapter. "Mānase" means in the mental sacrifice;
that is, by means of the mental consciousness (*citta*). And therefore:
Having established Bhairava, who exists in two states, within the pericarp—
resembling pure crystal and adorned with all mantras.

In two ways, by way of being both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*); [this is] for the sake of bestowing grace upon those to be graced, through His abiding in His own sovereignty. That which possesses a form with parts is the manifest aspect, while that which is without parts is the reality of pure luminosity. "Adorned" means surrounded by rays, like a sun. Thus...

Although the root mantra is partless (*niṣkala*) with respect to its thirty-two syllables, it nevertheless possesses a state of being with parts (*sakala*) when the phonemes beginning with *a* are in motion. He points out that reality which is truly partless.
There too, all around, the object of knowledge is indefinable and free from affliction.

There, above those two— the differentiated and the undifferentiated— the supreme nature of Bhairava is to be known as manifesting by itself in its entirely perfect form, surrounding them on all sides.

The meaning is that it is the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñeya*), because it is indefinable, not being an object of "this-ness" (*idantā*), and because it is free from affliction (*anāmaya*). That is to say, it is devoid of even the subtlest affliction, namely the touch of the Great Māyā whose nature is non-apprehension (*akhyāti*). And thus:
Where there is no duality,
because it consists of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of all things— beginning with the venerable *niṣkala* and *sakala* states— there is no conceptualization of mantras and the like.
One should designate that as the dissolution of the *oṃkāra*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*.
The meaning is that one should know it to be the bestower of rest for all that is to be measured by mantras;

as he will say: "As long as it is uttered by speech, so long is it considered to be with parts (sakala). Likewise: "How can there be liberation in syllables? The supreme reality is beyond syllables. And therefore:
Knowing that place to be difficult to attain, one should never arise from it— that state wherein there is neither top nor bottom, nor east, west, north, or south.
It is neither sound nor even space; by meditating upon that, one is liberated.
It is called a "station" (*sthāna*) because everything abides within it. Because its form is empty, its nature is ungraspable as either root or tip.
Because it is empty of the nature of syllables and the form of mantra, it is not sound.
Although it has been stated thus, with the intention that even so it is not empty, it was said: "Having meditated on 'not space'...
By resting in the uncreated *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (I-consciousness), having thoroughly churned [the mind], one is liberated;
the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is attained.
The water for rinsing the mouth, the arghya offering, flowers, unguents, the sacred thread, necklaces, earrings, crowns, anklets, and other ornaments such as upper and lower garments;
flowers, garlands, betel, the tasting of the six flavors, mouth-fresheners, and the water for rinsing the mouth.

One should contemplate the deity as being satisfied by means of canopies, umbrellas, chowries, dance, song, recitation, meditative absorption, fire-offerings, and so forth. Having thus gratified [the deity], one should meditate on the fire in the region of the *kanda* (the root-center) as having a blazing and radiant form.

Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with the Aghora mantra ending in *svāhā* and using the liquid nectar fallen from the *dvādaśānta*, one should meditate on the Lord in the form of the full moon between the eyebrows; then, one should perform the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), the union of the mantras (*mantra-sandhāna*), and the process of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*). As follows:
Having uttered the Śrī Niṣkala mantra, one should expel the luminous channel from one’s own heart through the left [nostril],

draw out one’s own consciousness, and cause it to enter within the right channel of Bhairava; then, having exited again through his left channel, one should proceed in this very same manner with the Varaṇās.

Having entered within oneself through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*) by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) according to the sequence of entry and exit, one should join [the breath] in the very center; this is the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). Now follows the joining of the mantra (*mantra-sandhāna*).
The mantra is recited in its sequential order: "O Viṣṇu, [place] myself along with my discus (*sacakra*) upon Your discus (*śacakra*)."

One should contemplate Viṣṇu together with the lotus-bearing Brahmā; Brahmā together with the trident-weaponed Īśāna; and following that, Īśāna together with the mace-bearing Dhanada—homage! In this manner, one should likewise contemplate Viṣṇu together with his mace-weapon and Dhanada.
First the mental sacrifice, and afterwards that accompanied by material substances—
he who is a teacher devoted to sacrifice should perform this constantly.
Having worshipped properly in one's own hand, in the *sūṇḍila* liṅga, in the maṇḍala, in the *caru*, as well as in water and in fire, one obtains the fruit of perfect initiation (*samyaṅ-dīkṣā*).

The primacy of the mental [initiation] is because it has been stated that without the state of Śiva, there can be no eligibility for the non-Śiva sacrifice. "The instructor" refers to the teacher whose purpose is instruction; "constantly" means because of the reality of perpetual worship. "In his own hand" refers to the occasion of bestowing the Śiva-hand. Regarding the *sūṇḍila*:

Thus, at the time of the consecration (*adhivāsa*): regarding the term "liṅga," by the word *liṅga*, the wise refer to the consciousness of the disciple (*śiṣyacaitanya*) which is appropriate for the introduction [of the teaching] as the cause of creation and dissolution, according to the etymological explanation (*nirukta*);
or else, it refers to the external form such as a *bāṇa*-linga, used in a figurative sense; or to the mandala whose form will be described below.

In the *caruka* (the sacrificial offering), which is essentially a specific form of oblation; in the water contained within the ritual jar (*kalaśa*); and in the fire that burns away the fetters (*pāśa*)—one obtains therein the fruit of initiation for disciples: the recognition of one's own true nature as being of the essence of Bhairava. This is the cause [of that attainment].

It indeed attains the capacity for agency. And thus, having first performed the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga), which consists of the state of becoming Śiva in every respect, one should then perform the external sacrifice (bāhyayāga).
Otherwise: "If one should commence another sacrifice without having performed the mental sacrifice..."

But that [state] should be known as inauspicious; it is not ordained for liberation. "Inauspicious" means that because there is no transformation into Śiva (śivībhāva) during the performance of the mental sacrifice, such a bound soul (paśu) is not ordained for liberation—that is to say, he is not made fit for that purpose—because of this.

When the sacrifice of the self (ātmayāga) has been performed, the purification of the body arises. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "cohu" (indeed/furthermore). The word "eva" (only/just) is to be joined immediately after the word "jāyate" (is born/arises); thus, because immediately following that sacrifice, [purification] occurs for the body which consists of both external and internal aspects.

The meaning is that purity indeed arises from the immersion into the state of Śiva; therefore, this [immersion] must necessarily be performed. For when that is so, one should not designate that teacher as being presided over by Śiva at all.
Because he moves together with Śiva, he will be called the Ācārya; furthermore,

regarding what he has said concerning the "burning of the self" and the "mental [suffering]," the meaning of "self" (ātman) here is the body, which is the locus of the various forms of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Having understood this correctly, the teacher is remembered as Śiva, the destroyer of bonds (*pāśahā*).
Correct knowledge consists in the dissolution of the egoity (*ahantā*) regarding the body and so forth, and the immersion into the state of "I am Śiva" (*śivāhambhāva*);
he now describes the power of this sacrifice.
In whatever place one may reside, whoever performs this rite in such a manner— even a killer of a Brahmin shall be liberated, let alone one who is devoted to Śiva.

Even one who has committed a great sin (mahāpātaka), if impelled by the will of the Blessed One and intending this very injunction, should sacrifice to and worship the Illustrious Lord; he too shall be liberated. Furthermore:
Even one who has fallen into every possible state and is enamored by sense objects is liberated by worshipping [the deity] just once; how much more so for one who does so day after day?

By the words "present in all states" and so forth, [it is shown that] one is capable of maintaining the *samaya*. Even one who enjoys worldly pleasures is liberated by worship once through the seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*). Therefore, this vision must be constantly practiced by the spiritual sons (*putraka*) and others; such is the supreme [teaching].

In the presence of Vāyu with his banner, [place] A; [worship] Vāyu with his banner. In the presence of Varuṇa with his noose, [place] A; [worship] Varuṇa with his noose. In the presence of Nairṛti with his sword, [place] A; [worship] Nairṛti with his sword. In the presence of Yama with his staff, [place] A; [worship] Yama with his staff. In the presence of Vahni with his spear, [place] A; [worship] Vahni with his spear. [Worship] Vahni with his vajra.

To Indra, to Śakra with the thunderbolt; to the King of Knowledge, to the King of Knowledge; to the King of Soma, to the King of Soma; to Meghanāda, to Meghanāda; to Manmatha, to Manmatha; to Vikarāla, to Vikarāla;
to Krodharāja, to Krodharāja; to Śikhivāhana, to Śikhivāhana.
*Kapāleśa* [is dissolved] in *kapāleśa*; *kapāleśa* and the *astra* in the *astra*; the *astra* in the *netra*; the *netra* in the *kavaca*;
the *kavaca* in the *śikhā*; the *śikhā* in the head (*śiras*); the head in the heart (*hṛd*); the heart in *Aghoreśvarī*;
*Aghoreśvarī* in *Aghora*; *Aghora* in *Niṣkala*; and *Niṣkala* [is dissolved].

One should contemplate [the deity] merged within one's own self; this is the union of mantras (*mantrasandhāna*). Now follows the process of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*): having made the tongue touchless and keeping the body, head, and neck straight, one should fix the gaze on the tip of the nose; this is called the divine instrument (*divyakaraṇa*). Thus...
First, by means of the divine instrument (*divyakaraṇa*), having raised the power (*śakti*) from the root (*kanda*) and caused it to reach the heart,
having pierced the two currents (*pravāha*), and having taken hold of the abode of Suṣumṇā—
the denotator of the cause consisting of *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the *nirodhinī*, and the *nāda*.
In the phonemic energies (*varṇakalā*) ending with *unmanā*— namely, *nādānta*, *śakti*, *vyāpinī*, *samanā*, and *unmanā*— there is the short (*bra*),
the long (*vi*), the protracted (*plūta*), the subtle (*ī*), the ever-subtle (*sadāsūkṣma*), and the supreme Śiva.
(Also in the *Āloka*: "Having thus become Śiva, one should worship Śiva," etc.

With this perspective, he states that one should perform the external sacrifice after having contemplated the state of being Śiva within the self, beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). In this way, [one contemplates] one's own consciousness from the vital breath up to the stage of space (*vyoma*).

"Having become Śiva through the practice of worship, one should thereafter perform the external rite. [The word] "thus" refers to the sequence of the internal sacrifice. "Vyoma" means the void. Now, one might object: "If the sacrifice has been performed internally, why is there an external one? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In view of the primacy of the external sacrifice..."

For when accomplishments (*siddhi*) and the like are conceptualized for the sake of purifying the internal sacrifice, the one who worships otherwise is a bound soul (*paśu*). But he who, being indifferent to accomplishments and the like, worships the Lord externally, achieves his purpose through this very means by means of the firm establishment of the great internal sacrifice. Accomplishments and the like are the cause for [the external rite] being primary.

Regarding the term "parikalpite" (in the imagined): it refers to that which was stated [in the previous verse], namely that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth undergo a transformation (*saṃskriyā*) in one way; however, if one were to undertake another sacrifice without performing the mental sacrifice (*mānasa-yāga*), he should be known as inauspicious (*aśiva*), for such an act is not ordained for liberation (*mokṣa*).

By that very means—namely, through the internal Great Sacrifice (*antarmahāyāga*) consisting of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth—the state of Śiva is attained by the body. Since this occurs through the internal sacrifice for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the void (*śūnya*), what remains that must be accomplished by the external sacrifice? [Thus it is said] here.
For those desiring to ascend, internal mastery arises through the external sequence.
14) One who meditates upon the supreme state should first examine the substances.

Sustaining a state of vibrant manifestation consisting of the possession by Bhairava, which is perfected through the supreme internal sacrifice (*parāntaryāga*), one [performs] the consecration (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites for the sacrificial substances prior to their imagined purifications, because they have attained the nature of oneness through the realization of supreme non-duality.
One should perform the great purifications; he now indicates them.
White sandalwood, camphor, excellent incense, two white garments, flowers of divine fragrance, sesame, rice, ghee, and so forth.
Mango sprouts, darbha grass, white mustard seeds, as well as chalk, a ruler, scissors,
and a cord for binding with nooses.

The water-vessel, the auspicious jar, as well as these enclosing-sticks (paridhis), the sacrificial fuel, the tooth-stick, the vessel for the oblation (caru), the large ladle (sruva), and the small ladle (sruc).
Rice grains, as well as milk, and many other such things.

Since initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of the purification of the self by means of its attainment of the state of Śiva, and since this purification is the effect [of initiation], white qualities (*guṇa*) predominate according to that suitability. There are two white garments and mango sprouts for the sake of the water-pots (*kalaśa* and *vardhānī*), and rice for the sake of the scattered offerings (*vikira*).

The *siddhārtha* grains are for protection at the time of going to bed and so forth; the chalk and the water-vessel are for the sake of the mandala; the scissors are for cutting the cords of the noose;
the sacrificial ladle is for the sacrifice; and the fuel-sticks previously mentioned are twenty-four in number, each measuring one cubit (*hasta*).

For the sake of satisfying the fire once it has been established: there are four enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one cubit in length and with leaves on their branches, placed outside the pit in the cardinal directions to protect against the entry of obstacles; and there are sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) originating from sacrificial trees, complete with bark, free of holes, and auspicious.

Those which were described as being "the size of a span in thickness and larger than the little finger" are for the purpose of producing a flame in the fire. The tooth-stick is for the sake of the disciple.
The rice and the milk-oblation (caru) are for the sake of the deity and the preceptor. The rest is clear.

Having thus observed the substances— such as the powders for the purpose of the mandala, indicated by the word "and so forth," as well as the five products of the cow, the eye-blindfold, the cloth, and so on, which are for the sake of the disciples.
White sandalwood (1), camphor (2), excellent incense (3), white garments (4), flowers (5), sesame seeds (6), rice (7), ghee (8), mango sprouts (9), *darbha* grass (10), white mustard seeds (11),
a small bedstead (12), a *karaṇī* (13), scissors (14), a cord for a noose (15), and a water-pot (16).

17. The auspicious water-pot (śivakumbha), 18. sacrificial fuel (idhmā), 19. the enclosing sticks (paridhi), 20. the kindling woods (samidhaḥ), 21. the tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha), 22. the vessel for the oblation (carusthālī), 23. the small wooden ladle (sruva), 24. the large wooden offering-spoon (sruk), 25. rice grains (taṇḍula), 26. milk (kṣīra), 27. colored powders (rajāṃsi), 28. the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and 29. silk cloths (tatastrepaṭṭāni).
Then, taking the vessel of offerings (arghapātra), one should wash it with water consecrated by the Astra mantra; having veiled it with the Kavaca mantra, one should worship it with the Praṇava.
O lady of excellent countenance, fill it with the eight constituents beginning with water.
Water, milk, flowers, *kuśa* grass, mustard seeds, rice grains, and barley—

these eight are the *arghya* offering for the eight forms (*mūrtis*) of the Lord for the sake of the *puryaṣṭaka*. Then, O Dear One, having consecrated everything with the *praṇava*, one should subsequently install the form (*mūrti*).
One should worship her, joined with the Bhairava enclosures, according to the proper sequence.
With perfumes, flowers, and likewise incenses, preceded by the application of mantras.
One should install [the deity] together with Bhairava and the enclosures (āvaraṇas). One should worship [her], preceded by the unification of mantras (mantrasandhāna). Furthermore:
That supreme reality is to be contemplated; through that, one indeed becomes immortal.

The meaning is that by reciting the supreme reality (*paramaṃ tattvam*), which is partless (*niṣkalam*) according to the reasoning previously stated, one should render it immortal (*amṛtī kuryāt*) by displaying the nectar-gesture (*amṛtamudrā*). And this is for the sake of the *argha* vessel.

One should arrange a triad of vessels for the mantras: likewise, the vessel for the *vidhyargha* (offering for the rite) is for the purpose of worship, while the vessel for the *nirodhārgha* (offering for cessation) is to be employed on occasions such as the dismissal (*visarjana*) during the ritual of cessation. As for what was stated regarding that which should not be performed with wine:
Afterwards, the *argha* offering should be presented with fragrant wine.
(The animal-argha vessel is for the purpose of sprinkling the sacrificial animal and so forth.
Having entered into the short and other measures (*mātrās*), and having passed through [the levels] beginning with Śakti and ending with Paramaśiva;

Up to the limit of the *dvādaśānta*, preceded by the recitation of the venerable *niṣkala* mantra according to the method from the mouth of the Guru, one enters the waveless abode; from that point onward, there are the *unmanā*, *samanā*, *vyāpinī*, and *śakti* [states], as well as *nādānta*, *nādanirodha*, *ardhacandra*, *bindu*, *makāra*, and *ukāra*.

Having descended through the sequence of the letter *a*, one should contemplate the entire Bhaṭṭāraka as being established within the heart-lotus and pervading it; thus it is for all the enclosures—this is the process of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*).
Then, having entered the tip of the nose at the station of *tuṭi* together with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and exhalations (*apāna*),

and having risen while supporting the essence of light (*jyotīrasa*), one should gaze with eyes consisting of supreme light upon the entire collection [of offerings] in order to remove its illusory nature.

The observation through the perspective of the other; now, the state of the Other (parā). That which is unobstructed, authentic reality, eternally free from conceptual construction—that state is declared, O Goddess, to be the supreme limit, that ultimate attainment. Thus ends the state of the Other.
Then follows the worship of the vessel for the animal-offering (paśvargha) according to the ritual procedure for cessation.

Now, having sprinkled the three vessels—made of gold and so forth down to clay, or of mother-of-pearl and so forth—with water using a cloth, and having covered them with the *kavaca* mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to the three vessels. Thus.

Having worshipped with the *praṇava* (Om), one should veil [the vessels] with: "Oṃ hauṃ, I veil the three vessels; namaḥ. Having thus veiled them, one should place there, in sequence, the *vidhyargha*, *nirodhārgha*, and *paśvargha* vessels.

Having established [the vessel], first worship on one's own left with the root mantra using the five principles (tattvas) of Self, Knowledge, Śiva, Prakṛti, and Puruṣa. Therein, with the mantras of Kṣiti, Rudra, Dhātṛ, Keśava, Sāvitrī,
Soma, Pitṛ, and Vāc, [place] rice, mustard seeds, barley, flowers, kuśa grass, and water.

Having consecrated sesame seeds and milk with mantras, one should fill [the vessels] with them. One should perform worship with the *saṃhitā* [mantras] and, through various meditative visualizations (*bhāvanā*), offer incense for the sake of purification.
Here, the eightfold nature of the *argha* offering is established by virtue of the intention to present the eight [substances].
The mantras for those [substances] are as follows:

"Lāṃ, obeisance to the Earth, the sustainer of the world. [With this, one offers] rice grains. "Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, who has three matted locks and an upright tawny [tuft]. [With this, one offers] mustard seeds. "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the eldest of the gods. [With this, one offers] sesame seeds.
*Namaḥ*. Barley grains: *Oṃ namo viṣṇave surapataye mahābalāya namaḥ*. Flowers: *Jrīṃ sāvitri pāpabhakṣiṇi hūṃ phaṭ*. Darbha grass: *Svāṃ svāṃ somāya svāhā*. Water: *Oṃ tatsadoṃ pitṛbhyo namaḥ*.
Sesame seeds: *Oṃ hūṃ vāgīśvari vākprade sarasvatyai namaḥ*. Milk: *Oṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ*. Ghee: *Oṃ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ sarvottamadravyebhyo namaḥ*. All substances.
15) (In brief, that collection of substances intended for sacrifice is to be sprinkled by him;
the remainder [of the sentence] is "having looked upon it with the support of the supreme *kartī*"; here, the sprinkling [is performed] because of its nature as consisting of light.)
[The mantra] *pādanam* ||) one should cast these into the vessels; by that, there is the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of all the ritual substances.
In its vicinity, with the root mantra alone, one should perform the offering for the cessation [of obstacles] until the conclusion of the sacrifice to the All-pervasive Lord.
Near that, separately on one's own right, is the worship of the animal-offering vessel (*paśvarghapātra*):
*oṃ ślīṃ paśu hūṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya phaṭ*.
[This is] the worship of the animal-offering vessel for the sprinkling of the disciple. Near that—
The separate ritual for the Śivāmbu: *Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Śiva*.

Thus is the worship of the Śivāmbu vessel. Thus is the worship of the Paśvargha, the Śivāmbu, and the Astrāmbu according to the prescribed rule. Within those [waters], one performs the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the Mṛta-mudrā. [One should likewise perform it] upon one's own self...
Having worshipped the form of Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; then, for the "Hand of Śiva" (śivahasta):
having sprinkled the palm of the hand with the water of Śiva and veiled it, and having washed the hand with scented water by means of another hand, [the hand] is smeared with perfume.
One should worship the God along with his limbs (retinue), but excluding the seat.
Endowed with the five Brahmans, presided over by Śiva,
auspicious, the cutter of bonds, and gentle— this is proclaimed as the Hand of Śiva (Śivahasta).
Having washed both hands with scented water:
*oṃ somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ* on the left hand; *oṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ* on the right hand. Then, with the middle finger and thumb of that [right] hand, one takes the flower placed in the other hand.

Having fully worshipped the root-mantra together with the seat (*āsana*), the limbs (*aṅga*), and the face (*vaktra*), one should perform the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), the joining of the mantras (*mantra-sandhāna*), and the act of consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*). Regarding this, [the author] states for what purpose the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*) should be employed: in this worldly rite of initiation (*dīkṣā-karma*).

While [the rite] is being commenced by the teacher whose self is Śiva, with his hand not distinguished [from the disciple's], how is there an instrumentality? For even one who has been consecrated by the installation of the daily rites (*nityakarman*), there is a specific occasional rite (*naimittikakarman*) characterized by the superior destruction of bonds (*pāśakṣapaṇa*) and the bestowal of the state of Śiva-ness.

First of all, there must necessarily be the state of being the Hand of Śiva (śivahastatā), which is essentially the firm support of the potency of the agent (kartṛvīrya) consisting of Śiva, cultivated through meditation on the identity of one's own self with that [Śiva] via the placement (nyāsa) of the radiant wheel of mantras received from the Guru.
"It should be performed.
