(He states the primary method for the conjunction of mantras:)
Recalling the root mantra, one should pierce through the heart, throat, and palate, reaching the space between the eyebrows— the peak of sound— which is the station of the fourth state (turya).
One should pierce the equinox at the crown through the left, right, and middle channels; having led [the breath] to the supreme *dvādaśānta*, the mantra-form resides in the hand.

The word "to be investigated" (*anusandheya*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The supreme root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) is the peak of sound (*śabdakūṭa*), consisting of all expressive words, having the form of a mass of mantras that has internally assimilated the collection of mantras,
and being a peak corresponding to sound— whose eternal nature consists of the supreme *nāda*.

The Teacher, with the intention of explaining merely the binding of the instruments (karaṇabandha) that will be described according to the *Manusmṛti*, says: "One should pierce the fourfold station consisting of the heart, throat, palate, and the space between the eyebrows. To the question "How? he replies:
"Vāma," and so forth. By means of the central path (*madhyamārga*), following the sequence of practice up to the center of the eyebrows;

with the mind fixed on the center of the eyebrows, having pierced the knot of the *bindu* by means of the sharp needle of the central vital breath (*prāṇa*)—attained through the method of expansion—into the left nostril.
The meaning is that one shall pierce even the knots of *nāda* and so forth without effort; and this will come to pass.

Then, having led the mantra to the *dvādaśānta*, the mantra-form residing in the hand should be contemplated through the very attainment of purity. Just as the instrument possesses the essence of the agent’s vitality (*kartṛvīrya*).

The joining of the channels has been explained. By this same method, one should enter the heart in reverse order; one should enter the heart through the exhalation (recaka) of oneself, and certainly not through inhalation (pūraka).
This indeed is the "joining of the channels" (nāḍī-sandhāna) proclaimed by the venerable Śiva:

having gone from the self upward by means of the upward exhalation (ūrdhvarecaka), one should then enter again from the heart into the dvādaśānta by way of reverse order for that Blessed Lord who resides in the state of bliss (itika). Then, having caused [the breath] to surge forth...
"That [breath] reaches the dvādaśānta, but it does not enter into one's own heart by means of *pūraka*.

This is the "joining of the channels" (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). It is distinct from the previously described "joining of the channels" according to the sequence of the nose; this is its specific pervasion as proclaimed by the venerable Śiva.
This indicates that the teacher is to be accepted as authoritative. Thus, having entered one's own heart by means of the union of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna).
One should meditate upon Śiva as all-pervading, presiding over the embodied form of the mantra;
one should meditate upon the venerable Lord Niṣkalanātha, who remains presiding over the entire embodied form of the wheel of mantras, situated within, without, and in the Hand of Śiva.
One should meditate on the all-pervading [reality].

While reciting the mantra, one should pierce the *bindu* situated between the eyebrows via the central channel (*suṣumnā*) within the middle abode, and, preceded by the tearing asunder of all knots, [attain] the supreme abode.

Having entered the *dvādaśānta*, and then having descended again from the *dvādaśānta* by way of the space between the eyebrows, one takes up the collection of mantras held in the hand— appearing in a blazing and radiant form— through the passage of the left nostril, and with that very [collection], as follows:

Having reached the space between the eyebrows by way of the left nostril, and from the space between the eyebrows as well, having pierced the cranial aperture with the very tip of a needle, one should cause [the breath] to reach the *dvādaśānta*;
this is the "junction of the mantra. Again, having caused it to reach the space between the eyebrows from the *dvādaśānta*...

Having performed exhalation (*recaka*) through the path of the right nostril from the midpoint between the eyebrows, one enters the heart of the All-pervading Lord who exists in the form of the mantra held in the hand; having reached the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths) by way of the heart of that All-pervading Lord held in the hand, one then performs inhalation (*pūraka*).
One should cause it to enter one's own heart through the right nostril; this is the joining of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna).

Then, from one's own heart, one should meditate upon the radiant Niṣkala Bhaṭṭāraka— resembling a rainbow— extending everywhere from one's own heart to the *dvādaśānta* and to his heart, as far as the aperture of the crown (*karandhra*). This is the process of supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*).

Having thus visualized his hand filled with the multitude of blazing mantras, one should recite the root mantra and place the right hand upon the heart. Having given a flower from the left [hand] into the right hand, one should place it upon one's own head. This is the ritual for the radiant Śiva-hand (*bhāsvaraśivahastavidhi*).

16) Having thus fashioned the Hand of Śiva, that very same Śiva [is present] in the maṇḍala by virtue of being the causal agent, in the fire by virtue of his authority over the rite of initiation, and in the Hand of Śiva as well.
Because it is the cause of that; and because it resides in the jar as the destroyer of all obstacles;
and because it resides in the body of the disciple for the purpose of loosening his bonds; I myself am present here directly as the performer of the initiation; and as for its mantras—

The higher and lower [initiations] are the direct cause; they belong to me alone. And that which is to be performed by him—the bestowal of enjoyment and liberation upon those to be graced—belongs to me alone.
Having thus grasped the "I-ness" of Śiva (*śivāhaṃbhāva*), he should prepare the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Now...

The Ritual for the Five Products of the Cow (*pañcagavyavidhi*). Having demarcated a nine-square grid using lines made of clay from a *mariyādā* tree or a *śāli* tree, one should bring nine vessels—ranging from gold down to earthenware—or seven vessels. [One recites: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I purify the vessels, haḥ phaṭ! Thus.

Having consecrated the vessels seven times with the Knowledge-Sword mantra (*jñānakhaḍga*), and having sprinkled them with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), one should arrange the seat, saying: "Oṃ haiṃ, I envelop the vessels, huṃ; Oṃ, obeisance to Anantāsana. Then:
Beginning from the central square, one should worship in sequence starting from the east:

Oṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva (in the center); Oṃ, salutation to the Sadāśiva-tattva (P); Oṃ, salutation to the Īśvara-tattva (Ā); Oṃ, salutation to the Vidyā-tattva (Da); Oṃ, salutation to the Māyā-tattva (Nai). Oṃ...
Salutation to Kālatattva. West.
(He speaks in order to describe the consecration of the five products of the cow:
"Having taken a blade of *darbha* grass and empowered it seven times with the Astra-mantra, [one prepares] for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)."...)
One should, however, cleanse the vessel with the auspicious water of Śiva.

The cows are supremely pure, the embodiments of all the deities. O embodiment of the earth, the cow-dung from the banks of the foremost of rivers is nectar; that divine milk is its transformation, and the curd resides within it. That clarified butter is contained therein.

The essence is that which always satisfies the immortals; thus, one should collect the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) which possess the excellence described in the *Śrīmat Parākhya Saṃhitā*. One should purify—that is, wash—the *pañcagavya* with *kuśa* water. One should wash it with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), and that [water]...

One should veil [the disciple] with the Kavaca mantra. For him, one should prepare a seat of Darbha grass with the Dhruva mantra and fashion a mandala—either circular or in the shape of a Svastika. Upon that, one should place a vessel and bring cow-dung and other materials, keeping them each in separate vessels.
Having sprinkled [it] with the Weapon-mantra and auspicious water, then...
Having consecrated the cow dung with the Heart mantra, the cow urine with the Head,
the curd with the Crest, the milk with the Armor, and the clarified butter and *kuśa* water with the Weapon mantra;
One should then consecrate [the substances] with the *dhāman* mantra and subsequently add the cow-dung and other ingredients.
Likewise, into a previously prepared vessel, one should add them after consecrating them with their own respective mantras—
namely, the cow-dung and so forth— with those very same mantras by which they were individually consecrated in separate vessels.

Having joined them together, one should subsequently consecrate [the deity] with all those very [mantras], beginning with the Heart-mantra and so forth, simultaneously. Even though [the deity] has already been consecrated here, he states the placement of the mantras upon the seat (*āsana*) first for the sake of a specific consecration:
"Having conceived Ananta as the embodied form with the Praṇava, [one should place] the abodes and the limbs."
But externally, one should worship those situated in the enclosure.
Having performed the union of mantras as well as the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should then contemplate that [liquid] as the nectar of Śiva, worship it, and install it.
The form is the nature of consciousness; the body is the venerable Sakalabhaṭṭāraka;
the abode is the root mantra.
In the light.
One should consecrate cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk, and clarified butter with the six limbs beginning with the head; then one should sprinkle them with water from kusha grass and with food.
One should set aside the remainder of the ground for the sake of the disciples and place the five products of the cow there;
wherever these five products of the cow are present in this water, it is called *kuśāmbu*.
One should recite the mantras over each substance separately placed in its own vessel. Regarding the phrase "with those ending in the upward direction" (*ūrdhvāntaiḥ*):
by this, the sequence is as follows—cow’s urine with *sadyojāta*, and so on, up to clarified butter (*ājya*) with *īśāna*.
*Oṃ* to the principle of necessity (*niyati-tattva*). *Oṃ* to the principle of the person (*puruṣa-tattva*). *Oṃ* to the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*).
"In the Īśāna [corner]," thus, having placed the nine internal principles (*antastattva*) within the nine compartments of the lotus-diagram.
One should place [the mantras] in the center, east, south, west, and north:
Oṃ supratiṣṭhāya namaḥ in the center; Oṃ suśāntāya namaḥ in the east; Oṃ tejovatyai namaḥ in the south; Oṃ amṛtākhyāya namaḥ in the west; Oṃ śukrodayāya namaḥ in the north.

Thus, when the five vessels have been consecrated: in the directions of Varuṇa, Kuvīra, Indra, and Yama, and in the center, one should place cow dung, cow urine, ghee, curd, and milk, measured respectively at half-an-aṅguṣṭha, one, two, three, and four palas; or alternatively, cow dung and ghee.

Measuring half a thumb [in height], having set aside one *pala* for each [other direction], one should place a *pala* measure of *kuśa* water in the northeast direction. Then, [reciting] the Netra-mantra once, twice, thrice, four times, or five times, together with its limbs (*aṅga*), [one should offer] cow dung, cow urine, curd, and milk.
One should consecrate the clarified butter with mantras as follows:

(once) *oṃ hāṃ hṛda* [to the heart] over the cow dung in the southwest; (twice) *oṃ hīṃ śirase* [to the head] over the cow urine in the north; (thrice) *oṃ hūṃ śikhā* [to the crest-lock] over the curd in the east.

(Four times: Oṃ haiṃ, in the midst of the cow's milk. (Mantra five times: Oṃ haḥ, for the weapon, in the ghee on the right. Oṃ hauṃ, for the eyes, in the water of *kuśa* grass. In the northeast. Alternatively: Oṃ laṃ, obeisance to the face of Sadyojāta, in the cow dung. Oṃ vaṃ, [obeisance] to Vāmadeva...
In the *Somaśambhu*, regarding cow urine:
"Half an *aṅguṣṭha* of cow dung and one *pala* of cow urine; [the same for] curd."
Three palas of sugar and five palas of milk are prescribed.
The measure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is two palas of ghee each.
One should take the dung and urine of a black cow, the ghee from a blue cow,
the curd from a tawny cow, and the milk from a white or copper-colored cow.
In the absence of vessels for all the [other] castes, a single Kapila vessel is praised; it may be made of gold, silver, Palāśa wood, or auspicious copper.
This is known as the Śivakūrca, performed according to the ritual procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Kuśa grass: *hauṃ* (5 times); curd: *hnaṃ* (3 times); cow’s urine: *hīṃ* (2 times); milk: *haiṃ* (4 times); clarified butter: *haḥ* (6 times);
cow dung: *hāṃ* (1 time).

Then, one should place cow dung with the *hṛdaya* mantra in the south, cow urine with the *śiras* mantra in the north, curd with the *śikhā* mantra in the east, and milk in the center with the *varman* mantra.
Having sequentially merged the water with the Īśāna mantra in the northeast, the ghee with the Astra mantra in the south, and everything else with the Mūla mantra, one should worship Śiva.
In the venerable Parākhyasaṃhitā as well: "Cow dung, cow urine, clarified butter, curds, and milk as the fifth—
with Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Rūpin (Aghora), Puruṣa, and Īśāna..."
One should consecrate the cow dung and the other substances in their respective order.
One should [offer] water with kusa grass using the Gāyatrī mantra, or by means of the Niṣkala-dhāman, or the Saṃhitā, or the six ancillary mantras (aṅga-ṣaṭka).

17) (And here, the venerable teachers Viśvāvasu [state]: "Now, for the procedure of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should bring seven auspicious vessels according to availability, ranging from those made of clay up to precious gems."*)

Having sprinkled [the vessel] with water from the ritual weapon (*astra*) and covered it with armor (*kavaca*), one should then worship the ninefold reality (*navatattva*) starting with Śiva in the center using the nine syllables. Then, the five vessels— characterized as well-established, peaceful, radiant, immortal, and possessing protection— should be placed within the central vessel.

One should place water consecrated with the *varma* (kavaca) mantra in the east; curd and ghee consecrated with the *śiva* mantra in the south; cow dung and cow urine with the *hṛdaya* and *śiras* mantras respectively in the west and northwest; and *kuśa* water with the *netra* mantra in the northeast.

One should place [the materials] consecrated seven times. One should gradually add four, three, two, and one *pala* weights, starting from the thumb upwards. Then, with the heart-mantra and the others, one should mix those [substances] into the seventh vessel while seated upon a seat of *kuśa* grass.
Kuśa grass, six times; curd, four times; cow’s urine, twice; milk, five times; ghee, three times; cow dung, once.

Oṃ raṃ, [offer] ghee to Aghora; oṃ yaṃ, [offer] curd to Tatpuruṣa; oṃ kṣaṃ, [offer] milk to Īśāna. One should consecrate the water with kuśa grass by means of the mantra together with its limbs (sāṅga-dhāman). Then follows the rite of conjunction: oṃ hāṃ laṃ, [consecrate] the cow dung as being of the nature of nectar; oṃ hīṃ...

*Vaṃ*, I join the cow’s urine, which is of the nature of Ratnodayā; *namaḥ*. *Oṃ hīṃ vaṃ*, [I join] the cow’s urine, which is of the nature of Ratnodayā; *oṃ haḥ raṃ*, I join the ghee, which is of the nature of Tejovatī; *ātmani*.
Oṃ haḥ raṃ, I join the self of radiant energy (tejas) with the clarified butter (ghṛta).

Oṃ hūṃ yaṃ, I join the well-pacified self (suśāntātman) with the curd (dadhi). Oṃ haiṃ kṣaṃ, I join [the self] with the milk (kṣīra) in the well-established self (supratiṣṭhātman); homage! Thus, each its own.

Having uttered the mantra and mixed the substances beginning with cow-dung and ending with milk, one should join that vessel of milk along with the kuśa-water to the root-mantra. Then: *Oṃ īśvaratattvam* (Oṃ, the principle of Īśvara). [One should join] the principle of Māyā into the principle of Māyā, and the principle of Niyati into the principle of Niyati.

One should unite [the offering] with the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*). Having placed all of that separately into a previously consecrated vessel upon a lotus, one should offer a seat beneath the vessel, saying: *oṃ anantāya namaḥ*. Then, one should stir it again with the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*). Having stirred it in this manner—

Having consecrated [the materials] with the *saṃhitā* [mantra], having rendered them nectar-like with the *amṛtamudrā*, and having worshipped Śiva there along with his retinue and performed the *mantrasandhāna* and other rites, one should purify all the collections of substances as well as the sacrificial abode by means of this.
Thus ends the procedure for the five products of the cow.
Then, to one's left, the worship of the Gurus should be performed in an upward sequence of rows.
Right here, the worship of Śrī Gaṇapati [is performed]:
Oṃ gūṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ gīṃ saḥ, [obeisance] to Gaṇapati’s beloved.
Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the Guru.

By means of the five applications (*pañcopayoga*), the vessels are purified with the *astra* mantra. Milk is placed in the central vessel; curd is placed in the eastern vessel with the *varma* mantra; and ghee is placed in the [northeastern] vessel with the *śikhā* mantra.
In the south, cow dung with the *hṛdaya* mantra; in the west, cow urine with the *śiras* mantra; in the north, [cow dung].
"The rule regarding the quantity of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is one *tulā* for a fortnight; for the eyes, there is water with *kuśa* grass at night.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrīgurupustikā*, and so forth.
Oṃ vāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī; in the northwest. Oṃ kṣāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla; [facing] the north.

Right here is the worship of the water-pot (*kalaśa*). Then, standing in the southern direction and facing north, one should sprinkle the sacrificial ground with darbha grass that has been consecrated seven times with the Astra-mantra. Then, mentally:

Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I perform the scraping here: haḥ phaṭ. Likewise, the removal of earth: ka. The extraction of impurities: [ka]. The filling with pearls: ka. The leveling: ka. Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya huṃ: the sprinkling: ka. The pounding: ka. I perform the sweeping: [ka].

Haḥ phaṭ! Having thus performed [this] mentally, the smearing is done with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and scented water: Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! "I perform the smearing, haḥ phaṭ!"—thus is the purification.
As it is said in the Mataṅga:
"Sesame, parched grain, barley, dūrvā grass, and white mustard seeds are auspicious;
likewise, white flowers that are fragrant in abundance."
"This auspicious scattering is mixed with sandalwood paste and camphor.

Then, one should perform the scattering of the *vikara* with water containing flowers, sandalwood, white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), *dūrvā* grass, parched grain (*lāja*), sesame, and barley, while reciting the *astra-mantra*. One should meditate upon the ground as being completely filled with pearls.

One should place [the vessel] in the northeast corner of the sacrificial altar using a *darbha* whisk. Having sprinkled the altar with fragrant water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should worship Śrī upon the seat facing the door.
The meditation on Śrī: Oṃ! Having invoked Śrī with the *dhruva* mantra—her who holds a lotus in her hand, possesses beautiful eyes, scatters white flowers, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
Dark as the petals of a blue lotus, gazing upon the sacrificial hall,
seated in the Brahma-position, and facing the door with an auspicious gait.
18) Having taken recourse to the northeastern direction, one should smear the mandala with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sprinkle it with fragrant water using the *śivāmbhas* mantra.
Having offered the Anantādi seat up to the *dhruva* [pillar] and the maṇḍala, one should prepare a jar smeared with sandalwood paste, completely free from all defects.
Having honored [the vessel] with the svastika and other [mudrās], with barley, white mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass, and having wrapped it with a white thread,
[one should sprinkle it] with water purified by a cloth.

Having filled it so that it was completely covered on all sides with the sprouts of mango, *aśvattha*, and other trees, and provided with gems, medicinal herbs, and groups of plants such as *sahadevā*;
Having sprinkled [the seat] with the Astra-mantra and gathered it together, one should cover it with the Kavaca-mantra and place it upon the seat while recollecting the Mūla-mantra.

"Up to the limit of the [five] maṇḍalas" means that, through the pervasive power of the Supreme (Parā), these fixed maṇḍalas of the Sun and so forth— which consist of the pervasion of the power of the Brahma-aperture (brahmavila) and are presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— extend up to that point, but not up to Śiva, due to the fierce powers of the mantras.

Since the body has been purified by means of drying, burning, and so forth, the consecration (*abhiṣecana*) is for that purpose; this is according to the future method, as it concludes the application of nourishment (*pyāyana*), because it is untenable for [the body] to remain as the primary seat for Śiva. Barley and so forth...

It is characterized by those [herbs] contained within; "by the thread acting as armor" means together with the groups of *sahadevā* and so forth. Regarding the herbs, it is said in the *Sārasaṅgraha*:
"The best of herbs is indeed *sahadevā*, known as *aśivā*. Thus, it is *sahadevā*.
The meaning is that it is joined with a collection of primary medicinal herbs, metallic ores, and seeds;
by the words "with the root mantra" and so forth, the fact that the pitcher consists of the form of supreme consciousness is stated.
One should worship the auspicious Fortune of Liberation (mokṣalakṣmī), which brings about well-being for the disciple and others who enter the sacrificial hall facing the door;
having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should thoroughly worship the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha).

Oṃ huṃ hāṃ huṃ, "O Śrī Lakṣmī, come," and so forth. Oṃ hāṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī. Śrām for the limbs. Na, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, tha, ca, dha, ī, ṇa, u, ū, ba, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, i, ha, va, bha, ya, ḍa, ḍha, ṭha, jha, ña, ja, ra, ṭa.

*Pa ka la a sa aḥ ha ṣa kṣa ma śa aṃ ta e ai o au da pha hrīṃ mālinyai namaḥ*. With this mantra, one should cast a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, one should draw two *svastikas* in the northeast (*īśāna*). [Next follows] the worship of the doors, the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), and the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
The mantra, the vessel for the *argha* offering, self-worship, and the worship of the Guru belong to the category of the seat (*āsana*).
(In the *Sutantra*, having assigned the seat beginning with Ananta [and the others] up to the *dhruva*,
"up to the *maṇḍala*" means that by means of the supreme pervasion (*paravyāpti*), they consist of the power of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmavila*) and the pervasive one (*vyāpinī*).)
The seat extends as far as the orbs of the Sun and others presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, but it does not extend as far as Śiva.
Oṃ, salutation to Ananta. [The sequence is: Ādhāra-śakti, Kadā, Aṅkura, Nāla, and Dharma.
"Salutation," and so forth; "To Adharma," and so forth; "To the Ṛgveda," and so forth; "To the Kṛtayuga," and so forth;
[salutations] to the lower covering, the middle covering, and the upper covering;
to the lotus petals, the filaments, the pericarp, and the solar orb upon the petals.
The lunar maṇḍalas are on the filaments, and the fire maṇḍala is at the pericarp. "Oṃ, homage to the pericarp of the lotus of knowledge.
Above that:
Oṃ glūṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. With "gām," [one should touch] the limbs of the one desiring enjoyment;
here, on the seat: Oṃ ślīṃ paśu hūṃ phaṭ, phaṭ to the Pāśupata weapon. Then:
Oṃ, obeisance to Indrāṇī, who holds a thunderbolt in her hand; Oṃ, [obeisance] to Āgneyī, who holds a spear; to Yāmyā...

*Daṇḍa* ha! To Nirṛti, *khaḍga* ha! To Vāruṇī, *pāśa* ha! To Vāyavī, *dhvaja* ha! To Kauberī, *gadā* ha! To the one holding the trident in her hand, the Mistress of the North-East, *namaḥ* (O Vijayā)!
Having placed the seat of the six objects (*ṣaḍdartha*), [one should place] upon it with the *praṇava*.
With the mantra "gām," one should worship Vighneśa with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having meditated upon the three-eyed one with an elephant face and a dwarf form, whose limbs arise from the letter *ga* joined with the six long vowels;
Having released [the weapon], one who desires success should worship the great weapon-mantra, having bestowed infinity,
as well as dharma, knowledge, and dispassion.
This seat consists of the six spokes, including the sovereign power and the pericarp;
having meditated upon [the deity] holding a sword and a shield, one should place him upon this.
Terrible with great fangs and a most fierce face knit with frowns,
he is endowed with his six limbs and surrounded by the Mothers of the Quarters.
O limb, having meditated upon that very form— the six limbs together with the *sārṇa* [syllables] and illuminated by the sound *phaṭ*— one should then request the eight measures (*mātrā*).

"Indrāṇīm on the eastern petals," etc.—thus one should worship the eight goddesses there for the sake of protection. This is the purification of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*). To its south, Kumāra is also to be worshipped: *Oṃ klūṃ*.
"Kāṃ" is for the salutation to the Kumāra; "kām" is for the limbs.

There, in the northeast, upon a maṇḍala marked with svastikas and other symbols, which has been smeared with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), fragrant water, and auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), one should place a vessel made of gold or other materials down to clay, filled with cloth, a goad, and water.
(The filling [of the vessel] is the contemplation that it consists of the entire universe.)

Having brought the Śiva-vessel (śivakalaśa) accompanied by boiled rice, horse-gram, sprouts, seeds, medicinal herbs, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains; containing within it fruits and jewels; provided with a sacred thread (upavīta); and furnished with a seat made of seven blades of darbha grass—one sprinkles it with the Astra mantra: *Oṃ haḥ phaṭ prokṣayāmi namaḥ*.

Having sprinkled [the vessel] thus: "Oṃ haiṃ, I veil you; namaḥ. Having veiled it with the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should worship it with the root-mantra (mūla). This left-hand vessel (vāmestravārdhānī), thus adorned, should be worshipped with the weapon-mantra (astra).
Having brought the sword of wisdom (jñānakhaḍga), which is thirty-six *tāla* in length and fashioned from thirty-six bundles of *darbha* grass, one should worship it with:

"Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! Homage to the sword of wisdom, whose nature consists of the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattva*). Then, having placed the sword of awakening to the lineage (*veṇībodhāsi*) between these two, one should touch the water-pot with the thumb.

With the fist [he touches] the *vārdhānī* vessel; thus at the time of eating. Then, at the time of release: first the *vārdhānī* with the fist, thereafter the water-pot (*kumbha*) with the thumb, having touched it. The touching of the eyes should be performed, having taken hold of the jar or the cloth-jar (*vāstrakakalaśa*).
"One should wander about, bringing down a stream of water upon the sacrificial chamber. Thus is the protection of the sacrificial chamber;
for [as stated in the Āloka]: "The marriage-thread with its upper knot serves as the sword of knowledge."

The arrangement of the *veṇī* (the ritual grass-bundle) is well-known and made of *darbha* grass. As it is said: "A *veṇī* made of thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass, measured by the length of the palate, and consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra of Śiva, is the most excellent means of awakening."
In the light.
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, what would be the purpose of worshipping the jar?",

he says: "The host of mantras, augmented by the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) within the water situated in the jar and contemplated as being of the nature of pure light, nourishes everything according to the ritual rule."
Therefore, the Guru should worship the entire collection of mantras within the pitcher— either the triad,
or those associated with Yamala and Tarkā, or a single mantra-deity.
"Every rite" refers to that which is about to be described; "from this" means because it causes the nourishment of all rites (sc.
One should place the jar, having cast [the substances] therein, at that spot. This is the sequence for the stable seat (*sthirāsana*).

Then follows the sequence of moving the seat: the placement of the *astrakalaśa* (weapon-vase) upon the *vikaras* (limbs), which are like the hands holding weapons; thereafter, one should perform the joining of the channels (*nāḍī*), the joining of the mantras, and the act of supreme consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*) through the left nostril.
Having entered the heart and attained rest within the subtle wind,

she should emerge through the right nostril. In the same manner, the Goddess, having performed entry, rest, and emergence through the lady of the mouth, [rests] in the fire that is a portion of that life-force.

One should contemplate one's own portion of the vital breath (*svajīvāṃśa*) as having entered within the deity; having meditated thus, it should emerge from the [deity's] left side and enter one's own heart through one's own left side. One should then perform the contemplation of the unification of one's own self and the divine self. This is the "joining of the channels" (*nāḍīsaṃdhāna*).

One should contemplate oneself as merged in Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu in Brahmā; then one should contemplate Brahmā as merged in the World-Guardian (Lokapāla), who is reciting the Brahma-mantra, and that Lokapāla in Īśāna; Īśāna in Vaiśravaṇa, Vaiśravaṇa in Vāyu, and Vāyu in Varuṇa.
To Nairṛta; to Yama, the [mantra] of Yama; to Agni, the [mantra] of Agni; to Indra, the [mantra] of Indra;
to Astra, the [mantra] of Astra; to Netra, the [mantra] of Netra; to Kavaca, the [mantra] of Kavaca; to Śikhā, the [mantra] of Śikhā;
to the Head, the [mantra] of the Head; to the Heart, the [mantra] of the Heart; to the Goddess, the [mantra] of the Goddess; to the Supreme Lord, the [mantra] of the Goddess.

One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord dissolved within the Self; this is the "unification of the mantra" (*mantrasandhāna*). Then, having uttered the root-mantra from one's own heart, by means of the sequence of piercing the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), [one proceeds through] the syllables *a*, *u*, *m*, and the *bindu*.

Having experienced rest in the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*) through the sequence of Ardhacandra, Nirodha, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā; likewise, one perceives the deity within the mantra, which is the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), presiding over all dimensions, and oriented toward grace (*prasāda*).
Having performed the descent (*avatāra*), one should meditate. Again, there is the worship of the two jars with the root-mantras and their limbs.
Then, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the partless mantra (*niṣkalamantra*) one hundred and eight times.
One should likewise perform the recitation of the partless weapon-mantra (*niṣkalāstra*). [This applies] to the jar of the Vikarāla-weapon as well.

One should meditate on [the deities] in the form of the weapons of Lokeśvara. Then, for the sake of destroying obstacles, one should meditate on the *Vajrārdhanī* weapon held in the right hand of the Blessed One— roaring, terrifying with the flames of the fire at the end of an eon, and bearing many faces and weapons.
Having offered clarified butter, milk, sugar, honey, and likewise grapes— the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)— as the food offering (naivedya), one should address the Lord.
Having thus presented the food offering (naivedya), one should, with knees on the ground and palms joined in añjali, address the God of gods:
"Oṃ! Come, accept this seat, protect [me], fill my mouth, and purify my defects."
O Supreme Lord, take away my evil! O Soul of the Universe, You are the power of the universe! Om, O Blessed One, by Your grace I shall complete this sacrifice;
O All-pervading Lord, grant me Your constant presence for the sake of removing all obstacles.
Likewise:
Oṃ, O Supreme Lord, you have been commanded by him who resides in the Guru; you should show grace.
The disciples were impelled by devotion to Śiva.
Thus, these [beings] have been declared to be of two kinds; by bestowing grace upon them, you shall enter my own body, and I shall not be your equal.
O Lord of the World, just as this temple of the Blessed One’s face has been constructed with effort, so must it be protected by you, the best of all sacrificial rites.
Having thus addressed the Blessed One, one should cover him with two garments. Then follows the worship of the flask and the mandala:
as prescribed, having drawn the lords of the directions, the planets, and the Bhairavas, each accompanied by their respective retinues and marked with their own emblems.
One should worship Gaṇeśa and Kumāra in front of the doorway, on the right and left respectively, and Śrī between them. First is the worship of Gaṇeśa in the northwest (Vāyu). The initial meditation:
*Oṃ glūṃ gāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*. *Gāṃ* is for the limbs. On the right...
The Worship of Kumāra:

Oṃ klūṃ kāṃ, salutation to Kumāra. With *kāṃ*, one should worship his limbs; between those two, one should worship Śrī: Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Śrī. With *hrāṃ* and *śrāṃ*, one worships her limbs.
Outside of that, on one's own left, in an ascending sequence upon the walnuts, is the worship of the Gurus.

Then, in the center, one should worship the manifest Lord (sakalabhaṭṭāraka) together with His Goddess, accompanied by the unmanifest (niṣkala). The visualization begins with "Oṃ, the three-and-five-eyed one," and so forth, using the venerable Aghora mantra in its unmanifest form.
And by which Amṛteśvara deity should that goddess worship the central lotus?
For those deities whose mantra-origination is not specifically mentioned in the scriptures,
one should employ the *praṇava* (OM) joined with their name.
Although the faces of the mantras such as Kapāleśa and others have not been explicitly stated,
nevertheless, the faces and limbs of the naiṣkala [mantra] should be employed by those who worship;
this is the tradition of our excellent Guru.

Oṃ, salutation to Kapāleśa Bhairava—[in the] east. Oṃ, [salutation to] Śikhivāha—[in the] southeast. Oṃ, [salutation to] Krodharājabhairava—[in the] south. Oṃ, [salutation to] Vikarālabhairava—[in the] southwest. Oṃ, [salutation to] Manmathabhairava—[in the] west. Oṃ, [salutation to] Meghanādabhairava—[in the] northwest. Oṃ, [salutation to] Somarājabhairava—[in the] north. Oṃ Gūṃ.
The Vidyārājas are in the northeast.
Then, first the worship of the planets (graha), and then the worship of the world-protectors (lokapāla):
*oṃ lūṃ* homage to Indra, who holds a vajra in his hand, in the east; *oṃ* to Agni, [who holds] a śakti... *oṃ*.

To Yama, the staff: *ha*. To Nirṛti, the sword: *oṃ khaḍga ha*. To Varuṇa, the noose: *oṃ pāśa ha*. To Vāyu, the banner: *oṃ dhvaja ha*. To Kuvīra, the mace: *oṃ gadā ha*. To Īśāna, the trident: *oṃ triśūla ha*. To Brahmā, the lotus: *oṃ padma ha*. To Ananta, the plow in hand: *oṃ halahastā*.
Then follows the worship of the planets (*grahapūjana*). First, in the center, with the root mantra: (2) Sūrya. *Oṃ raṃ agnaye* (1) *namaḥ*.
*Oṃ candramase* (2) *namaḥ*. *Oṃ vūṃ varuṇāya pāśahastāya*.
*Oṃ aṅgārakāya* (2) *namaḥ*. *Oṃ kuṃ kumārāya* (1) *namaḥ*. *Oṃ*...
Salutation to Budha (2). Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu (1). Oṃ, salutation to Jīva (2). Oṃ lūṃ, salutation to Indra (1). Oṃ, salutation to Bhārgava (2).
Oṃ aiṃ, speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech (1), svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Śanaiścara (2).

Oṃ praṃ, obeisance to Prajāpati (1). Oṃ, obeisance to Rāhu (2). Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ, obeisance to Ketu (2). Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Rudra. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda (2). Oṃ āṃ brāṃ.
Vraṃ Brahmamaṇe, homage! Oṃ Hrīṃ Agastyāya, (1) homage! Oṃ Hlāṃ (1) Anantāya Halahastāya, homage!
Thus ends the section on the planetary enclosure (*grahāvaraṇa*). Then, O Sudakṣe: "Oṃ, salutation to Agni and Āditya.
One should worship the planetary enclosure outside the mandala of the jars (*kalaśa*) according to the sequence of the upward rows.
Oṃ hrāṃ kṣaṃ kṣūṃ, homage to Heruka, Pū. Oṃ ai& hrīṃ lāṃ kṣeṃ, homage to Tripurāntaka, Agni. Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ kṣīṃ, homage to Agnivetāla, Da. Oṃ hrīṃ kṣūṃ hūṃ, homage to Agnijihva.

Not so. Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ, salutation to Kurpara in the west. Oṃ, salutation to Kāla in the north-west. Oṃ kṣāṃ yukṣīṃ, salutation to Karālin in the north. Oṃ ayuṃ kṣmīṃ, salutation to Ekapāda in the north-east. Oṃ kṣūṃ yuṃ kṣāṃ, [salutation] to Bhīmarūpa.

*Namaḥ* in the center; *namaḥ* to Ḍāmarāya above; *namaḥ* to Hāṭakeśvarāya below. Having worshipped other mantras of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) as part of the retinue (*parivāra*), then having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), and having given the *nirodhārgha* water, [one should perform the worship] with the *yonimudrā*.
One should perform a salutation.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the installation of the water jar (kalaśa).
Then, having brought the patron forward, one should perform worship with:
*oṃ naumi svāñme* and so forth; and *oṃ hrīṃ saḥ pavitrakam arpayāmi namaḥ*. Having bound the *tilaka* and the *kaṅkaṇa* with a benediction, [one should offer them] to oneself as Śiva.

Salutation to the form for the anointing; salutation to the fragrance. Salutation to the water offering (*argha*). Salutation to the flower. With the mantra "Oṃ *saṃsāra-marukāntāra*," [one offers] incense. With the mantra "Oṃ *kālāgni-rudrarūpa*," [one offers] the lamp. With the mantra "Oṃ *dvibhujaṃ caikavadanam*," [one offers] to the Sun. To the Self, whose nature is Śiva.

Through the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) regarding incense and lamps, may there be success. Incense, obeisance! Lamp, obeisance! Today, for Mahāgaṇapati, Kumāra, and so forth—incense, obeisance! Lamp, obeisance!
Then one should begin the inquiry:
*Oṃ gāyatryai namaḥ*. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ tatsaviturityādi*. *Bahurūpāya vi*, *koṭarākṣāya dhī*, *tanno ghoraḥ pra* 3, and so forth.
Now, first: "Of Mahāgaṇapati," and so forth.

For the sake of attaining the fruit of initiation on the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvadīkṣā*), I shall perform the worship of the jar (*kalaśapūjana*), the worship of the sacrifice (*yāgapūjana*), and the ritual adoration (*arcā*). *Oṃ*, do it!
Having scattered sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and barley.
Oṃ, to Mahāgaṇapati. This seat, obeisance! Having recited everything as before, one should offer the seat.
Again, taking two blades of *darbha* grass:
*Oṃ mahāgaṇapataye*, etc. ... I worship you all.
Oṃ, [reciting] "Mahāgaṇapati... and so forth, I shall invoke. Oṃ, invoke! Having scattered sesame seeds, one should then recite the invocations.
Oṃ, I invoke the god Gaṇeśa, who is honored by the gods themselves,
the eternal destroyer of obstacles, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Red in color, possessing great splendor, and adorned with red garlands and radiance; please accept this offering, flowers, sacrificial oblation, and incense.
Oṃ glūṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ, I invoke the auspicious god Kumāra, who has six faces,
who is mounted upon a peacock-throne, and who bestows boons upon his devotees.
Red in color; offering flowers; Oṃ klūṃ kāṃ, homage to Kumāra.
I invoke the goddesses Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.
In the same manner, one should worship Viśvakarman and the other deities of the door, as well as goddesses assuming various forms,
adorned with diverse garlands, garments, and ornaments.
The offering of flowers: Oṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Śrī.
Then, in the center, one should invoke Svacchandabhairava with:
"Oṃ! I invoke Maheśa, who has eight arms like the Vasus and the moon, who is Svacchanda, whose supreme self-nature is as pure as a flawless gem, seated upon Rudra, and three-eyed."
The five-faced one, auspicious like the crescent moon, supremely compassionate, and immeasurable.
22) *Oṃ hūṃ aghore*. This is the root mantra. *Oṃ āvāhayāmi* (I invoke).
For the sake of protecting the sacrifice, [I take refuge] in the Lord who wears a crown of crescent moons, the glorious Kapālin who holds a garland of skulls,
the five-faced and three-eyed one with ten beautiful arms, whose crest is the half-moon.
Oṃ kṣmryūṃ, obeisance to Kapāleśa Bhairava (1). I invoke Śikhivāhana Bhairava, who is red in luster,
adorned with a garland of beautiful human skulls, five-faced, three-eyed, beautiful with ten arms, and whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon.
For the purpose of protecting the ritual site:
Oṃ hrūṃ śikhivāhana bhai 2!
Oṃ, I invoke that stainless King of Wrath, who possesses a splendor like that of fresh clouds.
Wearing a garland of skulls, five-faced, Oṃ Kṣūṃ, O King of Wrath!
I invoke the formidable form of the Lord, radiant as fire.
Wearing a garland of beautiful young skulls, having five faces— Oṃ jhrūṃ, O Vikarāla, Bhai 4! Oṃ, I invoke the Blessed One, the form of the Lord, that Manmatha,
who wears a garland of beautiful young skulls, having five faces— Oṃ hvū-auṃ, O Manmatha, Bhai 5!
Oṃ, I invoke the one who possesses the luster of a smoke-colored body, the stainless Meghanāda, adorned with a garland of skulls and the five [faces]. Oṃ Hryūṃ Meghanāda Bhai 6!
I invoke him who holds a skull-ornament, who possesses a radiance like that of the moon, the sovereign of the moon, the five-faced one: Oṃ hūṃ somarāja bhairava!
Oṃ, I invoke the King of Knowledge (Vidyārāja), who resembles a white jewel.
Adorned with a garland of skulls upon his head, he has five faces.
Then, outside of that, are the invocations of the planets: *Oṃ, I invoke the Lord of Day (the Sun), who bears the cord of the sacrificial thread in his right eye, a smoke-colored banner, and a flag;
who is mounted upon seven horses, holds the reins with a pair of hands, and possesses a mass of rays and three eyes.*
The three-eyed refuge for the protection of the sacrifice: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Sūrya.
(1) Thus, in the center.
Oṃ, I invoke the Moon, who holds a rosary in his right hand and a banner with a smoky base; in his left hand he holds a deer and a mass of rays;
the three-eyed one, the refuge for those with three eyes, for the protection of the sacrifice.

Oṃ srūṃ! To the east, [I invoke] Candramas twice. I invoke Dharaṇī’s son, who carries a water-pot and a rosary and bracelets on his right hands, who is seated upon the peacock-vehicle, who holds a crescent moon in his left hand, and who is beautiful with a white complexion.
Tryakṣa: Oṃ Hrūṃ! Aṅgāraka, from the fire [region]!

I invoke the white one, adorned with a crown and necklaces, holding a rosary and a bracelet in his right hands, seated upon Garuḍa, holding a water-pot in his left hand, beautiful with a white complexion.
Tryakṣaṃ | Oṃ śrī ūṃ, to Budha on the right (four times):
I invoke the steadfast Guru of the gods, who holds a rosary and a ring in his right hand,
who is mounted upon an elephant, and who, in his left, carries a water-pot and is clad in yellow garments.
Tryakṣa: Oṃ RṢŪṂ,
I invoke the wise Lord, of fierce form, holding a sacrificial staff and a rosary in his right hand, the Seer.
Seated upon a peacock vehicle, holding a water-pot in his left hand, white in color, and three-eyed; Oṃ Hrīṃ Bhārgava, come from the north!
I invoke Śani, the end-maker of fierce form, who holds a rosary and a bracelet in his right hands.

Seated upon a man-borne vehicle, likewise holding a water-pot in his left hand, the three-eyed one—Oṃ kṣamarayarūṃ! Śanaiścara, I invoke you from the southwest; you who wear earrings and a garland, and have a head shaped like a vessel.
And having offered the *svadhā* oblation, [one should invoke] Rāhu, seated upon a lion-throne,
with an exceedingly terrifying face, possessing three eyes— [reciting] "Oṃ Dhūṃ, to Rāhu, svāhā"—
and accompanied by ten serpents, endowed with a right eye; I invoke him.
And the water-pot (kalaśa) is on the left. Ketu is in the northeast (īśāna), having a mass of darkness, a black body, very long, and three eyes. 9.
Oṃ, I invoke Dhruvarāja, the lord of the stars,

who possesses a thousandfold virtues, who is perfectly pure, whose footstool is worshipped by the hosts of gods and the primordial deity, and who is three-eyed— Oṃ Hrīṃ, to Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda.

Namaḥ! To the north, with devotion to the Lord, I invoke Agastya, the king of the twice-born, who joyfully drank the ocean, who is compassionate toward his devotees, and who is a devotee of the Supreme Lord—him of the three eyes.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Agastya. To the south.
Outside of this, one should perform the invocations of the world-protectors (lokapālas):
"Oṃ, I invoke the king of the gods, seated upon an elephant, holding a goad and a thunderbolt in his right hands,
honored and as radiant as the moon, bearing a parasol together with a spear."
The pure left eye for the purpose of protecting the sacrifice: Oṃ lūṃ, obeisance to Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand. (1)
Oṃ, I invoke Agni, who holds the Vedamudrā and a rosary in his own right hand, who is mounted upon a parrot, and likewise holds a fire-pit and a staff in his left;
he is three-eyed, devoted to the Three-Eyed Lord (Śiva), and intent on protecting the sacrifice. Oṃ Rūṃ, to Agni!
Śakti ha || 2 ||
Oṃ, I invoke Yama, the supreme lord, marked with a trident and a vajra, seated upon the back of a buffalo, possessing three eyes, holding a lute together with a staff, and wearing a garment;
O Makha, I [invoke] you with four arms. Oṃ ṭūṃ ya Makha! 3.

Oṃ, I invoke Nirṛti, who has the crescent moon upon his crest, who is intent on worship, and who holds a goad and a sword in his right hands; in his left, he is equipped with a shield and a noose, seated upon a grass mat for my sacrifice. Oṃ Kṣūṃ, O Nirṛti! 4.

Oṃ, I invoke Varuṇa, who has the crescent moon upon his crest, who is intent on worship, and who holds a goad and a sword in his right hands; in his left, he is endowed with a shield and a noose, seated upon a crocodile—him I [invoke] for this sacrifice. Oṃ vūṃ, the mantra of Varuṇa. 5.

O Lord of Sacrifice, I invoke you, who hold a vessel of wind in your pair of right hands and the supreme Wind-god in your left, together with your water-pot and seated upon a moving deer-throne: Oṃ Yūṃ, to Vāyu! 6.
Oṃ, I invoke Dhanada, who is seated upon a man-vehicle (naravāhana), holding a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) and likewise a rosary (akṣasūtra) in his own hands,
together with the lion-banner (siṃhadhvaja) and the auspicious book (śivapustaka).
O Lord, supreme sacrifice, you who cause the wandering; Oṃ Kuṃ Kuvīrā. 7.

Oṃ, I invoke Īśa, who wears a crown of crescent moons, holding a rosary and a trident in his right hands, and likewise a mirror and a *liṅga* in his left; he has three eyes, a bull as his vehicle, and is the Lord of Sacrifice. Oṃ Mūṃ, Īśāna. 8.
I invoke Brahmā, seated upon the lotus-throne, bearing the gesture of the Vedas and the rosary,
constantly holding the staff and the water-pot—
the supreme Lord of sacrifice. Oṃ Āṃ Brāṃ Braṃ.
To Brahmā, a lotus. || 9 ||

Oṃ, I invoke Viṣṇu, who is eternally situated on his own right side, bearing a rosary and a mace; who is joined by the Śārṅga bow and a pestle in his left hands; who is seated upon the tortoise, devoted to Śiva, and the sustainer of the earth. Oṃ hlāṃ, Ananta! 10.
Now, for the goddesses:
I invoke the goddess Mahātripurasundarī, who resembles ten million suns and is accompanied by Kāmeśvara.
paṃ paṃ paṃ mahātripurasundarī pādukābhyo namaḥ ||
Oṃ, I invoke Durgā, who bears in this sacrifice a trident,
a discus, a sword, a bow, a conch, a shield, and the threatening gesture.
Oṃ hrīṃ duṃ, obeisance to Durgā. Oṃ, I invoke the goddess Śārikā, the Supreme Sovereign, the bestower of all accomplishments, into this delightful sacrifice.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ āṃ śāṃ, obeisance to Sārikā.
Oṃ, I invoke the goddess Śāradā, the bestower of boons, in this sacrifice— she who is eternally worshipped as Śāṇḍilyā, who resides on Śrīśaila, and who possesses six arms.
Oṃ śmrīṃ, nectar for Śāradā. Oṃ, I invoke the Goddess who dwells upon the Mountain of Flames, Jvālāmukhī, accompanied by Mahādeva, at this great sacrifice.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ, obeisance to Jvālābhagavatī. Oṃ, I invoke the goddess Lakṣmī, the bestower of all prosperity.
Seated in the lotus posture, resting upon the chest of the lotus-navelled one: Oṃ hūṃ, grant the crushing of the hands of all! Hūṃ, to the Goddess of Wealth, svāhā!
Oṃ, I invoke the goddess Veḍā, the Blessed One, into this sacrifice—
she who holds a vessel of spirituous liquor in her hand, is adorned with necklaces, and has a smiling face.
Oṃ hrīṃ hsrūṃ ai& kraṃ maṃ vīḍā bhagavati haṃsarūpiṇi svāhā | Oṃ, I invoke the Goddess, the Queen who bestows sovereignty.
To her who occupies half the body of Bhūtīśvara, seated upon a lion-throne:
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Rāṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Queen.
Oṃ, I invoke the Lord of the Field, the most wonderful ruler of the sacrifice, who shines with serpents, wears a garland of skulls, possesses three eyes,
and holds a trident in his hand; he has a dark-blue countenance, removes misfortune and suffering, and is the sovereign of the gods.
Oṃ kṣāṃ, homage to Kṣetrapāla.
Then: *Oṃ Phaṭ*! *Astrāya Phaṭ*! *Kuṅkumam aguru*! *Mahāgaṇapataye* and so forth; this is the *pādya*, [offered] with *namaḥ*.
Again: Oṃ phaṭ! Astra-phaṭ! Svāṃ svāṃ to Soma, and so forth.
To Mahāgaṇapati: this is your arghya; obeisance!

To Mahāgaṇapati, [I offer] fragrance, water for honor, and flowers; obeisance! Incense, obeisance! Lamp, obeisance! Perfume, obeisance! This is the water for honor (arghya) for these deities. Food, obeisance! Obeisance! 2.

The *apośāna* rite; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); these deities are ever-present. Then, having offered as an oblation (*naivedya*) jaggery, sugar, ghee, curd, and various fruits, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) one hundred and eight times.

Then, having worshipped the world-protectors (lokeśas) along with the planets and the Bhairavas according to the previously mentioned sequence, he should proclaim the command of the venerable Sakalabhaṭṭāraka:
"Oṃ! Ho! Ho! Lord of the Gaṇas, now make this place free from obstacles."

"I shall perform the worship of Hara for the sake of protecting my disciple. O Blessed Planets, all you who are considered primary planets and those who are secondary planets— may you all grant your presence here for the pacification of obstacles."
Oṃ! O Indra, for the pacification of obstacles in your own quarter, you must remain vigilant until the completion of the rite, by the command of Śiva.
Oṃ lūṃ, homage to Indra, who holds a vajra in his hand.
"O Agni! O Yama! O Nirṛti! O Varuṇa! O Vāyu! O Kuvīra! O Īśāna! O Brahmā! O Viṣṇu!
Thus, with these mantras, [he addresses] the world-protectors with the command of Śiva."
Having caused [the mantra] to be recited, having presented the food offering (naivedya), and having offered the water of cessation (nirodhārgha),
one should proceed to the sacrificial ground, which takes the form of an altar suitable for drawing the Śrī Navanābha-yāga.
There, on the sacrificial ground, having prepared the three vessels in the form of the *vidhi-argha*, *nirodha-argha*, and *paśu-argha*,
and having worshipped them with their respective mantras according to the previously mentioned rule, one should sprinkle the sacrificial ground with the *vidhi-argha*.

Enveloping with the Kavaca [armor] mantra; striking with the Astra [weapon] mantra; and transforming into nectar with the Amṛta-mudrā. (2) From the east to the southeast, ending at Īśāna: *Oṃ gurave namaḥ*, *paramagurave*, *parameṣṭhigurave*, *paramācāryāya*, *ādisiddhebhyaḥ*. Thus.
Having performed the worship of the Śrī Guru (2), one should worship Śrī Gaṇeśa in the north-west corner (1):
*oṃ glūṃ gāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*. *Gāṃ* [and so on] for the limbs.
Having thus fully worshipped Śrī Gaṇeśa (1), [one prepares] the seat in the center of the sacrificial altar.
One should place them as follows: *oṃ anantāya namaḥ*. *oṃ* to the support (*ādhāra*); *ka* to the root (*kanda*); *aṃ* to the sprout (*aṅkura*);
*ā* to the stalk (*nāla*); *ṛṃ* to virtue (*dharma*); *ṝṃ* to knowledge (*jñāna*); *ḷṃ* to dispassion (*vairāgya*); *ḹṃ* to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
These sandals (*pādukās*) are white, red, yellow, and black, [to be placed] from the southeast (*agni*) to the northeast (*īśa*).
Those in the form of lions, possessing three eyes, are also to be worshipped.
Oṃ, Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya— these limbs are white in form, appearing as the planks of the lion-throne, extending from the east to the north.

One should meditate upon and install this fourfold Veda— the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, and *Atharvaveda*— as the form of the joints, sandals, and the central pin of the body, and thus worship it.
Oṃ, to the Kṛtayuga, Tretāyuga, Dvāparayuga, and Kaliyuga—thus [in the corners] beginning with the northeast (īśāna). Oṃ, obeisance to the lower covering, to the quality of darkness (tamas).
Here, "invocation" (āvāhana) is said to be the act of respectfully bringing [the deity] face-to-face. || 1 ||
And the wise have declared that devotion consists of both non-attachment and steadfast establishment.
O Jagannātha, that manifestation of acceptance—“I am yours”—is the presence of Your Lordship even in a state of separation;
it cannot be otherwise.
Up until the completion of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), there is a gradual exhaustion of presence;
even though Śambhu remains all-pervasive, this state is celebrated as "suppression" (nirodha).

That which is the non-manifestation of Śiva— who consists of bliss and consciousness, and who is composed of both consciousness and bliss— toward those who are not devotees, that is his veiling (avaguṇṭhana).
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa with the six mantras, one should then effect the unification of the limbs with the possessor of limbs, thereby bringing about the state of nectarization.
The seat (*pīṭha*) or throne of the venerable Supreme Lord, consisting of His own powers denoted by the term "yoga," begins with the Foundation Power (*ādhāra-śakti*) and ends with the Pretas.
The middle covering consists of the quality of passion (*rajas*), and the upper covering consists of the quality of purity (*sattva*).
Having thus worshipped the *yogapīṭha* beneath the pericarp of the lotus as the seat for the *mahāpreta*, [reciting]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva, whose seat is the great *preta*.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should invoke the Blessed Lord together with his consort there: Oṃ.
O Blessed One, together with your limbs and faces, with your retinue, both in your manifest and unmanifest forms, O Lord, accompanied by the Goddesses, come, come!
Be present, be present! Be near, be near! Be firmly established!
I perform the veiling; *namaḥ*. I render [you] nectar; *namaḥ*. Thus, having invoked [the deity].
One should worship.

First, the venerable Śrī Sakalabhaṭṭāraka—possessing all faces and limbs—is to be worshipped together with Netranātha; then Aghoreśvarī; then the six limbs of the partless (niṣkala) Bhaṭṭāraka: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras); obeisance to the Lords of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśvaras)."

Having performed the concise seven-fold enclosure worship (saptāvaraṇa-pūjā) to the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras), the Mothers, the Abodes, the Nāgas, and the Weapons, and having worshipped the mantras of other desired deities as part of the retinue, [one performs] the union of mantras and the union of channels (nāḍī).

One should perform the acts of supreme identification (*paramīkaraṇa*). For example: having issued forth from one's own right nostril and entered through the left nostril of the Deity, and having reached His heart, [one reaches] His *dvādaśānta*.
Having gradually taken up the nectar, one should exit through the left side of the deity and enter one's own heart; this is the junction of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*).

Having meditated upon oneself as dissolved into the enclosure of the World Guardians (Lokapāla), that [enclosure] into the enclosure of Bhairava, that into the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), the six limbs into the Śrī Devī, the Devī into the Bhaṭṭāraka with parts (sakala), and that into the partless Bhaṭṭāraka (niṣkala)— thus one should meditate.

The conjunction of mantras: Then, having uttered the root mantra from one's own heart, by means of the sequence of piercing the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra)— [one proceeds through] A-kāra, U-kāra, Ma-kāra, Bindu,
Ardhacandra, Nirodha, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā.

Having brought [the breath] to its limit, one should establish it there in the state of Śiva at the *dvādaśānta*. Then, by that same sequence, having brought it back to the heart, one should contemplate the Lord there together with the Goddess, along with his limbs and his retinue. This is the process of supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*). Thus.

Having performed the union of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*), the union of the mantras (*mantra-saṃdhāna*), and the act of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*), one recites the Aghora-utkīlana-vidyā: *oṃ ghore juṃ thaghore | saḥ ghoraghoratare | hrīṃ sarvataḥ sarvasarve | namaste rudrarūpe astrāya phaṭ*.

Having performed the satisfaction of the spirits (*bhūtatṛpti*) and the worship of the Lord of the Field (*kṣetreśa*), and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should proceed to the vicinity of the fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*). Now, the characteristics of the fire-pit:
there, the fire-pit should be twenty-five finger-breadths in width, measured by the thumb of the teacher’s left hand.

(25) In the center, a circular pit is dug half [the width] of that [altar]. Outside of that, there are three tiers (*mekhalā*) of equal size: the upper one is four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), the one below it is three finger-breadths, and the tier below that is two finger-breadths. [The area] is square and four finger-breadths [in width].
In this way, everything is equal; all is one, measuring exactly fifty finger-breadths.

The altar is square and four finger-breadths high. Then, one should perform the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) for Vāmadeva in an abbreviated manner. Others hold that there is no separate worship of the doors in a single-shrine temple, but rather it is performed by another means; this is considered to be done with twenty-five [offerings] using the thumbs of the Guru’s right hand.
Its circular base is excavated to half its height, with three tiers of molding (*mekhalā*) rising from it;
the uppermost is four *aṅgulas* high, the middle three, and the other two likewise.
Its width at the bottom is thus [the same], and the altar (*vedi*) is four *aṅgulas* in height.
The navel, due to its nature as the form of a horse, should be nine finger-breadths in height; a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with a three-finger-breadth rim at the top is recommended for daily rites.
Now, there is another intention of the treatise.
Then, in a pit one cubit in measure, the upper girdle (mekhalā) shall be one-sixth [of the depth];
the middle [girdle] shall be two-fourths [of that], and the lowest shall be one-twelfth.
Its length and sides are likewise; there are three finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in the middle and at the tip.
The upper girdle is four finger-breadths wide, which is one-sixth of the hand's width;
that is to say, it is three finger-breadths, being one-eighth of the middle part increased by two [units].

The lower part should be twelve finger-breadths less [than the upper]. The excavation below is empty. The navel is shaped like a vulva (yoni), with its specific internal features visible within the space between the lip, the girdle, and the excavation;
it resembles the form of a horse's hoof. The navel is of this shape.
In front, there is a specific part characterized by length; on the sides, it is nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas) wide;

and in the middle and at the tip, it is six finger-breadths and three finger-breadths respectively—this is the *kuṇḍa*. This has been described in the context of a *sāhasrika* homa, meaning a sacrifice consisting of a thousand oblations.

And it is held that for ten thousand [offerings] (ayuta), the [fire-pit] should be double; "and" (ca) is used in the sense of "but. For ten thousand—that is, ten thousand [or ten thousand times ten thousand]—in the case of a homa of fifty-three ayutas, however, that which is endowed with the proper characteristics is prescribed as double; such a fire-pit is praised for a homa of one hundred thousand (lakṣa).

For a *homa* of thirty thousand up to fifty thousand, it is double [the previous size], thus four cubits (*caturhasta*). For a *lakṣa-homa*, it is double that as well, thus eight cubits. "Double" refers to the measurement of the hand (*hasta*) endowed with its characteristics, following the appropriate proportions for the girdles (*mekhalā*) and other features, like the eye of a crow (applying to both). Thus it is said.
It is stated in the *Gurupustikā* and in the *Amṛteśavidhāna*:
"In the [work] of Śrī Somaśambhu, it is said: 'The excavation should be equal to that for animal births, together with the head-line and the girdle.'"
The neck is one finger-breadth wide on the outside; according to some scriptures, it is two finger-breadths.
Outside of that, there are three girdles measuring four, three, and two *aṅgulas* respectively;
or else, there are five girdles measuring six, five, four, three, and two *aṅgulas* in sequence.
These pit-makers are considered to be six or one finger-breadth [in depth];
above them, there should be a *yoni* shaped like the middle petal of a lotus.
Its height is one finger-breadth (aṅgula), its width eight finger-breadths, and its length half the measure of the pit (kuṇḍa).
The navel, equal in depth to the neck of the pit, is shaped like the hoof of a horse and twelve finger-breadths high; [the base] is nine finger-breadths.
It is broad; six finger-breadths in the middle and three finger-breadths at the tip;
and the rim is one finger-breadth. This is the pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit. When there is an increase in materials, the pit should be two cubits; in that case, one should double everything.
"A wise man should likewise make an opening between the two girdles for the placement of the enclosure, as well as above the second girdle.
(If the fire-pit is in another's house while the water-jar is in one's own house, then [one should perform] the worship of the door...)

And one should perform the Vāstupūjā. If, however, both the water-pot (kalaśa) and the fire-pit (agni-kuṇḍa) are located in the very same house, then one need not perform the worship of the door-guardians and so forth. As it has been said:
"When the abode of the fire is elsewhere than the place of worship, then one should perform the worship of the door-guardians."
The binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) is the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*). When the fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed in the temple of the image (*arcālaya*), this [binding] is not employed;
however, others say that it must indeed be performed.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*). Having thus approached the perfected fire-pit,

Having taken the sacrificial offering from the Lord of Sounds residing in the *kalaśa*, and having performed prostrations with the sound *huḍuṅkāra*— the *huḍuṅkāra* being the synonym for the mouth-instrument, a sound consisting of the awareness of the resonance (*nāda*) manifesting through the intensity of devotion— one should sit upon the exalted seat.

"Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Self. Having thus performed the purification of the seat, one should prepare the *argha* vessel to one's right. One should worship around the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with "Oṃ, obeisance to Umā," and so forth. One should perform the worship of the door with "Gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati."

*Namaḥ* and so forth. Having thus performed the worship of the door, and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and self-worship (*svātmapūjā*), one should worship the *vidyārghya* with the root mantra together with its limbs as before. In its vicinity, one should worship the *nirodhārghya* with the root mantra alone.
(“O lady of beautiful hips, having formed fists with the thumbs placed in the middle of the palms—this is known as the *niṣṭhurā* mudrā, the ‘crying’ mudrā of the Lord.
One should display the *niṣṭhurā* mudrā; then, on one’s own right side near the navel...

With the root mantra together with its ancillaries and the Pāśupatāstra, one should prepare the *paśvargha* for the purpose of sprinkling the disciple. Nearby, one should perform the worship of the vessel of Śiva’s water with the mantra: *Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Śiva*. Thus [is the worship] of the five jars with their respective [mantras].

Having worshipped with one's own mantras: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, salutation to the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) which consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). Thus, having worshipped the sword of knowledge, [one offers] the weapon-offering (*astrārgha*) with that [sword].
One should perform the purificatory rites for the vessel and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). As follows: *Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the sprinkling, phaṭ.* (1)
(Through the specific mention of sprinkling, striking is included.
(The veiling is for the purpose of protection: "Oṃ haiṃ, I veil, huṃ.
Thus, the veiling is performed with the *liṅgamudrā*. These two purifications are direct. || 2 ||
(And these thirteen rites, beginning with sprinkling and ending with drying,

must be performed through meditative visualization— either at the time of preparing the sacrificial pit or even after it has been prepared— in order to achieve the perfection of the Supreme Lord’s form, whose essence is the power of action.)
Now, by means of meditation: Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I perform the scraping, phaṭ.
(Scraping is digging. || 3 || Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! [I perform] the removal of the soil (the clearing away of impure earth), ka. || 4 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ. Sprinkling (prokṣaṇaṃ) [is performed for the sake of purification after the gaze of supreme vision]. || 5 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ | The filling is *ka*. || 6 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ | Equalizing (the equalizing [is] the plaster), ka || 7 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ | Sprinkling (the joining with water). || 8 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! Crushing (crushing is the removal of hardness). || 9 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ. Cleansing (sammārjana) is *ka*. 10.
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ. The smearing [with cow dung]. || 11 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ. Again, perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa). Ka. 12.
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I perform the drying; haḥ phaṭ! || 13 ||
In the light.

By the contemplation that "the sacrificial pit is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) of Śiva," this indeed constitutes the supreme consecration (*saṃskāra*), even without other ritual sequences. Now, in this context, one should perform the consecration with the *astra-mantra* in order to render [the site] fit for the descent of Vāgīśvarī.

Regarding the acts of making [the site] adamantine (*vajrīkaraṇa*) and taking possession (*gṛhīkaraṇa*): in the presence of light, by the contemplation that "the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of Śiva," this indeed constitutes the supreme consecration (*saṃskāra*),
even without other ritual actions or smoke.

Thus are the consecrations of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). "Oṃ, salutation to the fire-pit, whose essence is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). With this *praṇava*, perform the worship of the fire-pit (having worshipped it with perfume and flowers). "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I consecrate the fire-pit; salutation. With this, perform the consecration using the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I perform the vajrīkaraṇa, phaṭ! || 2 ||
The vajrīkaraṇa consists of three lines drawn east-to-west using the Astra mantra, and one line facing north;
this is proclaimed as the "Vajra" [arrangement].
This task is to be accomplished by the act of scratching alone; alternatively, having thrown a single blade of *darbha* grass extending from south to north between the three previously dug lines,
one should produce the stability of the pit in the form of a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! Phaṭ! I cover both the exterior and the interior with darbha grass.
Furthermore, O Īśvarī, for the purpose of the house, that fire-pit should be covered inside and out with *darbha* grass blades pointing eastward, in order to accomplish a home free from obstacles.
Thus, both types of formative forces (saṃskāra) are likewise [to be understood]. || 16 ||

(The seat for Vāgīśī and Mahattaraka is prepared with pure cow dung. Then, to the right of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should place Brahmā, who was previously fashioned from fifty-four blades of *darbha* grass, in the center of a ball of pure cow dung. There, [one should offer] a flower.
Therein:
(On the southern side of the sacrificial pit, one should prepare a seat of pure cow dung, a grass mat,
and flowers with the syllable Om).
Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Brahmā. Then: Oṃ, O Brahmā, come, come! Be seated, be seated! Be present, be present! Be firmly established, be firmly established!
Oṃ, I veil you; obeisance! Oṃ, I render you nectar; obeisance! O Brahmā, accept the water for washing the feet; obeisance! And so forth. Now, the meditation.
Brahmā has four faces and is red in color; he is adorned with four arms, wears a black antelope skin as an upper garment, and is seated upon a lotus throne.
O Goddess, the God holds a water-pot and likewise a staff in his hand; he wears a rosary of beads, holds a lotus in his hand, and possesses beautiful eyes.
Having meditated upon him as the destroyer of all sins, one should place him upon the leaves with the mantra: *oṃ brahman sannihito bhava namaste* (O Brahmā, be present;

salutations to you). Alternatively, one may worship him with water for the feet and other offerings using: *oṃ hlāṃ bhagavate caturvedeśvarāya gāyatrīsahitāya brahmaṇe namaḥ* (Oṃ hlāṃ, salutations to the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Four Vedas, accompanied by Gāyatrī, to Brahmā).
With the two [ends] facing the east and the north, one should place a seat upon it; then a flower upon that.
One should not worship [the deity] directly in the heart.
Having invoked Vāgīśī with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, one should draw a triangle, a hexagon, and a circle; this is the seat of Vāgīśī.
Although mentioned in other scriptures, a crossroads [should be drawn] for the sake of obtaining the center of the house.
Following that, having prepared a four-way crossroads in the center of the pit with two blades of darbha grass, one should place a flower there upon a seat;
this is Vāgīśī, the supreme power of Vāgīśa.

Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Vāgīśī. Having thus performed the worship of the seat with the Praṇava, [one recites]: Oṃ hāṃ, O Blessed Vāgīśvarī! Come, come! Be present, be present! Abide near, abide near! Be firmly established, be firmly established! Oṃ, I veil [thee], salutation! Oṃ.
I make [the water] immortal, *namaḥ*. Then:
(The water for the feet is the *pādya*)—*oṃ hāṃ bhagavati vāgīśvari pādyaṃ gṛhāṇa namaḥ*. Thus.

Having worshipped with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows: *Oṃ*, [I meditate upon her] whose eyes are beautiful and dark like the petals of a blue lotus, and who possesses all the auspicious marks (*sarvalakṣaṇa*).
Complete and adorned with all her limbs.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess in this manner, one should establish her in the middle of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
lying supine like during the fertile period, with her head directed toward the northeast.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, while recollecting the *bhava-mantra*:
*oṃ hūṃ hāṃ vāgīśyai namaḥ*.
[One should worship] the Goddess, the radiant power of speech (*vāk-śakti*), who is of the nature of the *kriyā-śakti* of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

One should place her in the center; one should bind her in a state of stability. She is face-upward in the upper abode, whose nature is expansion and whose form is extension. For this very reason, she has beautiful eyes, for she is light (*prakāśa*).
Her dark-blue color, like the petal of a blue lotus, is her *māyīya* (illusory) form; her season is the time of menstruation (*ṛtukāla*).

What does he do? He [perceives] Śuddhavidyā, whose nature is fire and so forth, who is intent on generating [the universe], who is eternally connected and established within the Lord Īśāna—the Sovereign of Freedom—in His supreme form, with her head fixed in the northeastern direction; by that, he becomes [one with] each and every [aspect of] the Sakala.
"By means of the form of the breaking of Brahma and so forth"—thus [speaking], Śrī Bhava is the Niṣkala Bhaṭṭāraka; recollecting His mantra, one becomes permeated by His existence.
(Having made the middle fingers curved and positioned above the index fingers, with the ring fingers placed between them...)
In the same way, indeed, for the little finger.
"Having joined all [the fingers] together in one place and pressed them with the thumbs— this is indeed the supreme mudrā, which is known as the Yoni-mudrā. Thus,
one should worship [her] with perfumes and other offerings, [visualizing her] with the head of Īśa, face upward, and most excellent.

Having meditated, one should display the *yonimudrā* for the purpose of invoking the presence of Vāgīśī. Then, having brought fire—obtained from a fire-drill (*araṇi*), from the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*), or from the house of a twice-born (*dvija*)—one should bring the Knower of the Vedas (*jñātavedas*) [into a vessel]. [One should bring it] into a copper vessel or a clay bowl, [reciting]: "The semen of Śiva."
Having meditated thus, one should cast [the mantra] into the womb of the Vidyā.
(The flesh-eating fire of the cremation ground:
*Oṃ haḥ phaṭ*, I expel the flesh-eater here, *haḥ phaṭ*. Thus [with] a blade of Darbha grass.

Having ignited two [fires], one should cast [the remains] into the south-western fire with five oblations of sesame seeds, saying: *oṃ bhairavāgneḥ kravyādaśuddhirastu svāhā*. Having thus performed the purification from the flesh-eating spirits (*kravyāda*), one should say: *oṃ haḥ phaṭ saṃprokṣayāmi namaḥ*.
Having thus sprinkled [the water]. || 1 ||
Oṃ haiṃ, I veil [you], obeisance. Having thus veiled [it]. || 2 ||
Having worshipped with "Oṃ Raṃ, obeisance to Agni," thus [ends the third].
One should perform his worship in the form of the feet of Parāmṛtā, having meditated upon him as [the letter] ŚU. 4.
(Having performed the meditation: "This fire is indeed of the nature of the *śukra* [semen/seed].")
