Above that:
"For the protection of the newborn child, may Brahmā and the others who are worthy of worship be honored."
One should worship Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Sadāśiva with perfumes and other offerings. For example: *Oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ* in the east; *Oṃ rudrāya namaḥ* in the south; *Oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ* in the west;
*Oṃ sadāśivāya namaḥ* in the north. Thus is the worship. Thus [it is said].
Having worshipped the gods, beginning with Brahmā, upon the seat, [he worships] Agni.

The first three [mantras], and again five each for the next five [sections], and the final three should be added with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) by the preceptor for the success of the sacrifice. Having strewn *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward, arranged from south to north, and with the tips pointing northward, from the eastern to the western [directions].

Likewise, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the grass seats (*viṣṭara*). The enclosing sticks are branches one cubit in length, with their tips joined together by a knot; the seat (*viṣṭara*) is made of *darbha* grass. One should worship the world-protectors (*lokeśa*) above the girdle of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with perfumes and other offerings, as follows:
Oṃ, I meditate upon Indra, the lord of Śacī, who always holds a vajra in his hand, is mounted upon an elephant, possesses a thousand eyes, and abides by the command of Śiva.
Thus is the meditation. "O Indra, come! Come! and so forth. *Oṃ lūṃ, homage to Indra, who holds a vajra in his hand;
in the east.* *Oṃ, [I invoke] him who always holds a spear in his hand, is mounted upon a peacock, and is accompanied by Svāhā.*
In the southeast, I meditate upon the nine-tongued Fire; *oṃ rūṃ*, obeisance to Agni, who holds a spear in his hand. [Twice] in the southeast.
Likewise, [I meditate upon him] who has a staff in his hand, is black in color, and is likewise joined with Yami.
I meditate upon Yama, mounted upon his buffalo throne.

Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand; [he is] in the south. Oṃ, [I meditate upon] Nirṛti, who always holds a sword in his hand, accompanied by his goddess, seated upon a grass mat (vṛsī), for the sake of the worship of Śiva; [I] meditate upon Nirṛti in the southwest. Oṃ kṣūṃ, homage to Nivṛti, who holds a sword in his hand.
O Nirṛti! Oṃ, I meditate upon Varuṇa, the lord of the sacrifice, who holds a noose in his hand, possesses great majesty, is seated upon a crocodile throne, and is accompanied by his goddess.

Oṃ vūṃ, to Varuṇa in the west: I meditate upon Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand, is mounted upon a deer, is accompanied by his goddess, has two eyes, and is the executor of the command of Trilocana.
Oṃ yūṃ, to Vāyu, in the wind. (Sc 35; p.
34) Oṃ, [I worship] the lord of the yakṣas, who holds a mace in his hand, is mounted upon a man, is accompanied by his goddess, and is dear to Śiva.
And I meditate upon Nidhīśa and Kuvīra.
Oṃ kuṃ, to Kuvīra in the north, seven times. Oṃ, I meditate upon Īśāna, the Lord of Gods, who holds a trident in his hand, is mounted upon a bull, is the consort of Umā, and resembles pure crystal.

Oṃ sūṃ, to Īśāna, in the northeast, [svāhā] 8. Oṃ, I meditate upon the god Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand, who has four faces, who is the promulgator of the four Vedas, and who is accompanied by Gāyatrī.
Oṃ āṃ brāṃ braṃ to Brahmā in the zenith. || 9 ||
Oṃ, I meditate upon Viṣṇu, who holds a discus in his hand, who resembles a dark cloud, who is worshipped with nectar, and who is mounted upon the seat of Garuḍa.
Oṃ hlāṃ, hail to Ananta; hla, below. || 10 ||

Then, having filled a vessel prepared with *darbha* grass (*sapavitra*) on his own right and on the left of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having filled it with flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and sesame seeds, he should worship Śrī Viṣṇu therein.
(Some maintain that one should worship Viṣṇu to the right of the pit, not on one's own right; thus it has been stated.)
To the south of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and outside the seat (viṣṭara),
one should prepare the Praṇīta vessel there, filled with water.
Our teachers, however, state that one should worship Viṣṇu to the north of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus is the opinion of others.
Regarding that, the procedure for worship is as follows:
Oṃ, [I salute Him] who resembles the flax flower and who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The god wearing yellow garments and adorned with a forest garland.
Adorned with a network of tinkling bells from the rubies of his shimmering crown,
wearing divine earrings, and seated upon the throne of Garuḍa.
"I invoke Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, for the pacification of the multitude of obstacles.
Having thus performed the meditation, [one recites]:
"We know Vāsudeva; we meditate upon Lakṣmī’s half; may that Viṣṇu inspire us. (3)
Thus is the Gāyatrī. Oṃ, Blessed One Viṣṇu, come, come! [In the independent rite, on the northern part of the sacrificial pit and outside the seat, the Praṇītā vessel...]
There, one should cause a water-filled cup to be placed.
One should place there a sacred thread (pavitra) mixed with flowers, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds,
joined with the disciple’s name, accompanied by a beautiful meditation, and ending with the word "namaḥ."
One should not perform worship by placing Viṣṇu in the vocative case.
There was a seat made of *masaṃda* wood for the *rudrāśraya* grass-mat, and there was also a seat for Viṣṇu, who sits upon the destruction of the sacrifice.
Thus is the tradition of our most excellent Guru.
Santiṣṭha 2 | Sannidhatsva 2 | Sanniruddho bhava 2 | Haiṃ, I veil you; obeisance! Oṃ, I render you nectar; obeisance! O Viṣṇu!
"Welcome, O Guest, seated in the cup! Then, from the vessel for the *arghya* offering: "Oṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ, Viṣṇu, accept the *pādya*; homage! Likewise for the *ācamanīya* and the *arghya*.
[Offer] flowers, incense, and lamps. "Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Viṣṇu"—thus with the perfumes and other offerings.

One should perform worship. Having worshipped Viṣṹṇu, one should make this request: (The term "for the sake of the animal" is to be applied in the case of occasional rites; "for the purpose of the injunction of initiation" in the case of obligatory rites; and "O Blessed One, for the sake of desired results" in the case of optional rites.)

Oṃ! Whether the sacrifice has been commenced for the sake of cattle or even for the sake of the self by the practitioners, O Blessed One, may there be freedom from defects in our sacrifice through your grace.
Then, upon the flame above the *liṅga*, one should worship the Lord in the *śānti-kalaśa* (peace-pitcher), which contains water, a jar, and is provided with a seat made of seven *darbha* grasses.
[Reciting: "Oṃ, [I worship] Sudhākumbha, Vidhu, Śaiva, Vara, and Abhaya."
I meditate upon Bhairava, who is held in his hands and seated upon a lotus.
Oṃ! [I salute] the one established as Rudra, stainless, three-eyed, five-faced, with the moon as his crown-jewel,
and possessed of nine right arms and likewise nine left arms, each holding various weapons.
Adorned with a garland of human skulls, yet always graced by the wreath of the celestial river;
he is the ornament of ash that brings prosperity to all beings, the leader of the *nāgas*, worshipped by the *vināyakas*.
I take refuge for the sake of prosperity in Śiva, who is praised by the goddess Jayā with fragrant powder of moon-like sandalwood,
and who is gratified by the hymns of Nandin and the other lords of the Gaṇas.
Having thus recollected the meditation:
Oṃ, Blessed One, Sakalabhaṭṭāraka, Svacchanda Bhairava, come, come! Be present, be present! Draw near, draw near! Be firmly established, be firmly established! Haiṃ, I veil you.
*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ hūṃ amṛtīkaromi namaḥ*. Having thus rendered [the substance] immortal, [one says]: *Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Aghora-Bhairava, who is of the nature of flame and resides within the flaming liṅga;
in that Self which consists of knowledge and is of the form of pure light.*
Having meditated upon Aghoreśvarī, who is blazing like a streak of lightning,
one should worship Aghoreśvarī with the *sakala-mantra*. Then, having visualized the *saṃhitā-mantra* in that vessel as resembling a spark of blazing fire, [one worships] Śrī Bhairava.
He should announce as follows:
"Oṃ! Blessed One, even by a single glance from you, the lords of the gods seek your grace;
those who have been served by me in the sacrifice [attain it] merely through your presence."
For they become fully armed and provide protection for the sacrifice, by which means the child attains [his goal].
"O Lord, may I attain the state free from affliction through your grace.
Thus is the worship for the peace-vase (śāntikalaśa). 7.
Then follows the release of the bracelet of Vāgīśī: "Oṃ hūṃ, I perform the release of the bracelet of Vāgīśī, svāhā. [Recite] three times. "May it be accomplished," [recite] three times.
With these words, one should untie the seat (viṣṭara) previously fashioned in the form of a bracelet. || 8 ||

(Since the fetus has been born and since protection for the subsequent [period] has been prescribed, the obligation regarding the protection of the fetus has ceased; thus, there is the "releasing of the bracelet" (*kaṅkaṇa-mokṣa*).

Likewise, there are the purification of birth-impurity (*sūtaka-śuddhi*), the opening of the mouth (*vaktra-udghāṭana*), the purification of the mouth (*vaktra-śuddhi*), and the sprinkling of the mouth (*vaktra-abhighāra*).)

Having performed the eight intermediate purificatory rites—namely, the placement of the seat (*viṣṭaranyāsa*), the installation of the deities, their worship, and the release of the bracelet—the final purificatory rite called *nāmakaraṇa* (the naming ceremony) is as follows:
*Oṃ hauṃ, I perform the emergence of the fire; svāhā* (three times). Having completed [the rite], *Oṃ hauṃ*.
I perform the visualization of the Sun within the fire; svāhā! 3. It is accomplished! 3. (In this consecrated fire, which is indeed light, he speaks in order to bring about its state of Śiva.)
Likewise, O Lord of Mantras, the fire that suddenly blazes forth through the power of a true resolve becomes composed of the nature of Śiva,
because it has attained identity with the resolve of Śiva.

Likewise, by the power and majesty of the resolve— such as "Śiva is truth"— of the preceptor who, through the aforementioned method, is joined with the mantras and the Lord and has attained oneness with Him, he blazes forth just like that resolve which fulfills the intended purpose.

The meaning is that, just as fire blazes when fanned by the act of stoking, so too, through identification with Śiva who is being meditated upon, the sacrificial thread itself becomes essentially Śiva.

And saying that this has been declared by us as it was received through the lineage of gurus, and is therefore worthy of discernment, he says: "Śrī Śambhu explained this reality of purification to me; I too have shown it. O pure-minded ones, let it be entered into."
"Oṃ hūṃ, be the auspicious fire; obeisance!"—this is the request. Thus one should assign the name.
"Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the auspicious fire"—this is the worship. "Oṃ kṣaṃ, svāhā to the auspicious fire," three times. "Oṃ haiṃ, svāhā to the auspicious fire," three times. (9)
Thus, the rite known as the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) is accompanied by these intermediate purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*).
The formative forces together with the previous [consciousness] are the cause.
Then, having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā," and having gratified him with "Oṃ, svāhā to Brahmā" three times, one should ask for forgiveness: "O Brahmā, may you forgive me.
O Lord Brahmā, you have performed the protection of this Śiva-fire; now..."
One must not obstruct him; let him go directly to his own abode.
Thus, one should release the seat in the eastern direction.
Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra. Oṃ, svāhā to Rudra, three times. O Rudra, may you forgive [me].
Oṃ, O Lord Rudra, protection has been performed by you for this Śiva-fire; now you must not cause any obstruction. Go, O God, to your own abode.
One should release the southern seat.

Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. Oṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu, three times. O Viṣṇu, may you forgive me. O Lord Viṣṇu, you who are the fire of Śiva, protection has been performed by you; O All-pervading One, you must not remain obstructing [us] now. Go, O God, to your own abode.
One should release the western seat.
SC 37; p.
36) Oṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva. Oṃ, svāhā to Sadāśiva, three times. Sadāśiva, may you forgive me.
Oṃ! O All-pervading Lord, protection has been afforded by you to this Śiva-fire known as Sādākhyā;
now it must not be obstructed—go, O God, to your own abode.
Thus, one should release the upper seat: *Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Vāgīśvarī*.
This is the worship. *Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Vāgīśvarī*. O Vāgīśvarī, may you be forgiven.
Oṃ! O Śivā, who are skillful in creation, maintenance, and dissolution; O bestower of enjoyment and liberation; O Mistress of Speech, salutations to you! Go, O Goddess, to your own seat.
Thus he should dismiss [the deity].

Then, for the purpose of consuming [the oblation] in the fire, there are twenty-four fuel-sticks (samidh) each twenty-four finger-breadths long: Oṃ Hūṃ, I satiate the auspicious fire, Svāhā—[repeated] twenty-four times.
Now follows the consecration of the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles.

Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the heating [of the *sruk* and *sruva*] (the heating of the wooden ladles and so forth for the purpose of warding off worldly existence). Haḥ phaṭ. One should heat the *sruk* and *sruva* in the fire. || 1 ||
"Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the sprinkling; haḥ phaṭ. With this, one should sprinkle with the auspicious water (śivāmbhas). || 2 ||
Oṃ haiṃ, I veil [you]; with hūṃ, one should veil [it] with the armor-mantra (kavaca). || 3 ||
In the fire [recite]: "Oṃ haiṃ, I cause [it] to revolve, obeisance. One should cause it to revolve three times. || 4 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I perform the sprinkling; haḥ phaṭ! || 5 ||
The touching of its tip with the tip of a blade of darbha grass.
Oṃ haiṃ bhrāmayāmi namaḥ. One should rotate it three times. || 7 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the sprinkling, haḥ phaṭ. Thus is the sprinkling with the water of Śiva. || 8 ||
Through the middle [of the body], there is contact with the middle. || 9 ||
The fuel sticks (*samidh*) should be offered according to the sacred site (*dhāman*); they should be one cubit (*hasta*) in length and number twenty-four for the propitiation of the fire of Śiva.
With the stainless radiance [of the deity], the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) are unsplit, straight, and possessed of branches; likewise,
having colored the ritual preparations with sesame seeds, one should proceed with the ritual acts involving clarified butter (*ājya*),
beginning with the act of pouring the supreme clarified butter.
He speaks for the purpose of consecrating the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles:
Having heated the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles in the fire, one should sprinkle them with auspicious water while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).
Having veiled them with the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*), one should cause them to be whirled three times around the Śiva-fire.
One should wipe it with water using the Astra-mantra, then touch it with the Bhāga-mantra; having again whirled it over the fire, one should sprinkle those two with auspicious water (śivāmbhas).

Without touching it in the middle of the *darbha* grass, one should again heat it by rotating it over the fire; having cleansed it with the auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), one should touch it with the root-end of the *darbha*.
Then, one should place the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with their roots downward and their openings facing upward.
The wise should always worship [the deity] behind the darbha grass and to the south of the fire.
Wiping, sprinkling, and heating wood and other materials are for the purpose of removing their state as wood.

As it has been said: "One should heat them three times in fire; thus heated, they turn away from the state of being wood. Here, in the order of emanation, [this applies] to the tip of the *darbha* grass.

By touching the middle base with the tips [of the two blades] and rotating them three times, the state of consisting of the three powers—will and the rest—is produced in the *sruk* and *sruva*; "by the *sruk* and *sruva*" means by the two ladles. After the twelve purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), they are to be worshipped below.
*Mukhāvi* (with the intention of being oriented toward creation): *Oṃ haiṃ bhrāmayāmi namaḥ*. Threefold rotation. || 10 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the heating; haḥ phaṭ, the heating in the auspicious fire. || 11 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the cleansing; haḥ phaṭ. || 12 ||
Washing with auspicious waters; touching the root-mantra with the root-mantra. 13.
(Somaśambhu)
Having taken up the *śruk* and *sruva* ladles with their faces upward and downward respectively, and having heated them three times in the fire,
one should touch them with *darbha* grass at the root, middle, and tip.
On the surfaces of the *kuśa* grass, one should sequentially deposit the three principles (*tattva*) consisting of the auspicious Self-knowledge,
using the syllables *hāṃ*, *hīṃ*, and *hūṃ* for Śambhu in their respective order.
Having placed Śruci-Śakti [on the ladle] and Sruva-Śambhu [on the spoon] with the heart-mantra (hṛdayāṇu),
their necks wrapped with three threads, they should be worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
Then, one should worship them as the forms of Śiva and Śakti.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), at the root location. Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), in the middle. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), at the tip. Having turned [the two swords of knowledge] face downwards.
(Having turned the two swords of knowledge face downwards.)

(The phrase "on the right of the worshipful one and on the left of the mouth" is intended to signify the orientation toward creation; by being simultaneously connected with both through radiance and nourishment— [the former] on the right of Agni and [the latter] on the left of the Hotṛ— the state of consisting of both Agni and Soma is attained.)

Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva. Oṃ, obeisance to Śakti. Having turned [the hands] upward, [one says]: Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva and Śakti. Equal water-offering (argha) and flowers, obeisance. To the right, obeisance.
First, one should perform the cooking by placing [the vessel] upon the fire. Then follows the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya).
The placing of the clarified butter on the fire, and its placement in a consecrated vessel after it has flowed forth.
Heating the vessel is called "placing upon the fire. *Oṃ haḥ phaṭ*, I perform the sprinkling; *phaṭ*, the sprinkling with auspicious water. || 1 ||
Oṃ haiṃ, I veil [you]; huṃ, the veiling with the *liṅgamudrā*. || 2 ||
Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I heat [it] phaṭ; one should heat it with the Astra-mantra in the Śiva-fire. || 3 ||
Oṃ haiṃ, I perform the dismissal; huṃ—this is the dismissal by means of the armor-mantra (kavaca). || 4 ||
"Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I whirl [the weapon], phaṭ. Thus, one performs three whirling motions over the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Astra-mantra. || 5 ||
Oṃ hīṃ, I establish [you], obeisance! Thus one should place [the image] upon the womb[-seat]. || 6 ||
(The span from the extended thumb to the index finger is a *prādeśa*.
Taking two blades of *darbha* grass, each the measure of a *prādeśa*, shaped like a serpent’s noose (*nāgapāśa*),
with the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands, [he should offer them] three times into the clarified butter while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
One should perform the turning away [of the fire], the leaping over,
the consecration of the clarified butter (consisting of placing the butter on the fire and so forth), the placing [of the vessel] upon the fire,
and the pouring of the flowing [butter] into the consecrated vessel.
In some places, the reading is *adhiśrayam*; in that case, the meaning is "heating in the vessel which is the locus. He states the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) indicated by the word "etcetera":
"Having sprinkled the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the Weapon mantra (*astra*), one should veil it with the Armor mantra (*kavaca*) in the Śiva-fire."
It should be heated with the Astra-mantra and removed with the Kavaca-mantra, but not otherwise.
O Goddess, having rotated it three times above the *kuṇḍa*, one should place the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyapātra*) situated within the womb (*yoni*).
Heating is for the purpose of illumination in the southeastern direction; taking it out of the fire and holding it upright is for the sake of making the light more distinct. Furthermore:
"Then its overflowing and its immersion": the meaning is that one should perform the overflowing and the immersion of that clarified butter (*ājya*). To the question "By what means?", he says:
Having placed two tips of darbha grass joined at their middles with a knot the length of a span, this is prescribed as the *pavitra*; by means of it, one performs the sprinkling and the cleansing.
The *prādeśa* is the measure from the extended thumb to the index finger. To explain how this is so, he says:
Holding this purifier with the thumb and the ring finger, one should turn it away three times and likewise toward oneself three times.

By means of the weapon-mantra alone, one should perform an upward leap (*utplava*) for the removal of the insubstantial parts, and a downward plunge (*saṃplava*) for the extraction of the essential parts. Furthermore:
The illumination is by means of the fire of Śiva; the remainder is that it must be performed by the Astra-mantra alone. He explains that [as follows]:

Having taken hold of a bunch of *darbha* grass, one should gaze into the vessel of clarified butter (*ājya*). With that [grass], one should illuminate it. At this juncture, the meaning is that by gazing at the light from one's own eyes, one should make the clarified butter consist of the supreme light (*paratejomaya*). Thereafter, one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) completely.
One should consecrate the king by brandishing a flaming blade of darbha grass on all sides with the *dīpana* mantra.

Then follows the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire). How? Having recited the *dhāman* weapon-mantra, one should cast a firebrand (*ulmuka*) into the fire. Together with the root of the *dhāman*, the *paryagnikaraṇa*—the act of performing the circumambulation on all sides—is the attainment of a state of fiery radiance. Then [proceeds as follows].

One should sprinkle [the materials] with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra according to the prescribed rite. The "rite" (vidhi) consists of the mental resolve of non-difference from Śiva; furthermore, having consecrated them with the six limbs, one should effect immortality through Śiva.
The consecration by means of the partless [mantra] along with its limbs, using the Amṛta-mudrā, is itself immortality.
Thus [are performed] the sprinkling of clarified butter, the veiling, the heating, the removal, the circling, the floating upward, the floating together,
the illumination, the lustration, the circumambulation with fire, and the sprinkling known as "immortality."
Having performed the twelve preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*),
one should worship with the Bhairava-mantra by means of a single utterance,
using the partless (*niṣkala*) form alone. [This applies to] the agent, the object, the instrument, the locus, and the action.

Having performed the rites of purification for the sacrificial post, the argha-vessel, the sruk-ladle, and so forth, as well as for the sacrificial ground, the fire, the clarified butter, and other materials, one should effect the unification with the deity Bhairava, who is the nature of the recipient.

One should perform the leading forward facing east and the immersion for the purpose of removing the insubstantial portion and extracting the substantial portion. For example: *Oṃ haḥ phaṭ* (the upward movement, leading upward, and leaping up). "I perform the leaping up, phaṭ. Thus.
With the mantra, one should lead the two *darbha* blades away from oneself. (Leading them back toward oneself in the correct manner is "submerging" [*saṃplavana*]).
With the mantra: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the submerging, phaṭ," one should lead the two *darbha* blades, together with their central knot, back toward oneself. || 7 ||

Thereafter: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, phaṭ to the weapon-mantra. Having thus ignited a tuft of *darbha* grass with this weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should gaze at the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyapātra*). By gazing with the brilliance of one's own eyes, one should make the clarified butter consist of the supreme light; this is the consecration known as *āvadyotana*. (8)

Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the *nīrājana* rite, phaṭ. With that very same blazing *darbha* torch—(the *dīpa-rāja*, a lamp made of a flaming *darbha* blade)—one should perform the *nīrājana* by waving it in all directions. || 9 ||
One should cast that very flaming darbha torch, which has attained the state of being composed of radiant energy, into the fire with the root mantra:

*Oṃ hūṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the encircling with fire; obeisance*. (The encircling with fire on all sides is the attainment of the state of being composed of radiant energy. Thus one should cast it into the fire. 10
Oṃ hūṃ, I perform the sprinkling; homage! Thus is the sprinkling with the water of the weapon-mantra.
Having consecrated [the offering] with the root mantra—*oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ hauṃ haḥ*—and with the limb-mantras, one should render it nectar-like by means of the Amṛta-mudrā. || 12 ||

"Having consecrated [it] with the six-limbed [mantra], may Śiva lead [the disciple] to immortality. The consecration is performed with both the partless and the whole [mantra]. Immortality [is attained] by means of the Amṛta-mudrā.
Having thus performed the twelve purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should worship the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root-mantra. 13.
(The consecration of the clarified butter is performed) with the *naiṣkala* mantra. Then, one should perform the joining of the faces with three oblations of sesame seeds, as follows:
*Oṃ laṃ*, with the face of Sadyojāta.

(The meaning is as follows: Because the oblation consists of sesame seeds alone and the purificatory rites for the clarified butter have not yet been completed, one should rest upon the head facing west; this is because, for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), this [westward orientation] is primary.
The upward-facing mouth is known as the primary one, while the others possess the status of qualities. For one desiring liberation, the upward-facing mouth holds primacy in initiation.
*Oṃ vaṃ*, I contemplate the Vāmadeva face, svāhā. (3 times). *Oṃ vaṃ*.

With the face of Vāmadeva: *oṃ raṃ*, I contemplate the face of Aghora, svāhā! (3 times) With the face of Aghora: *oṃ raṃ*. With the face of Tatpuruṣa: *oṃ yaṃ*, I contemplate the face of Tatpuruṣa, svāhā! (3 times) With the face of Tatpuruṣa: *oṃ yaṃ*. I contemplate the face of Īśāna: *oṃ kṣaṃ*.
"svāhā" three times; thus, with sesame seeds, there are three oblations for each [deity].

Now, he speaks in order to bring about the threefold nature of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the fire: "Then," [meaning] by the offering of two *darbha* blades situated in the middle, the construction of the three paths (*vartman*), that is,
the three channels (*nāḍī*) in the form of the three pathways, must be performed.

Having uttered Bhairava by means of the three paths of the *vartman*s, one should bring about a restful repose with the vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*)— which consists of will, knowledge, and action— abiding within the three portions present in the clarified butter (*ājya*);
[this] threefold portion consists of the three abodes (*dhāma*) composed of fire, moon, and sun.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) and maintain the connection:

*Oṃ hūṃ, I perform the conceptualization of the three channels; homage.* Thus, by throwing two blades of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing eastward into the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyapātra*), the conceptualization of the three channels is established therein. In that [vessel], the clarified butter...
In the center: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Icchāśakti. Oṃ oṃ, salutation to Suṣumṇā, whose abode is fire.
Thus, in the center.

Then, on one's left: *oṃ hūṃ kriyāśaktaye namaḥ* | *oṃ saḥ somadhāmne iḍāyai namaḥ* | thus on the left. Then, on one's right: *oṃ hūṃ jñānaśaktaye namaḥ* | *oṃ juṃ sūryadhāmne piṅgalāyai namaḥ* | thus.
In the right [hand].
Then, from the fire as well: "Oṃ hūṃ, I perform the visualization of the three channels; obeisance.
Having thus placed two fuel sticks facing east in the fire, one should meditate on the three channels. There, in the middle of the fire: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the power of will (icchā-śakti). Oṃ oṃ."
Salutation to Suṣumṇā, the abode of fire.

Then, on his own right [side] is Vahni and on the left: *oṃ hūṃ kriyāśaktaye namaḥ*; *oṃ saḥ somadhāmne iḍāyai namaḥ*. Then, on his own left [side] is Vahni and on the right: *oṃ hūṃ jñānaśaktaye namaḥ*; *oṃ jūṃ sūryadhāmne piṅgalāyai namaḥ*.
p. 38) (Having thus made the clarified butter consist of the three abodes, he says "To Agni, svāhā! in order to make even the fire consist of that through its oblation.)
Then, during the bright fortnight, from the southern portion of the clarified butter, toward the south-eastern direction: Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Agni!

From the left portion of the clarified butter (ājya), into the left part of the fire: *oṃ hūṃ somāya svāhā*. From the middle portion of the clarified butter, into the middle part of the fire: *oṃ hūṃ agniṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*.
Thus for the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).
Then, during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), the Sun should be placed in the position of the Moon.
For the Sun should occupy the lunar portion; indeed, the designation "Agni" [for that position] remains as before. Of Agni...
One should indeed offer the oblation into the center of the sun.
Since you shall indeed enter into the sun at the new moon (amāvāsyā) in its center;
for example: from the southern portion of the clarified butter (*ājya*) into the southern portion of the fire—*oṃ hūṃ agnaye svāhā*;
from the northern portion of the clarified butter into the northern portion of the fire—*oṃ hūṃ sūryāya svāhā*.
From the midst of the clarified butter, into the midst of the fire: Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Agni and Sūrya!
Then, with clarified butter.
(The *prāśana* is the consumption of the future bonds and so forth; it is the laying of the fire-altar.
Oṃ hūṃ kṣaṃ, I perform the *prāśana* in the Īśāna face of Agni, svāhā, thrice. Oṃ hūṃ yaṃ, I perform the *prāśana* in the Tatpuruṣa face of Agni, svāhā, thrice. Oṃ...

HŪṂ RAṂ, I perform the consumption [of the offering] in the Aghora face of Agni, SVĀHĀ 3. OṂ HŪṂ VAṂ, I perform the consumption [of the offering] in the Vāmadeva face of Agni, SVĀHĀ 3. OṂ HŪṂ LAṂ, I perform the consumption [of the offering] in the Sadyojāta face of Agni, SVĀHĀ 3.
(The sacrificial fuel-sticks are prescribed to be eighteen finger-breadths long.

First, one should perform the *sampāta* (sprinkling of the remnants) with the root mantra together with its ancillaries upon all the substances, such as the fuel-sticks, barley, sesame seeds, and so forth. Thereafter, one should cause the disciples to behold the clarified butter (*ājya*).
For example:
Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is the supreme remover of sin. Clarified butter is the food of the gods; in clarified butter all the worlds are established.
With the mantra *vedākara*, the sacrificer, together with his wife, should joyfully show his head, which brings about sons, grandsons, and victory.
If he desires his own welfare, he should behold his own self reflected in clarified butter.
With sesame, rice, gold, silver, copper, barley, and so forth.
The twice-born should perform the consecration of the ghee according to the prescribed rite:
"Whatever sin has come upon you— whether celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial— may it all go to total destruction through contact with this ghee."
I offer this clarified butter for the sake of attaining the fruit of initiation into the six paths; obeisance!
Then, he should bestow a blessing upon all and give them a *tilaka* and a flower, [reciting]:

"Oṃ! I bind this bracelet for you, so that your mind may be fixed upon the destruction of the fear of worldly existence; through devotion to the skillful, immovable, and stainless [Lord], may there be the attainment of the eternal state, free from rebirth."

May the divine Śiva protect your out-breath and in-breath, your eyes, ears, nose, mind, head, and hands—whatever has been taken up even in your primordial nature. May the blessed Lord Śiva, the remover of sin, grant you auspiciousness; and may the hosts of all beings be for your welfare.
May Nārāyaṇa protect my heart with effort.

(From the word "etcetera" [ādi], it is understood that those rites beginning with the initiation ceremony [upanayana] which are established for the child and ending with the instruction in the Veda, as well as marriage and so forth, conclude at that point.)

Then, having recollected the visualization as "kheṭaka" in the left [hand], the full offering (pūrṇā) should be given: *oṃ hūṃ śvāgneḥ cūḍādyāḥ brahmacāri-vratāntāḥ sarve saṃskārāḥ saṃpūrṇāḥ santu vauṣaṭ svāhā*. Thus is the full offering.
Then, on the following day, having taken out the fire for the sake of the milk into a new vessel—(as it is said:

"The *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings are [prepared] in the fire consecrated by the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*); the *homa* is performed in the Śiva-fire when it has not been summoned, but in the Śiva-fire when it has been invoked").

Oṃ haiṃ, I envelop you, huṃ! Having thus enveloped [the vessel], one should place it so that it is well-protected, so that on the following day the preparation of the milk-rice oblation (kṣīracaru) may be successfully accomplished without being harmed by fire.
Furthermore, the worship of the cup-vessels is as previously described.

Then, for one desiring worldly enjoyment, the Sadyojāta face [is primary]; for one desiring liberation, the Īśāna face [is primary]. It is taught that the upper face is the principal one, while the others possess a secondary status; for one who desires liberation through initiation, the upper face holds primacy.
Having first meditated upon the five faces, one should resolve that whichever face is desired for a particular rite shall be the principal face.
Having conceived the primary face, one should then worship the flame of the tongue upon the liṅga as follows:
Oṃ, obeisance to Prabhā; obeisance to Dīpti; obeisance to Prakāśā; obeisance to Arcā.
"Salutation to Marīcī, to Stāpinī, to Ruci, to Karālā, and to Lelihānā.
Thus one should contemplate the nine tongues as being in the form of flames upon the Jvālā-liṅga. Then, one should worship those tongues with the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Oṃ, obeisance to Rājyārthā in the east; Oṃ, obeisance to Dāhajananyā in the southeast; Oṃ, obeisance to Mṛtyudā in the south; Oṃ, obeisance to Śatrukāriṇyā in the southwest;
Oṃ, obeisance to Vaśīkartrī in the west; Oṃ, obeisance to Uccāṭinī in the northwest. Oṃ.
"Oṃ, salutation to Dhanadā in the north; Oṃ, salutation to Muktidā in the northeast; Oṃ, salutation to Sarvasiddhipradā in the center.
Thus, the oblation (homa) is performed with [the mantra] ending in svāhā.
Oṃ rājyārthāyai svāhā, and so forth.
Having recollected the meditation with "Oṃ madhyaprāṇa," [one recites]: "Oṃ hūṃ, I fashion the tongues of Agni, vauṣaṭ. This is the single *apūrṇā* offering.

Having recollected the visualization with "Oṃ, in the left [hand] is the shield," one says: "Oṃ hūṃ, may the presence of the tongue of Agni be here, svāhā vauṣaṭ. This is the second full oblation (pūrṇā).
Then, having grasped the tip of the flame imagined as consciousness through the heart-mantra, *oṃ hāṃ sṛṅgṛhṇāmi namaḥ*,
and having taken it in by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) through the left nostril, one unifies it with the fire of consciousness residing in the heart.

Having made Bhairavī one's own through meditative absorption, she should go to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). There, having milked the two-breasted Anaṅgadhenu and churned her milk, one should visualize that the ghee of separation has emerged; then, taking that ghee, one descends into the heart.

When the fire of consciousness has become one with the external flame of fire within the heart, [one should offer oblations] with the mind, ending with "svāhā," O Aghora (according to the *Svatantrecara*).
Now, he carries out what was proposed— that one should first perform the supreme consecration of the fire and then visualize Ananta and the others—
by stating: "Having grasped the tip of the flame with the heart-mantra, [one should place] the fire-consciousness imagined [there] into the Self residing in the heart."
Having thus resolved, one should then mentally construct the yoga-pīṭha.
Following the middle of the tongue, one should meditate on the stalk reaching from the fire-abdomen lotus-root bulb up to the heart,
and there one should contemplate a lotus.
Having meditated upon the tip of the flame as being conceived in the form of the consciousness of fire,
and having grasped it with the heart-mantra through the nostrils, one should assimilate it by means of its unification with the fire of consciousness residing in the heart,
thereby transforming it into Bhairava— both the external fire and the subtle body.

To manifest his state of Bhairava—according to the principle stated in the *Mataṅga* that "his own powers flash forth everywhere as yoga"—one should conceive for him a seat consisting of power (*śaktirūpam āsanam*), beginning from the *yogapīṭha* and ending with Sadāśiva. How so? [It is said: "with the tongue in the middle."
One should visualize there the infinite [Maṇḍala], endowed with eight petals, white in color, and of great splendor,
extending from the Dharma-wheel to the feet.
And [the sequence] from Oṃ to Śiva; this has already been explained. Then, one should fashion the form of Agni, which was previously bound by means of the syllable itself. Furthermore:
The crest-lock (śikhā) which resides in the heart, one should again unfasten with the eyebrow-center (dhruva);
by means of exhalation (recaka), one should cast it into the fire—that is the form whose nature is Bhairava.

One should nail that [impurity] with the *dhruva* mantra, which is partless (*niṣkala*), and having unified it with one's own consciousness as Bhairava, one should extract it. Then, through the right nostril, one should cast it into the external fire-form (*vahnimūrti*). In this way, their form becomes identical with Bhairava. Now:
Having thus conceived [the deity] as having become incarnate and endowed with thirty-eight kalās,
one should perform the visualization for purification and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) at the time of initiation, O fair-faced one.

The thirty-eight *kalās* previously mentioned— intended as indicators for the *daṇḍa*, *vaktra*, *bhaṅgī*, and so forth— are the path to be purified (*śodhyādhvan*), by means of which the venerable Guru now desires to perform initiation. Having done thus...

Having worshipped Bhairava according to the ritual procedure prescribed in the scriptures— meaning, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with mantras through the sequence of offering water for honor (argha) and so forth mentally, up to the end of the enclosures as described— one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Oṃ hūṃ! Blazing with the oblation of dharma and adharma, with the mind as the ladle, I offer the eternal fluctuations of the senses within the revolving channel of the *suṣumṇā*—svāhā, vauṣaṭ!

Having thus performed the mental *homa*, that fire of consciousness (*caitanyānala*) is made into Bhairava. Just as by meditating on the shield in the left [hand], one should remember the form of Bhairava as the fire of consciousness within the heart-lotus and worship it with mental offerings such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth.

In this way, having made the fire of external objects into the fire of consciousness, one should mentally arrange the seat— beginning with Ananta and ending with Sadāśiva— as the Yoga-pīṭha known as "Bestower of All Siddhis," following the central tongue (the middle channel), in order to bring about the state of Bhairava for the subtle body. One should do so by means of the mind.
The meaning is that one should meditate according to the prescribed rule. For example:
following the central tongue [of the lotus], at the navel, "Oṃ, salutation to the bulb (kanda).
From the navel up to the heart, "Oṃ, salutation to the stalk (nāla). At the heart is a white eight-petaled lotus.
Upon those petals: *Oṃ vāmāyai namaḥ*, *jyeṣṭhāyai*, *raudryai*, *kālyai*, *kalavikaraṇyai*, *balavikaraṇyai*, *sarvabhūtadaminyai*. In the center:
*manonmanyai namaḥ*. Having thus meditated upon the deities, [one offers] *oṃ dharmāya namaḥ*.

Having visualized these sandals— white, red, yellow, and black— as representing knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and [the absence thereof]; and having visualized these "limbs" (*gātraka*) in the form of the panels of the lion-throne as representing unrighteousness (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*).
Oṃ! To the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda—these [I join] with the sandals of my limbs. (Sc 41; p. 40)
Having visualized them in the form of ritual stakes (kīlaka): Oṃ, salutation to the Kṛta Yuga, the Tretā Yuga, the Dvāpara Yuga, and the Kali Yuga;
Oṃ, salutation to the lower covering, which is the quality of darkness (tamas); to the middle covering, which is the quality of passion (rajas);
to the upper covering, which is the quality of goodness (sattva); Oṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva, whose seat is the great corpse (mahāpreta).

Salutation! Having visualized these [deities] beneath the pericarp of the lotus: *Oṃ hāṃ namo 'gnimūrtaye*. (According to the *Śrī-svacchanda*, with the *Haṃsa*-syllable, the *Praṇava*, and likewise with the *Oṃ* syllable ending in *Śiva*, one should propitiate the form of Agni. Thus, the form of Agni.
I have fashioned it by means of the Imperishable.
Having uprooted the flame previously established in one's own heart by means of the *niṣkala* mantra,
one should, through exhalation (*recaka*) via the right nostril, cast it into the external fire upon the visualized seat;
in this way, this form of fire becomes identical with Bhairava.

Having thus conceived the fire as having become manifest in form, endowed with the thirty-eight *kalās*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the path to be purified (*śodhyādhvan*). For example:
"Homage to the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*), to the path of words (*padādhvan*), to the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), and to the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*)."
Having thus performed the placement of the paths to be purified— namely the path of reality (*tattvādhvan*) and the path of limited powers (*kalādhvan*)— one should worship Bhairava,
together with his Goddess, his retinue, and his limbs, by means of the mental rite, beginning with the offering of water (*arghya*).
Then, with clarified butter:

*Oṃ laṃ*, I offer the face of Bhairava known as Sadyojāta into the fire of Śiva at the Sadyojāta face; *svāhā* (three times). *Oṃ vaṃ*, [I offer] the face of Bhairava known as Vāmadeva into the fire of Śiva...

Oṃ vāṃ, I unite the face of Bhairava known as Vāmadeva with the face of Śiva-Agni known as Aghora; svāhā! (3) Oṃ raṃ, I unite the face of Bhairava known as Aghora with the face of Śiva-Agni known as Aghora; svāhā! (3) Oṃ yaṃ, I unite the face of Bhairava known as Tatpuruṣa with the face of Śiva-Agni known as Tatpuruṣa.
Svāhā 3. Oṃ kṣaṃ, I unite the face called Īśāna-Bhairava with the face of Śiva in the northeast; svāhā 3. The same applies to the tongues.
Oṃ laṃ! I unite the tongue of the Bhairava face known as Sadyojāta with the Śiva-fire in the tongue of the Sadyojāta face; svāhā! (3 times).
Oṃ vaṃ! [I unite] the tongue of the Bhairava face known as Vāmadeva with the Śiva-fire...

I join the tongue of the face called Vāmadeva to the tongue of the face of Śiva’s Aghora-fire; svāhā! 3. Oṃ raṃ, I join the tongue of the face of Bhairava named Aghora to the tongue of the face of Śiva’s Aghora-fire; svāhā! 3.
Oṃ yaṃ! I unite the tongue of the Bhairava face called Tatpuruṣa with the Śiva-fire of the tongue of the Vāmadeva face; svāhā, thrice.
Oṃ kṣaṃ! [I unite] the tongue of the Bhairava face called Īśāna with the Śiva-fire of Īśāna.

"Oṃ, [I] join [myself] to the tongue of the mouth, svāhā"—three times for each. Then, the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*). First, having meditated upon one's own self and the fire of Śiva as being one and the same: "Oṃ hūṃ, I go forth, namaḥ. Then...
Having recited the root mantra, which is the heart of Agni, one should exit through its south, proceed to the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
enter through its north, and exit through its south; thus, one should mentally follow the sequence of entry and exit for the deity throughout all the enclosures (āvaraṇas).
Therefore, there should be a junction of the channels; he says this:
Having recited the root mantra, she emerged with the fire; one should then unite her, who is seated upon the sacrificial mound and joined with Śiva, as a single essence.
Having recited the root mantra through visualization from the heart of the fire, one should exit by its right side,
enter the sacrificial ground or the seat by the left, and exit again by the right;
having followed this sequence for all the mantras of the protective enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), one should enter by the left side of the fire.
"Of one meaning" means non-different, consisting of the glorious Svacchandabhairava, which is the form of the deity who is the signified. (Sc 42;

"One should enter through the left of the fire"—this refers to the junction of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). As for the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*): it should be produced from a sacrificial tree, stripped of its bark, free of blemishes, auspicious, one *prādeśa* in length, and in thickness it is prescribed to be slightly greater than the little finger; these are for the kindling of the fire.

O Seven-faced One of excellent countenance, one should perform the oblations; thereafter, for the sake of inflaming the fire, one should perform the *siddhahoma* with seven oblations each. In that regard, there is a group of seven for Aghora and Aghorīśvarī in their aspect as partless (*niṣkala*), as well as for the faces, the limbs, the goddesses, Bhairava, the world-protectors, Gaṇeśa, and the others.
Three each should be given, as they are not distinct from one another.
If there is an excess of days, then one should perform the *dravyahoma* of food and other materials for Gaṇeśa and the others.

(Having made a mandala on one's right, having taken down the vessel [with *oṃ hūṃ saṃpātaṃ karomi svāhā*], and [having offered] the sacrificial porridge [with *carau*] and the fire [with *hā agnau*]). When only a few days remain, it should be done exactly in that manner.

Then, for the sake of bestowing grace, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root mantra to effect the rite— [first the oblation of wood, then the oblation of grain, and then the oblation of clarified butter]— turning away from [any lack of] favor.
(In the *Svatantre*— )
O fair-faced one, one hundred and eight oblations of pure clarified butter should be offered to Bhairava;
one-tenth of that amount should be offered to the consort of his face,
and one-tenth of that again to the eight Bhairavas and the world-protectors.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-half for the Goddess and Bhairava, and with a tenth part for the faces, limbs, the eight Bhairavas, the world-protectors (lokeśas), and so forth. Then, one should offer three full oblations (pūrṇāhutis).
Having recited the root mantra, one should cause a single full oblation to be offered.
For the purpose of satisfying the entire wheel of mantras, he says that one should offer a second full oblation even beyond that, for the sake of primarily satisfying the root [mantra].
Likewise, one should pour out the full oblation for the purpose of nourishing Bhairava; even more than that.
Furthermore, for the purpose of correcting what is deficient or excessive, and for making [the ritual] free from flaws.
The remainder [of the instruction] is that one should pour out the full [offering] with the root mantra alone.
The making of it leak-proof is for the purpose of preventing deficiency or excess.
First, the visualization; then: *oṃ hūṃ sarvamantracakratṛptir astu svāhā*.

*vauṣaṭ*. This is the first. Then the second: *oṃ vāme kheṭaka* (Oṃ, [O Goddess] with the shield in the left hand). *oṃ hūṃ bhairavāpyāyanam astu svāhā vauṣaṭ*. This is the second. Then the third: *oṃ madhyaprāṇa* (Oṃ, [O Goddess] of the central breath). *oṃ hūṃ nyūnātirikta-vidhipūraṇam* (Oṃ hūṃ, may there be the fulfillment of any deficiency or excess in the ritual procedure).

"…cāstu svāhā vauṣaṭ. Thus, three full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, having brought fire from another source, performed the *vaiśvadeva* rite, and offered the food offering (*naivedya*), [one should recite] "Āloke..."
That awakening which is above, reflected in the sacrificial pit, is the fire;
the vital breath is the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; and the essence of consciousness, consisting of volition, is the clarified butter.
Having thus understood from the beginning the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva), the clarified butter (ājya), and the mantras,
one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) after restraining them within the fire of awakening at the dvādaśānta.

Having first reflected upon this: that fire which, while situated above in the state of perfect awakening, is by its very nature reflected below in the sacrificial pit; and likewise, that vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is of such a nature—these two constitute the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; and that essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*), whose nature consists in the reflective awareness of duality, is the clarified butter (*sneha*). Having thus contemplated, at the outset...

Having firmly restrained the [elements] beginning with the *kuṇḍa* up to the *dvādaśānta* within the fire of awakening (*vibodhāgni*), and having brought about a state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) there at each stage through the process of ascent— [an ascent] which consists primarily of the reflection— one should cast the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) so that these external things, which consist primarily of reflections, descend further and further downward.

It should remain so. Now, anticipating the objection—"If the original object (bimba) is situated higher and higher, the reflection (pratibimba) would have to be situated lower and lower; what kind of logic is this?"—the author provides an illustration while internalizing that doubt.
For just as a swan flies up into the sky, its reflection sinks into the water;
such is the principle here as well.
"Bimba" means the form of the reflection.
Having performed [the recitation] up to "O Blessed One, free from disease," one should perform the worship of the Guru and the Brahmins.
Just as [in the previous rite], one should recite "To that Maheśa," etc., and other Gāyatrīs.

"From this day forward," and so forth: "For the sake of attaining the fruit of initiation, I shall perform the worship of the Guru Śiva, as well as the deities worshipped during the previously mentioned jar-sacrifice (kalaśayāga).
One should perform [this] daily in this sequence, beginning with the seat (āsana) and ending with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Having performed that—
One should offer the full oblation.
Oṃ! To the one whose chest is adorned with a captivating necklace, whose wide eyes are the ornaments created by the Lord of the Earth,
who has five faces, who is radiant with white luster, whose crest is decorated with a peacock feather,
and who holds aloft a noose, an arrow, a bow, an excellent khaṭvāṅga staff, a vīṇā, and a bell.
I meditate upon the Blessed One as he strikes here with his staff and club, holding in his nine left arms a sword,
a goad, an arrow, the gesture of fearlessness, a skull-cup, a hand-drum, a trident,
a thunderbolt, and an axe; and in his nine right arms, he bears these same objects.
The upper face of the deity is white, the one in front is yellow,
the right is dark blue, the left is red, and the western face is beautiful with white luster.
One should thus meditate upon him, who is adorned with the appearance of the lord of the world, the bull-bannered Śiva.
[And] even the goddess Aghorīśvarī seated upon her lap. Oṃ hūṃ!
May there be the fulfillment of the rite for the cessation of the expiation for actions performed whether deficient or excessive; svāhā vauṣaṭ. Thus is the full oblation (pūrṇā).

Then, having performed the offerings to the quarters (*digbali*), the propitiation of the spirits (*bhūtatarpaṇa*), and so forth, and having offered the *arghya* for the restraint of the breath (*camyanirodha*)— where "restraint" means remaining there without wavering— one should spend the remainder of the day diverting oneself with stories of Śiva. This constitutes the ritual duties of the first day on the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
The ritual procedure for the first day.
Oṃ, salutation to the venerable Guru, whose nature is that of Supreme Śiva.

Oṃ. Then, on the second day, having performed the worship of the water-pot (*kalaśa*) at dawn as previously described, one should proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). There, having worshipped the seat with "Salutation to the Seat of the Self" (*ātmāsanāya namaḥ*), one should worship the vessel for the weapon-offering (*astrārgha-pātra*). [One should also worship] the deities of the door and the deities of the directions.
Having performed worship; having worshipped the water for the *arghya* of the bound souls (*paśu*) according to the rules, as well as the water of Śiva (*śivāmbu*).
[Offering] "Obeisance to the planets" (*grahabhyo namaḥ*) on one's right; "Obeisance to the gurus" (*gurubhyo namaḥ*) on one's left;
"Obeisance to the seat of the yoga-throne" (*yogapīṭhāsanāya namaḥ*) in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having worshipped Śiva there along with his retinue (*sāvaraṇa*).
Then, at the base of the sacrificial pit, upon a clump of *kuśa* grass: *oṃ hūṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*.
Then, one should perform the worship of the world-protectors (lokapālas) in order, starting from the east as before.
Then, in a very fine cup (camasa): *oṃ hūṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*.
Then, upon the jar above the flaming liṅga: *oṃ hūṃ śāntikumbhāya namaḥ*. Thus.
Having performed the worship in brief.
Then, with sesame seeds: *oṃ hūṃ brahmaṇe svāhā* (three times); *oṃ hūṃ viṣṇave svāhā* (three times); *oṃ hūṃ rudrāya svāhā* (three times); *oṃ hūṃ īśvarāya svāhā* (three times);
*oṃ hūṃ sadāśivāya svāhā* (three times). Then, for the occasional rite (*naimittika-vidhāna*), with sesame seeds: *oṃ*.
"HŪṂ! O Bhairava, be present in the fire of Śiva; svāhā!

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds, and having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations with the root mantra for the sake of the occasional rite (*naimittika-vidhāna*), one should then perform the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*).

Having applied the *tilaka* to all [the disciples], one should cause them to behold the clarified butter (*ājya*). Reciting: "I offer this clarified butter for the sake of attaining the fruit of initiation on the six paths;
*namaḥ*," and meditating upon the visualization of the shield (*kheṭaka*) in the left hand.

Oṃ hūṃ! May there be satisfaction for the entire wheel of mantras of the Śiva-fire; svāhā vauṣaṭ! Oṃ hūṃ! To the Śiva-fire, svāhā (three times). Oṃ hūṃ! May there be the presence [of Bhairava] in the Śiva-fire of Bhairava; svāhā vauṣaṭ!
Thus concludes the *pūrṇā*. Then, having brought the sacrificial pap (*caru*) together with fish and meat, one should perform the *sampāta* offering.
Reciting "Oṃ hūṃ, I perform the *sampāta*, svāhā," [one offers] into the fire; reciting "he," [one offers] three times into the *caru*.

Having performed the *sampāta* in this manner, and having offered the *naivedya* to the *kalaśa*, the *yaga*, and the fires, this is the procedure for every day from the time of the commencement until the conclusion of the initiation rite (*dīkṣākarma*). On that day [of the initiation] itself, however, there is no food-oblation (*annahoma*) on other days; at the beginning, there is first the fuel-oblation (*samiddhoma*).

Thereafter follows the oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*). Then follows the oblation of barley and rice (*yava-taṇḍula-homa*): *Oṃ hūṃ, may there be the presence of the entire wheel of mantras (*sarva-mantra-cakra*) for the initiation rite (*dīkṣā-vidhi*) of [Name]; svāhā vauṣaṭ*.
At the conclusion of the food-oblation (*anna-homa*), there is no application of the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) on that day. Herein...
The oblation is to be performed using only milk.
(Āloke—
Then, the sacrificial oblation (caru) is to be prepared with fire previously established and consecrated by the recitation of mantras.)

He consecrates [the oblation] with a mantra, as it has been said: "The sacrificial porridge and cakes are to be offered when the fire has been purified by the five purificatory rites; however, the oblation is performed in the Śiva-fire even if it has not been formally invoked."
Now follows the procedure for preparing the *caru* offering (the ritual performance).

There, having washed a flawless vessel with auspicious water, [one should perform the veiling rite] with "Oṃ haiṃ, I veil you, namaḥ hūṃ" and thus veil it. Then, having anointed it with sandalwood paste and other substances, [one should say]: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to this vessel, the cooker of the six flavors. (Thus.)

One should fumigate with refined incense. Reciting: *oṃ haiṃ, I bind a thread around the neck of the vessel, huṃ namaḥ*, one should tie the thread around its neck. Upon a circular mandala made of darbha grass and sprinkled with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), one recites: *oṃ anantāya namaḥ*.
And so forth.
(In the *Svatantra*: "Then one should cook the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). Should one cook it oneself, or have someone else cook it? How so? [One should prepare] the pot..."

Having taken it up and washed it with auspicious water from a vessel of *nirvāṇa*, one should veil it with the *kavaca* [mantra]. One should smear it with sandalwood and other unguents and fumigate it with refined incense. O lady of excellent vows, one should bind it around the neck with a thread that has become the *varma* [mantra]. Then...
Of the pot.
O Dear One, one should fashion the maṇḍala with *darbha* grass in the form of the weapon-mantra; having sprinkled it with the auspicious waters of Śiva, one should veil it with the armor-mantra.
One should arrange the seat there, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva. And there,
one should place the vessel which has become the embodiment [of the deity], and worship Bhairava residing therein,
together with his three enclosures (āvaraṇas), using perfumes and flowers in due order, by means of mental application.
With flowers of pure being, O fair-faced one.
Since the sacrificial pit (*caru*) might become tasteless due to being mixed with flowers and other such things, worship is not mentioned here [in this context] (cf.
Then, having sprinkled the hearth (*culi*) with the *śaṃ* mantra and with the *astra* mantra, one should worship it just as one would the sacrificial fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is intended as an indicator for the subsequent consecrations mentioned in the context of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, having placed the vessel upon the fire, one should subsequently set the fire beneath it;
then, having sprinkled with the water of Śiva the milk previously prepared and extracted, as well as the rice grains, into the vessel.
Having cast it [into the fire] with the mantra recited one hundred and eight times, one should cook it gently.
O Goddess of the Gods, with a single-pointed mind and composed,
one should proceed slowly so that the vessel does not break; and therein,
one should perform the shaking, opening, and other such acts with the *astra* mantra.
"One should cause [it] to be made" means by a disciple who has been previously initiated.

*Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Sadāśiva*—ending thus. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the series of seats beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva, one should [place] the vessel (*sthālī*), which constitutes the [divine] form (*mūrti*), upon that.

Having established [the deity], one should worship Bhairava there— along with his retinue of face-manifesting limb-bhairavas (*vaktrāṅga-bhairava*) and his retinue of weapon-bearing world-protectors (*sāstra-lokapāla*)— with mental flowers (*bhāvapuṣpa*) or with rice grains. (The reason for using "mental flowers" is so that the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) does not become unpalatable due to being mixed with physical flowers and other such items.)
[The section on] Worship: There, the fire is [placed] on the hearth to the right, or facing west or south;

the consecration (*saṃskāra*) is performed as in the case of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). From the *argha* vessel of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), it is as follows: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I perform the sprinkling; haḥ phaṭ. Thus, the sprinkling is done with the weapon-mantra. Oṃ haiṃ.
"Avaguṇṭhayāmi namaḥ. Having thus veiled [the site], [he says]: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ;

I perform the scraping here, haḥ phaṭ. In this same manner, [he performs] the removal of earth, the sprinkling, the filling, the leveling, the watering, the pounding, the sweeping, and the smearing again.

"I perform sprinkling and drying: *haḥ phaṭ*. Having thus consecrated [the vessel] and empowered it by reciting the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should place the pot upon it after wiping it with cow-butter (*gavyājya*) over which the mantra has been recited seven times. Below that, on the previous day...
The fire extracted from the hearth and kept separately: *Oṃ hūṃ raṃ, I cast the fire;

hūṃ haḥ phaṭ*. With this, one should cast the fire into the hearth. Although these two purificatory rites, beginning with the spreading of grass beneath the hearth, [are prescribed], they apply to all sacrificial sessions (*stakeṣu*).

Nevertheless, it must be examined, because it is seen in scriptures such as the *Sutratantra*, the *Tantrāloka*, and the manuscripts of the gurus, and because it is absent from our own guru-lineage and because it is contradictory.
Oṃ hūṃ, I satisfy the moving fire, svāhā! [Recite] ten times with the *ānya* vessel. Then, having rinsed the rice four times and sprinkled the milk with auspicious water, [recite]: Oṃ haḥ.
"Phaṭ! I wash; homage! Having thus purified the milk with the Astra-mantra through a cloth filter, one should pour it into the vessel, reciting:
"Oṃ haiṃ, I cast [the essence] into the water and milk, huṃ, homage. Then, one who has previously received initiation should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
One who has obtained the power of the mantra.

Being composed and one-pointed in mind, or in his absence, one born of that same lineage performing the recitation (*japa*), he should cook it very slowly. With the mantra: *oṃ haiṃ kriyāśaktyātmikāṃ darvīṃ veṣṭayāmi huṃ namaḥ*, he should tie a thread around the ladle (*darvī*). Then: *oṃ haḥ phaṭ*.
"I perform the shaking, opening, and so forth, phaṭ. Thus, one should not have the shaking, opening, and so forth performed by the hand of one previously initiated.

In the rite for a single disciple, one should take five handfuls (*prasṛti*) of rice; likewise, by increasing it by one handful at a time, one should prepare three [handfuls] more. And in that regard, having reflected that there is danger of disease if it is uncooked and danger of death if it is burnt, one should perform it well.
One should cook it.

Then, once the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) has been steamed, one should perform three oblations with the three limbs (*aṅga-mantras*)—consisting of sprinkling the heated clarified butter (*taptābhighāra*), spreading it over the fire (*agnivyāpti*), and pouring the nectar of the *caru* as an ignition (*uddīpana*)—in order to pacify the defect of insufficient steaming. One should pour half of the *caru* with the *sruva* ladle, but not into the fire, as follows: *Oṃ hāṃ*.
*Oṃ sutapto bhava svāhā* (3 times). *Oṃ hīṃ sutapto bhava svāhā*. *Oṃ hūṃ sutapto* (3 times). *Oṃ haiṃ sutapto* (3 times). *Oṃ hauṃ sutapto* (3 times). *Oṃ haḥ sutapto* (3 times).
Thus is the *taptābhighāra-homa* performed with the *sruva* ladle.
O Dear One, one should offer the heated oblation while the limbs are not yet perspiring; one should sacrifice with three portions of clarified butter at a time using the *śruva* ladle.

This [grain] has been heated by the pervasive fire and sprinkled with clarified butter (*ājya*)— the nectar-like pouring that serves to kindle it. In accordance with the meaning of the verbal root, this [process],
consisting of offerings made from the vessel with mantras ending in *svāhā*, results in the state of being well-cooked, which serves to destroy defects.
Having drawn a mandala on the ground, one should cause [the vessel] to descend with the syllable *praṇava*;
then, having smeared the pot with clarified butter, one should perform the *śītāghāra* oblation.
With the Bhairava-mantra consisting of six limbs and joined with the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, [one should perform the rite].
By the pervasion of Soma, "it is cool"; for the destruction of the *doṣas*, there is excessive sweating.
In this interval, having uttered "svā" over the sacrificial food (*caru*) and "hā" over the fire, one should offer the oblation—so say the venerable Gurus. Thus.
And the sacrificial pap (*caru*) consisting of Agni and Soma is perfected through consecration (*saṃskāra*). As it is stated in the *Śruti*:

"Whoever offers that oblation consisting of Agni and Soma as clarified butter (*ājya*), for him that [offering] becomes immortal. Also in the *Mṛgendrottara*: "These two streams consist of the nature of Agni and Soma."

The two *carus* have been prepared; for the attainment of immortality, they should come from Agni and Soma. One should pour the *caru* [into the vessel]. Then, on the ground to the right of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), upon a *maṇḍala* with *darbha* grass, one should lower the vessel [with the mantra]: "Oṃ hīṃ, I lower the vessel; obeisance. Having thus lowered the vessel, [one recites]: "Oṃ lāṃ..."

"I smear; obeisance. This is the mantra for smearing. Having performed the smearing, one should offer oblations with the root mantra joined with the six limbs and the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, using cool clarified butter (*śītābhighāra*)—which is like the pervasion of Soma—to alleviate the heat and distress caused by the afflictions. [The word] "svāhā" is used for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).

[Offering] into the fire: as follows—into the sacrificial porridge (caru): *oṃ hūṃ svaśīto bhava vaṣaṭ svaḥ*. Into the fire: *hā*. *oṃ hāṃ svasīto bhava vaṣaṭ svāhā* (three times). *oṃ hīṃ svaśīto bhava vaṣaṭ svāhā* (three times).

(Having prepared the maṇḍala near the sacrificial pit, one should lay down a seat of darbha grass; having placed the cooking vessel upon it, one should perform the *sampāta* oblation while reciting the collection of mantras.)
One should cause each individual [offering] to fall as a single oblation with the Bhairava mantra.

That which is partless (*niṣkala*) is preceded by the utterance of its limbs and faces; first, "svā" in the fire, then having uttered "hā," which consists of the vowels and the four oceans, one should offer oblation—this is the sequence for the *sampāta*.
(Oṃ hūṃ svasīto bhava vaṣaṭ svāhā 3. Oṃ haiṃ svaśīto bhava.)
Vaṣaṭ svāhā 3. Oṃ hauṃ, be cool yourself, vaṣaṭ svāhā 3. Oṃ haḥ, be cool yourself, vaṣaṭ svāhā 3.
Then, on a small mandala made of darbha grass to his right, near the earrings, he should place the seat-pedestal [with the mantras]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti; Oṃ, obeisance to the Yogapīṭhāsana.
Then, having whirled the vessel over the fire, he should place it upon the mandala.
With the partless [mantra] and the one with limbs and faces, one should perform the *sampāta* offering with each individual oblation.
(In the *Āloka*:
"Thus, in the fire, *svāhā*—this is the portion of Soma; *nicarau hā*—this is the nature of Agni from Soma...")
And a portion should be set aside by which both [substances] become of the nature of Agni and Soma. For example:
*oṃ hūṃ saṃpātaṃ karomi svā*—thus over the fire; *hā*—thus over the sacrificial porridge (*caru*); *oṃ hāṃ*.

(With lights)
He demonstrates the etymological significance of the word *sampāta*:

"Because of the simultaneous convergence (*ekānusandhāna*) of the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment at the moment of falling (*pātataḥ*), and because of their mutual falling together (*saṃpātāt*) into one another, it is thus called *saṅgama* (union). Herein, the meaning is that of simultaneity."
The meaning of *vaya* is the sense of "union" (*saṅga*), which is the collective meaning [of the syllable]. Oṃ vaṃ, may there be fulfillment. Oṃ laṃ, may there be fulfillment.

Again, recollecting the supreme nectar while performing one hundred and eight recitations of the Niṣkala mantra, one should cast the oblation of clarified butter into the *caru* itself; thus the *caru* becomes of the nature of Agni and Soma. (In this context, he describes the *sampāta-homa* everywhere for the purpose of manifesting the state of being Agni and Soma. Thus [it is said].
The means of accomplishing the sacrificial pap.

(The two lines for the *khaṭṭikā* are for the sake of the mandala. Then, with the root mantra accompanied by the six fires (*ṣaḍagni*), one should draw the line (*karaṇī*) made from the powder of chalk (*khaṭikā*) and the sacrificial implements such as clarified butter, sesame seeds, and so forth, as before. This is for the fire. With the syllable "Hā," [one draws] on the chalk and other materials.
One should perform the *saṃpāta* (the pouring together of the remnants).
Then, having divided the caru into three parts, [he should offer] the foremost portion to the Lord residing in the jar, on the sacrificial mound, and in the fire.

One should present [the offering] with the mantra: *oṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ dravyasvarūpiṇe ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. Regarding the specific procedure for the universal offering (*vibhu-naivedya*): having taken the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in a vessel, one should worship it with the Bhairava-mantra; having worshipped it with flowers, incense, and so forth, one should present it to the Universal Lord (*vibhu*) with the Bhairava-mantra.
Oṃ hūṃ, I offer this supreme nectar-caru to the Lord; homage!
(One should perform one hundred oblations for Bhairava and a tenth part for his limbs. Whatever remains, O Dear One, one should cover and set aside for the practitioners.)

"Remainder" (śeṣa) means that which is left over; one should set it aside because the initiates—the disciples who have not yet been consecrated—possess the entitlement to eat the consecrated sacrificial porridge (caru). This same procedure applies to the jar (kalaśa) as well, along with its retinue.
One should offer a tenth part to the enclosures.
One should offer one hundred oblations with the root mantra for the second portion, and a tenth part with the ancillary mantras.
Therefore, one should set aside a third part for the sake of the teacher and the disciple, protected by the vowels; after that, the fire offering (homa).
One should offer one hundred oblations for Bhairava and a tenth part [ten] for those who are ignorant. *Oṃ gāṃ, I satiate Vināyaka, svāhā.* 108.
Oṃ hāṃ, I satiate Bhūta-dhātrī; svāhā. (108 times)

Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ, may there be the pacification of the reverse [order]—svāhā! (Three oblations each should be offered for every instance of the reverse order, inversion, deficiency, excess, or ill-performed rites. Thus.

Salutation to Bhairava—thus is the worship. In the same manner, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed with [the mantras] ending in *svāhā*: *oṃ kṣraṃ* for the upper direction;
*oṃ yraṃ* for the east; *oṃ traṃ* for the south; *oṃ vraṃ* for the north; *oṃ lraṃ* for the west; *oṃ āṃ* for the heart; *oṃ īṃ* for the head; *oṃ ūṃ* for the crest-lock; *oṃ aiṃ*.

Oṃ raharakṣamalavaya-ūṃ, obeisance to Navātmabhairava. Oṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to the upward-facing mouth. Oṃ yaṃ, to the eastern face. Oṃ raṃ, to the southern face. Oṃ vaṃ, to the northern face. Oṃ laṃ, to the western face. Oṃ āṃ, to the heart. Oṃ īṃ.
*Śira*: Oṃ ūṃ. *Śikhā*: Oṃ aiṃ. *Kavaca*: Oṃ auṃ. *Netra*: Oṃ aḥ. *Astra*: [Oṃ aḥ]. Thus, the fire offering (*homa*) is performed with the ending "svāhā."
Oṃ rayalava-ūṃ, obeisance to Ratiśekharabhairava; likewise, svāhā, three times. Oṃ aṃ, to the east, va. Oṃ iṃ, da va. Oṃ uṃ, u va. Oṃ eṃ, pa va. Oṃ oṃ, ū va.
Oṃ āṃ, to the heart, hṛda. Oṃ īṃ, to Śiva, śiva. Oṃ ūṃ, to the crest-lock, śikhā. Oṃ aiṃ, to the armor, kava. Oṃ.
Oṃ, for the eyes; Oṃ Aḥ, for the weapon. Thus, svāhā three times.
Oṃ hrīḥ sauḥ, homage to Parā. Oṃ saṃ, eastern direction. Oṃ sīṃ, south-eastern direction. Oṃ sthaṃ, southern direction. Oṃ seṃ, south-western direction. Oṃ soṃ, upward direction.
