Oṃ saṃ pū; Oṃ siṃ da; Oṃ staṃ u; Oṃ seṃ pa; Oṃ soṃ ūrdhva;
Oṃ sāṃ hṛda; Oṃ sīṃ śira; Oṃ sthaṃ śikhā; Oṃ saiṃ kava; Oṃ sauṃ netre; Oṃ saḥ astrā. Thus, the *homa* is performed with [the mantras] ending in *svāhā*. Then, the *āhuti*...
With the three [mantras], there is also an oblation for Gaṇeśa and the others: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā* (three times); *oṃ hāṃ vāstupuruṣāya svāhā* (three times).

The reverse of the sequential order (*anuloma*) is its inversion (*viloma*). Regarding that, "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) refers to the penance prescribed for deficiencies or excesses; *prāya* means austerity (*tapas*) and *citta* means resolve. For that purpose, the oblation ending with "I offer with the root mantra for expiation, svāhā" is called *prāya*.
Penance (*tapas*) is said to be the mind and indeed resolve (*niścaya*).
The wise know that penance conjoined with resolve is expiation (*prāyaścitta*),
[applying] to those [acts] performed in direct or reverse order, and to those that are deficient or excessive.
Oṃ hūṃ, I offer this into the fire for the sake of expiation; svāhā! || 108 ||
Then, the visualization for the full oblation (*pūrṇā*) is: "From *ā* to *kṣa*. *Oṃ hūṃ, may the success of the consecration (*adhivāsa*) be attained, svāhā vauṣaṭ*. Thus is the full oblation.
Thus begins the section on the upper garment (*adhi-vāsa*).

Now follows the consecration of the disciple. Having worshipped Bhairava in the ritual jar (kalaśa) and having approached the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should offer a hundred oblations of the root mantra. Then, meditating on a shield in the left [hand], one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra and enter the sacrificial pavilion.

There, having performed the ritual of cessation and worship of the three vessels with animal-offerings (*paśvargha*), and having performed a special worship of the Blessed One as before, he should place his knees upon the ground,
seat the disciples near him, and take hold of them by the hand.

One should cause [the disciple] to receive the permission of the Blessed Lord, as follows: "Oṃ! O Śambhu, I have already been appointed by you for the Śiva-sacrifice; standing as the Guru in both the higher and lower [realms], act for the benefit of the worlds. By your power, [I am] smelled..."
"O Blessed One, this heart has been seen by me; I have set out for the sake of bestowing grace, not out of greed. In this matter, O Blessed One, you alone are the authority regarding all actions."
The supreme Śaṅkara, the auspicious one, is himself the agent and the witness;
having specifically presided over me alone, he remains in close proximity.
Act in such a way that she may be made equal to your feet; having placed your command in my heart, I shall perform all the necessary rites.
"O Lord, can even the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) act otherwise? By Your command, such-and-such a person, possessed by Śakti, is to be initiated by me."
"O All-pervading Lord, I shall report whatever action I perform; grant me your command, O Lord of the World, and be gracious unto me, O Blessed One."
Thus, this is the reception of the command for each disciple. Having thus received the command, he should draw a circular mandala at the door of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa).
If there is no space there, then he should draw a small mandala within the sacrificial pavilion near the door.
He should act thus: having reflected in this way and having prepared the mandala,

the Guru— facing east— should look upon the disciple, who has fasted, is gentle, facing north, standing upright with a serene countenance, by means of the flame arising from the *kanda*-station, [uttering] "Oṃ Haḥ."
"Phaṭ! I sprinkle; obeisance. Having thus sprinkled with the water of Śiva using the Astra-mantra, [one says]: "Oṃ haiṃ! I veil; obeisance huṃ. Having thus veiled with the Kavaca-mantra (p. 47).

Having struck [the disciple] three times on the head with the sword of knowledge— [making him] a son of [the lineage], free from fear, a celibate student, and one committed to the final goal— and having [anointed him] with ashes,
he should then touch [him] three times from the navel to the head with *darbha* grass blades pointing upwards, as follows:

Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I kindle the power of will (icchā-śakti), haḥ phaṭ; likewise [I kindle] the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). Having said this, one should cast those darbha grasses into the fire.
Again, with the tips of the *darbha* grass pointing downwards: "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! I cut the *āṇava* bond here, phaṭ!
Likewise, [I cut] the *māyīya* bond."

"Kārmapāśam. Thus, reciting this three times, he should touch [the disciple] from the navel down to the feet and cast those [impurities] into the fire. With the mantra "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ, I sprinkle the disciple, namaḥ haḥ phaṭ," he should sprinkle him three times downward to remove the three impurities (*mala*), and three times upward.
One should sprinkle from the animal-offering vessel (paśvarghapātra) in order to kindle the three powers;
"with the sword of knowledge," so say the Gurus.

Then, having projected Śiva along with His limbs (the ancillaries) from his own body into the body of the disciple, he should worship the disciple with flowers and other offerings using the Bhairava-mantra.
Then, having brought a white cloth with its fringes intact for use as a blindfold,

having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra and enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, and having thoroughly fumigated it and worshipped it with the Mūla-mantra, [one should say]: "Oṃ hauṃ, I bind the eyes of [Name], hauṃ namaḥ."
With this mantra, one should bind [the eyes].
Then, supporting him with both hands, he should lead the disciple into the vicinity of the altar of the vase, facing the deity; having placed a single flower in his hand with the root mantra.

In order to prevent the outward diffusion of the organs of action and to turn inward the light of Bhairava placed within, one should cover the mouth which is the locus of the sense organs of cognition.
For the purpose of restraining the sense organs and the organs of action, he should first cause the disciple to enter while supporting him by the hand, which is the primary means for such restraint.
Having grasped him with both hands, one should enter behind the curtain; even from there...
Having turned [the disciple] toward the deity, one should place a flower in his hand—
only a single flower consecrated with the root mantra— and give it for the purpose of determining the result of the flower’s fall.
And therefore: "One should employ that [mantra] with the thought, 'The flower has been cast by the power of the [deity's] abode';
and at the moment of its falling, the Guru should recite the root-mantra"—this is the meaning.
One should not perform elaborate rituals regarding the source of existence; for it is stated in the *Śrīgamaśāstra* that "O Supreme Goddess, such a person never attains the fruit."
In the light—

[the yogin] whose eyes have been consecrated with mantras and bound with fine cloth, who is not fickle and whose heart has become focused on nothing else, should thus forcibly restrain [the senses]; [thereby,] pearls, gems, and so forth [are perceived].

The Guru, having led the disciples who hold their hands cupped with flowers to the front of the sacrificial ground and having had them sit upon their knees, should cause those disciples of purified souls to cast that handful of flowers; then, having refilled their cupped hands, [he should cause] them...
[The teacher] should quickly [hold up] a cloth to shield the eyes; that too, the disciple sees as if it were not there.

By those [disciples] thus led in, by means of the agent who employs them, "quickly" means so that the sight of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) occurs exactly as it was before; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding "in the light"—
anticipating the question of what would happen to him upon seeing the mandala in this way, he says:
"When the place is suddenly beheld, illuminated by the splendor of the mantra, there is absorption into that."
Through that [influence], the disciple attains identification with it.
He brings this very point home by means of an illustration.
For just as one whose heart is impassioned perceives various qualities of the beloved in a woman,
so too does one refined by the descent of power perceive the presence of the mantra.
"By itself" means not by depending on another form; for if that were the case, its perception would not occur instantaneously.

Surely, qualities such as beauty and charm are visible and belong to beloved women; therefore, those whose hearts are impassioned may indeed behold them. But how can these [qualities] be seen by those with physical eyes, given that they are invisible, even though they are present?
Furthermore, how could they be perceived by the eyes of all?
Fearing that they might fall within the range of the sense faculties such as the eye, he says:
For if such a cooperative cause for the sense organs, such as the eye, were absolutely unseen even previously, then their capacity [to produce cognition] would have arisen even before.
When there exists a cooperative cause characterized by the descent of power (śaktipāta) for the benefit of the sense organs such as the eye,

there arises a fitness for the visual act even with respect to mantras and the like— which were previously entirely unseen and thus lacked the latent impressions of experience and are not objects of conceptual cognition.
The meaning is that it should be understood as being possible in that manner.

Anticipating the question, "What is the proof for this?", he says: For those of perfected wisdom, perceiving the body, water, land, images, and so forth, as being infused with mantra, understand its presence and absence.
In the Svatantra [Tantra] ||
Having uncovered his face,
he should reveal the Cause, Sadāśiva, together with the hosts of Vidyās and Mantras.
"The cause" refers to Śrī Niṣkalanātha, who exists together with Sahasradāśiva and Śrī Sakalabhaṭṭāraka. Now, he...
Freed from the veil of ignorance, the awakened one beholds [the Lord], having fallen prostrate like a staff upon the earth,
bowing down again and again.

By the word "ignorance" (ajñāna), the pervasion [of the means] in the removal of the veil is stated. The bound soul (paśu) who was in a prior state has now become awakened; for this very reason, filled with wonder from beholding the true nature of the Lord after thousands of previous births, he gazes upon the Lord again and again.

By moving like a staff, he casts aside the state of being a limited subject (pramātṛtā) regarding the body and so forth; thus, his fitness for following into the absorption of Śrī Śiva is demonstrated. For this very reason, he is [described as follows].
Having accomplished his purpose, with a joyful soul, he should raise up that child whose eyes were filled with joy,
take him by the hand, and bring him to the southern image.
Having raised [the disciple] with eyes wide with joy through the touch of one's own nature, which consists of consciousness and bliss—
the meaning being that he has emerged from that state by means of the method after having long been submerged in the ground of the body and so forth—
he [is led] along the favorable southern path, which is essentially Śiva-natured and not of the nature of bonds (pāśava) consisting of the body.
And he should place it directly in front of the venerable Lord Aghora.

Then, he should cast that flower upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*); at the moment of its falling, the Guru should recite the root mantra. Thereafter, having removed his blindfold, [the disciple should be led forward].

Having displayed the assembly of mantras worshipped upon the sacrificial ground (or the worshipped vase), one should cause him to perform a prostration like a staff. [This is the removal of the eye-cloth and the liberation from the veil of ignorance:
*Oṃ, homage to all yogins and to the Siddhas, salutations again and again*.]
Obeisance to the Lord of the Embodied and the Unembodied, who grasps the multitude of powers. Having raised him up,
with the cloth over his eyes bound, having led him thus to the front of the sacrificial altar,
one should remove the eye-cloth [and reveal] the host of deities situated upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the form of mantras.

Having shown [the disciple] this, the Guru should cause him to perform a prostration with a staff, saying: "Homage to all. Having spoken thus, the Guru should bow down even without the eye-veil. Taking the disciple by the hand, he should go near the fire and, on his own right side, place him upon a seat consisting of the *praṇava* (oṃ) within a maṇḍala made of *darbha* grass.
Having seated the disciple facing north within a circular space, the subsequent consecrations must be performed for each disciple individually with separate effort. Until its completion,
a distinct consecration must certainly be performed for the disciple’s attainment of the status of an Ācārya.
The Gurus maintain that even when there is a group of practitioners, only one person may at times perform the rite;
for example: *Oṃ haḥ phaṭ tāḍayāmi* (striking with the weapon-mantra of the *vidyārgha*), having struck with the weapon-mantra *haḥ phaṭ*, [one says] *Oṃ haḥ phaṭ prokṣayāmi haḥ phaṭ*.
Having thus sprinkled [the area] with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), one should veil it with: *oṃ haiṃ avaguṇṭhayāmi namaḥ huṃ*.

Having veiled it and rendered it immortal (*amṛtīkṛtya*) by means of the *amṛta-mudrā*, [one should place the vessel] there near the sacrificial altar (*yāgavedi*) on one's own right, upon a mandala of *darbha* grass together with grains (*sākṣata*).

Having seated the disciple facing north, if there is no space in front of the sacrificial altar due to its proximity to the *saṅghaṭṭa* and so forth, then one should lead him near the fire after considering the deity;
for the one facing north, one should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites, having struck him with the *vidyā-argha*.
And regarding the one who has been sprinkled, it says in the Guru’s manuscript:
48) Having prepared a mandala there, one should place a seat of *praṇava* with flowers; upon that—
Having laid the infant with his body upright and facing north, [one should proceed].
The Guru, standing facing the east, should perform the sprinkling and other preliminary rites.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [one should understand] the support for striking as before. Regarding the phrase "he should cause [it] to be done":

while performing the mantras, one should employ them by entering into their potency. Then, having seated [the disciple] here on the seat, one should then perform the rite of *sakalīkaraṇa* (the ritual of making [him] complete).
For the sake of accomplishing the fruit of separation, for one who desires liberation or for a practitioner.

For one who has undergone general consecration and has beheld the true form of the Blessed One, even when performing the worship of Śiva, fire rituals, and so forth, the body must be rendered "sakalīkṛta" (endowed with all parts); it cannot be otherwise than in its prior state, as will be explained later; furthermore, this is for the sake of enjoyment according to what is appropriate.

The connection with the distant [verb] is as follows: "Having performed the rite of *sakalīkaraṇa* for the sake of liberation, or for the attainment of all fruits such as the fitness for worshipping Śrī Śiva, one should subsequently deposit the path of the *kalās*"; thus he indicates the *sakalīkaraṇa* in its proper sequence.
Having smeared the two hands with fragrance, one should purify them with the Astra-mantra;
having enveloped them with the Kavaca-mantra, one should then drench them with nectar.

"Anointed with fragrance and so forth" means permeated by fragrance such as that of *kulaka* and other substances; the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa* (the act of making complete) is performed for the sake of attaining the specific fruit consisting in the fitness for the worship of Śiva and other rites.
And for those two alone:
having prepared an infinite seat, one should install the limbs of Bhairava.
"Bhairava and the limbs" is a copulative compound (dvandva).

One who desires specific fruits, a seeker of liberation, or a practitioner should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa in this manner: having smeared the hands of both the teacher and the disciple with fragrant substances, one should purify them with the Astra-mantra, veil them with the Kavaca-mantra, and drench them with the Amṛta-mantra. Then: *Oṃ anantāsanāya*.

Salutation! To the lotus seat; to the seat of Sadāśiva. Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seats in this manner, one should place one's own mantra between the two hands. Then, having gazed upon the disciple for a moment with eyes consisting of supreme light, and having entered the disciple’s heart through exhalation (*recaka*), [one should perform the following] for him.
Then, having caused the self [of the disciple] to reach the *dvādaśānta* from the heart through meditation, one should perform the drying and other rites for the disciple. For example:
"Oṃ kṣyūṃ, I dry up the body of the disciple, obeisance. Thus, [one visualizes] the form of the Sun.

Having meditated upon the *praṇava* as pervading the entire body, one should contemplate the body by means of it as resembling a withered tree. Reciting: "Oṃ rakṣaraya-ūṃ, I burn the disciple's body; obeisance," one should visualize the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) rising from the big toe of the right foot.

Having meditated, one should contemplate the body as reduced to ashes by that flame. Reciting "Oṃ ylūṃ, I cause the body to float up; namaḥ," one should visualize the bodily ashes being dispersed in the ten directions by the wind. [Then recite] "Oṃ vaṃ, I flood the body."
*Namaḥ*. Thus, one should contemplate that place as being washed by streams of the nectar heard from the *cidbindu*.

Just as the poisonous nature of a venom is neutralized by the power of a mantra without its essential form being destroyed, so too is the identification with the body and vital breaths dissolved through the practice of *āharaṇā*.

Then, having contemplated the body of the disciple as being like empty space and consciousness like fire within gold, one should meditate upon the *jīva* in the void of that emptiness as having the form of lightning. Then, having visualized the divine body as completely filled with the nectar of the *bindu*, [according to the method taught in the Svacchanda Tantra].

Below the disciple’s *kanda*: "Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti. Having thus placed the Śakti, above the Śakti: "Oṃ, salutation to Padmāsana. Having thus placed the lotus with the *praṇava*, one should meditate upon the Self as consisting of light upon the lotus.
One should conceive of it as having become embodied by virtue of its possessing form.
Or else, according to the principle stated in the *Gurupustikā*: ||
For the seated disciple, [one should visualize] below the *kanda*: "Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti"—thus having meditated upon Ādhāraśakti; then at the navel: "Oṃ, salutation to Dhātrī";
above Dhātrī, at the station of Kalanā: "Oṃ, salutation to the Ocean of Milk"; and at the heart-lotus-seat: "Oṃ, salutation to Padmāsana."

*Namaḥ*. Thus is the heart-lotus. *Oṃ candramaṇḍalāya*. Thus, externally, within the seven constituents (*dhātu*), it is encircled by a moon-maṇḍala. It consists of the letters *A*, *U*, and *M*, representing the principles of Self (*ātmatattva*), Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), and Śiva (*śivatattva*).
[The lotus] with its pervading petals, filaments, and pericarp: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Oṃ jhrūṃ, [obeisance] to Sūkṣma. Oṃ mūṃ, [obeisance] to Śivottama. Oṃ krūṃ, [obeisance] to Ekanetra.
Oṃ kṣyāṃ, [obeisance] to Ekarudra. Oṃ ylūṃ, [obeisance] to Trimūrti. Oṃ hjūṃ.
Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha. Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Śikhaṇḍin. Thus ends the leaf of the Vidyeśvaras.
The filaments of the mantra: Oṃ vāmāyai, jyeṣṭhāyai, raudryai, kālyai,
kalavikaraṇyai, balavikaraṇyai, sarvabhūtadamanyai, manonmanyai.
Thus is the reality of the nine seed-syllables beginning with Vāmā. Having meditated upon the lotus of knowledge (vidyābja) with Śakti as its pericarp, [one recites] above that:
"Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hūṃ oṃ, I cause the self of the disciple to descend; obeisance. Thus.
Having brought down the disciple’s life-force from the *dvādaśānta* and meditated upon the disciple’s self as consisting of light atop a lotus,
one should conceive of it as having become the form [of Śiva] with the mantra: *oṃ laṃ sadyojātamūrtaye namaḥ*.

One should nourish [the disciple] with immortality-drenchings. Thus, for the disciple who has become Śiva, one should perform the mental placement (nyāsa): first, the placement of the faces, the placement of the limbs, and briefly the placement of the kalās.

Oṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to Tārā and the other powers of Īśāna; on the head. Oṃ yaṃ, obeisance to Śāntā and the other powers of Tatpuruṣa; on the face. Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Tamā and the other powers of Aghora; on the heart. Oṃ vaṃ, [obeisance] to Rajā and the others...
"Oṃ, salutation to the Vāmadeva-kalās at the secret place (guhya). Oṃ laṃ, salutation to the Siddhas and others, the Sadyojāta-kalās, on the entire body.
After performing the placement of these mantras (mantranyāsa) in this manner, one should perform the placement of the path to be purified (śodhyādhvanyāsa), as follows:
In that regard, regarding initiation (dīkṣā), there are five kalās.
One should install the five paths within the womb in the order of emanation: Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and the one called Śāntyatītā.
From the *brahmarandhra* to the forehead is the *śāntyatītā* digit.
(The ritual placement [nyāsa] is declared according to the order of emanation, but the purification is performed by a different sequence.
(It is like crystal, black, red, white, and yellow.)
The knowable principles beginning with Śāntyatītā are the kalās that have been praised as being real entities.

"Consisting of the *tattvas*" means that [the elements] beginning with space and ending with earth have attained the nature of the *tattvas*; for this very reason, meditation upon them in such a manner is declared to be appropriate. Thus, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five *kalās* for the purpose of the creation of the pure *tattvas* has been stated here as a preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).

However, regarding the *putraka* and others, it will be explained later in another chapter that this [initiation] will take place according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) for the purpose of initiation; therefore, one should not be deluded into thinking that this is not relevant to the present context.

Her maṇḍala is circular, marked with a drop (or marked with a banner), and has the luster of crystal; it is her visualization. She has one face, and her hands bestow boons and fearlessness. Within that [maṇḍala] is the single reality, the Śiva-tattva. || 1 ||

In that regard, according to the *Samanāta*, the sixteen worlds (*bhuvana-ṣoḍaśaka*), which constitute the objects of knowledge (*prameya-rūpa*) on the ground (*bhūmikā*), are pervaded by the half-moon and the point (*bindu*).
Therein, in the form of Mahāmāyā who is *samanā*, Śiva—mounted upon that power and performing the fivefold cosmic act—resides in that world. || 1 ||
Following that, in Vyāpinī: (2) the world of Anāśrita, (3) the world of Anātha, (4) the world of Ananta, (5) the world of Vyomarūpa, and (6) the world of Vyāpin.
In the Śakti-āvaraṇa (the enclosure of Power): the world of Parāśakti is surrounded by a quartet of powers—Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, Amṛtā, and the one called Amṛtākhyā. || 7 || At the end of Nāda (Nādānta):
there is one [world] presided over by Suṣamṇeśa, the Supreme Brahman. || 8 || In the Nāda-āvaraṇa (the enclosure of Sound).
Ūrdhvagā bhu || 9 || Rocikā bhu || 10 || Mocikā bhū || 11 ||

*Dīpikā* [is] *bhu* || 12 || *Ṛndikā* [is] *bhu* || 13 || Then, in *Nirodhinī*, there is *Rundhanī*, *Rodhinī*, *Raudrī*, *Jñānabodhā*, and *Tamopahā*; surrounded by their respective five *lepa*s, *Nirodhinī* [is] *bhu* || 14 || Then, in *Ardhendu*, there are *Jyotsnā* and *Jyotsnāvatī*.
Lustre, beautiful radiance, and the stainless [state] joined with the half-moon belong to the Earth element.
[The seed-syllables] Bindu and Śakti are surrounded by Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, Śāntā, and Śāntyatītā.
Bhu || 16 || Thus are the worlds || 16 ||
The word "Oṃ" is the mantra; it is Lord Īśāna, inseparable from the eye that consists of the three abodes.
The vowels are: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ. || 16 ||

The mind (*manas*) is a portion of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city); herein lies the subtle path (*sūkṣmādhvā*). Within the seed-syllable (*bīja*), there are the resonance (*nāda*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). The two channels (*nāḍī*) are the *kuhu* and the *śiṅkhinī*. The two vital airs (*vāyu*) are the *devadatta* and the *dhanañjaya*. Among the senses, they are speech (*vāk*) and hearing (*śrotra*). The object (*viṣaya*) is sound (*śabda*).
And the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*); the quality (*guṇa*) is sound; the state (*avasthā*) is that beyond the fourth (*turyātītā*);
the cause (*kāraṇa*) is Sadāśiva. Having thus internalized the higher paths, one should deposit the *kalā* of Śāntyatītā. || 1 ||

Then, having meditated upon the Śāntākalā, which contains within it the five paths of the higher order (*tara-adhvan*), starting from the forehead and ending at the palate according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*). It is as follows:

In this [mandala], one should meditate upon a circular black hexagon marked with a dot; it has one face and its hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. Within its womb are the three principles (tattvas) known as Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā, and within those are seventeen worlds (bhuvanas).

In the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva, there is the world-pervading Sadāśiva-bhuvana, which encompasses the eight [deities] beginning with Brahmāṅga and Sakala, as well as the Śiva-rudra division and the infinite Rudra-worlds contained within its enclosure. || 1 ||
In the principle of Īśvara, from the syllable *rudra-om* up to the end of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), there are fifty-nine worlds;
for the powers of knowledge and action (*jñānakriyāśakti*), there is one world. || 2 ||
(Above the subtle veil, they know there are three powers; Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrā are declared to be the powers.
There is one world for Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. 3.
Therefore, understand from Rudra that form and its state exist therein: dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty as the fourth.
[These are] the ground of sovereignty (4), the ground of dispassion (5), and the ground of knowledge (6).
Dharmabhu || 7 || Ananteśabhu || 8 || Sūkṣmabhu || 9 ||
Born from Śivottama (10); born from Ekanetra (11); born from Ekarudra (12).
Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and Trinetra are thus proclaimed.
Śrīkhaṇḍa and Śikhaṇḍin are to be known as the Vidyeśvaras in their respective order. [They are assigned as follows:
Śrīkaṇṭhabhuja (13), Śrīkaṇṭha (14), Śikhaṇḍibhuja (15);
in the Īśvara-tattva, Īśvarabhuja (16); and in the Śuddhavidyā-tattva, Bhṛguṇī.
Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, Rūpiṇī, Mandinī, and Jvālā—these constitute one world-system. || 17 ||
Bhṛguṇī, Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, Parā, Rūpiṇī, Mandinī, and Jvālā— these seven are their respective lords.

The Vidyārājas are thus fully enumerated. (Because they bestow [attainments], they are called "steps. The steps are eleven: the *ha*-step, the *ra*-step, the *kṣa*-step, the *ma*-step, the *la*-step, the *va*-step, the *ya*-step, the *ūṃ*-step, the *ha*-step, the *oṃ*-step, and the *ra*-step.
The syllables are: *ka-varṇaḥ*, *kha-va*, *ga-va* (three times). This is the weapon mantra (*astramantra*) and the person mantra (*puruṣamantra*).
The subtle path is that which obstructs consciousness (*cidrodhinī*). The two seed-syllables are *biṃ* and *ya*.
The two channels are *yaśā* and *lambuṣā*. The two winds are *kūrma* and *kṛkara*. The two senses are the skin and the sense of touch.
The object is touch, as well as the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*). The two qualities are sound and touch. The state is...
The Fourth State (turyā), the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), the intellect (buddhi) and ego (ahaṅkāra), and the Lord as the cause—
having thus internalized these paths and having meditated upon the peaceful power (śāntā-kalā) as abiding, pervading from the forehead to the palate, one should perform the placement (nyāsa). 2.

51) Now, the pervasion of Vidyā extends from the palate to the navel.
Its mandala is triangular, red, and marked with svastikas;
it has one face and two hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. In this interval, there are seven principles (tattvas):
the first is the principle of Māyā.
And then Gopati, O Goddess, is situated in the lower knot.
Situated above the *granthi* are Viśva, Trikāla, Kṣema,
Brāhmaṇādhipati, and Śiva as the fifth.
Beyond this, however, it is infinite:
by time (2), by limited power (kalā) (3), by necessity (niyati) (4), by knowledge (vidyā) (5), by attachment (rāga) (6), and by the person (puruṣa) (7).
There are twenty-seven worlds (*bhuvana*). Above the *māyā-tattva* are: 1. the world of Viśveśa; 2. the world of Trikāla; 3. the world of Kṣema; 4.
the world of Brahmādhipati; 5. the world of Śiva. In the middle of *māyā* is 6. the world of Ananta. Below *māyā*, within the *kāla* and *kalā* principles, is 7. the world of Gopati.
(“O Great Goddess, within the principle of Time (kālatattva), the triad of Mahādeva resides: Mahādeva, the one of great splendor, and the powerful Mahājyotis.
Mahādevabhu 8; Mahātejobhu 9; Mahājyotirbhu 10. [These reside] in the principles of Niyati and Vidyā.
Manonmanābhu 11; Vāmābhu 12; Jyeṣṭhābhu 13; Raudrābhu 14; Kālābhu 15; Sarvabhūtadamana-bhu 16; Kalavikaraṇābhu 17; Balavikaraṇābhu 18;
Balapramathanābhu 19; [and the two] of Rāga and Puruṣa.
And above the principle of Vidyā, listen indeed to the world therein: Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Raudra, Kāla, and likewise Vikaraṇa.
Balavikaraṇa, Balapramathana, Sarvabhūtadamana, and likewise Manonmana;
[the lords] Ananteśabhu (20), Sūkṣmabhu (21), Śivottamabhu (22), and Ekanetrabhu (23).

The two mantras are the *kavaca* (armor) mantras. Now, the subtle path (*sūkṣmādhvan*): [the elements] obstruct consciousness (*cidrodhin*). The two seed-syllables (*bīja*) are the two tastes (*rasa*).

The two channels (*nāḍī*) are Hastijihvā and Pūṣan. The two vital airs (*vāyu*) are Nāga and Vyāna. The two sense organs (*indriya*) are the eye and the feet. The object (*viṣaya*) is form (*rūpa*), which is the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*). The qualities (*guṇa*) are form...

The [tattvas] are touch and sound; the state is Suṣumṇā; the two portions of the *puryaṣṭaka* are smell and form; the cause is Rudra. Having thus meditated upon the *vidyā-kalā*, which contains within it the entire path (*adhvan*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). || 3 ||
Then, she is situated pervading from the navel up to the ankles.
Within her is a white mandala in the shape of a half-moon, marked with a lotus;
it has one face, and its hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. Within that [mandala] are the principles (tattvas). 24.

The principle of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva) 1; the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva) 2; the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva) 3; the principle of mind (manas-tattva) 4; the principle of hearing (śrotra-tattva) 5; the principle of touch (tvak-tattva) 6; the principle of sight (cakṣus-tattva) 7; the principle of taste (jihvā-tattva) 8; the principle of smell (ghrāṇa-tattva) 9; the principle of speech (vāk-tattva) 10; the principle of hands (pāṇi-tattva) 11; the principle of feet (pāda-tattva) 12; the principle of the anus (pāyu-tattva) 13; the principle of the generative organ (upastha-tattva) 14; and the principle of sound (śabda-tattva) 15.

The principle of touch (16), the principle of form (17), the principle of taste (18), the principle of smell (19), the principle of space (20), the principle of air (21), the principle of fire (22), and the principle of water (23); and because of the coexistence of the qualities of *prakṛti*, there is the principle of qualities (24).
52) Beginning from Prakṛti and ending with the Śatarudras, this is the domain of Śrīkaṇṭha.
(The Bhairava, Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, Kaumāra, Auma, and Śrīkaṇṭha [mantras], both unmanifest and manifest.
Therein, in Prakṛti: Śrīkaṇṭhabhu 1; Aumabhu 2; Kaumārabhu 3.
Vaiṣṇava-bhu 4; Brāhma-bhu 5; Bhairava-bhu 6; Kṛta-bhu 7; Akṛta-bhu 8. Thus ends the group of eight yogas.
Chagalāṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara,
Kālāñjana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara.
The eight Sthāṇus are thus enumerated:
[in the intellect (buddhi)]— Pitāmaha-bhu 1, Prajeśa-bhu 2, Amṛta-bhu 3,
Vibhūti-bhu 4, Svarūpa-bhu 5, Svabhadra-bhu 6, Karāla-bhu 7.
Sunandabhū 8. Thus ends the group of eight divine origins.

This eighth [tattva] is designated by the term *sthāṇu* because it stands like a pillar (*sthāṇuvat tiṣṭhati*) through its presiding over the subtle elements and the sense organs, providing the perfection of all enjoyment.
Pervading from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) down to the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*), it remains as the pervasive ground, like the "goat-testicle" (*chāgalāṇḍa*) and other such [metaphors].
The Sthūleśvaras are the Rudras.
The group of eight Sthāṇus resides pervading everything from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) down to the principle of smell (gandha-tattva).
In the sacrifice to Ākāśeṣṭi, [the deities] begin with Rudra and Astra and end with Sthāṇu;

this is the group of eight purifiers (*pavitrāṣṭaka*). Its status as a purifier arises from its abiding in the state free of veils (*nirāvaraṇa-pada*), owing to its superiority even over the preceding [eight].
Namely: Cchagalāṇḍabhu 1; Dviraṇḍabhu 2; Mākoṭabhu 3; Maṇḍaleśvarabhu 4; Kāliñjarabhu 5; Śaṅkukarṇabhu 6; Sthūleśvarabhu 7; Sthūleśvarabhu 8; [and so on] all twenty-four.
(Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa,
Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu as the eighth.)
This group of eight purifiers has indeed been proclaimed in brief. [These are located] in the element of space (ākāśatattva): 1. Vastrāpada-bhū, 2. Rudrakoṭi-bhū, 3. Avimukta-bhū, 4.
Mahālaya-bhū, 5. Gokarṇa-bhū, 6. Bhadrakarṇa-bhū, 7. Svarṇākṣa-bhū.
Sthāṇubhu 8. Thus ends the eightfold pavitra.
"Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākhala, and likewise Kanakhala; Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Māhendra, and Maṇi as the eighth— this, which is more secret than the secret, should indeed be known with diligent effort."

In the element of air (*vāyu-tattva*): Gayābhūmi 1, Kurukṣetrabhūmi 2, Nākhala-bhūmi 3, Kanakhala-bhūmi 4, Vimala-bhūmi 5, Aṭṭahāsa-bhūmi 6, Mahīndra-bhūmi 7, Bhīma-bhūmi 8. Thus is the group of eight, more secret than the secret (*guhyātiguhyāṣṭaka*).

(Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jālmamāmrātakeśvara, Mahākāla, Madhyama, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava— these are declared to be the most secret [shrines], following the sequence from the East to the Northeast.)
Now, regarding the principle of fire (*tejastattva*): 1. Haricandrabhu; 2. Śrīśilabhu; 3. Jālmabhu; 4.
Āmrātakabhu; 5. Mahākālabhu; 6. Svamadhyamabhu; 7. Kedārabhu; 8. Bhairavabhu—this is the group of eight called the "Extremely Secret" (*aty-uguhya*).
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara; Āṣāḍhi, Diṇḍimuṇḍa, Bhārabhūti, and Calākula—
this is known as the Guhyāṣṭaka, O beloved, situated within the enclosure of water.

Regarding the state of being an authoritative source (*āptatva*), there are the eight secret sites (*guhyāṣṭaka*): 1. Āmareśabhū, 2. Prabhāsabhū, 3. Naimiṣabhū, 4. Puṣkarabhū, 5. Āṣāḍhabhū, 6. Diṇḍimuṇḍabhū, 7. Bhārabhūtibhū, and 8. Lakuleśabhū. All these are on the mountain (*parvata*). 6.

The qualities (*guṇas*) are taste (*rasa*), form (*rūpa*), smell (*sa*), touch (*sparśa*), and sound (*śabda*).
All objects of the senses, such as the object of sound, the object of touch, the object of form, the object of taste, and the object of smell; likewise, all the sense faculties. For example:
The auditory faculty, the tactile faculty,
the visual faculty, the gustatory faculty, the olfactory faculty, and the vocal faculty.
The faculty of the hand; the faculty of the foot; the faculty of the anus; the faculty of the generative organ.
All the subtle elements (tanmātras) are as follows: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell.
These reside in the subtle body.
Even the six sheaths exist in a subtle state.

The state is dream; the essence is the *puryaṣṭaka*; the cause is Viṣṇu. Having thus meditated upon the *Pratiṣṭhā* [tattva], which contains all the paths (*adhvan*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). || 4 ||
Now, the pervasion of the *nivṛtti-kalā* extends from the ankle to the end of the foot;
its visualization is a yellow square mandala marked with a thunderbolt (*vajra*).

"With hands granting boons and fearlessness," and so forth. Within that is the single earth-tattva (*pṛthvī-tattva*), extending for one hundred million *yojanas*, and the one hundred and eight worlds (*bhuvana*).
Above is Lord Vīrabhadra. And therein are: 1. Śambhubhuvana, 2. Vibhubhuvana, 3.
Gaṇādhyakṣabhu, 4. Tryakṣabhu, 5. Tridaśeśabhu, 6.
Saṃvāhabhu, 7. Vivāhabhu, 8. Nabhobhu, 9. Lipsubhu.

Endowed with sovereign power, these great gods wander about, well-honored by Brahmā himself:

Avyayabhu (7), Śāstṛbhu (8), Pinākibhu (9), and Tridaśādibhu (10).
"Patibhu" (10). Thus [ends] the first section.
Kapāleśa, Aja, Bradhna, Vajradeha,
Pramardana, Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākin, and Tridaśādhipa.
Having overcome the power of Indra, these great gods, endowed with sovereign might and honored by Indra, roam about. (1) Agnirudrabhu, (2) Hutāśabhu, (3) Piṅgalabhu, (4) Khādakabhu.
Harabhu 5, Jvalanabhu 6, Dahanabhu 7, Vabhrūbhu 8, Bhasmāntakabhu 9, Yamāntakabhu 10— thus [they are] in the southeast.
Agnirudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala, Khādaka, Hara, Jvalana,
Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Yamāntaka.
Having overcome the power of Agni and being endowed with sovereign might, the great gods, highly honored by the King of Fire, move about. [The five realms are:
1. Yāmyabhu, 2. Mṛtyubhu, 3. Harabhu, 4. Dhātṛbhu, 5. Vidhātṛbhu.
6. Kartṛbhū, 7. Saṃyoktṛbhū, 8. Viyoktṛbhū, 9. Dharmapatibhū, 10.
Adharmapatibhū—thus in the southern direction.
He is the southern one, the remover of death, the sustainer, the ordainer, and he who is known as the agent; he is the uniter and the disuniter, as well as the lord of dharma and adharma.
Having overcome the power of Yama, the great gods, endowed with sovereign might and honored by King Yama, roam about.
1. The realm of Nairṛta; 2. the realm of Māraṇa; 3. the realm of Hantrī; 4. the realm of Krūradṛṣṭi.
Bhayāntakabhu 5; Ūrdhvakeśibhu 6; Virūpākṣabhu 7; Dhūmrabhu 8; Lohitabhu 9; Daṃṣṭribhuvana 10—thus in the southwest (nairṛta).
The son of Nirṛti, the slayer of Māra, with a cruel gaze and the ender of fear; with hair standing erect, deformed eyes, smoke-colored and blood-red fangs.

Having overcome the army of Nairṛta, these great gods, endowed with sovereign power and highly honored by the Lord of Nairṛta, roam about. (1) Balabhuvana, (2) Atibalabhu, (3) Pāśahastabhu, (4) Mahābalabhu.
Śvetabhu 5, Jayarudrabhu 6, Dīrghabāhubhu 7, Jalāntakabhu 8,
Meghanādabhu 9, Sunādabhu 10— thus [are they] in the west.
Bala, Hyati, Bala, Pāśahasta,
Mahābala, Śveta, Ajaya, Bhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka.
The channels beginning with Meghanādī have been briefly described;
they possess the power of mastery by overcoming the water-element force.
The great gods, honored by Varuṇa and Indra, roam about.
(He is) swift, light, with the speed of the wind, subtle, sharp, and terrifying.
The ender of the five, the one with five locks, the one with matted hair, he who has the clouds as his vehicle.
Relying upon the power of Vāyu and endowed with sovereign might, the great gods, highly honored by the king of the winds, roam about: 1.
Śīghrabhū, 2. Laghubhū, 3. Vāyuvegabhū, 4. Sūkṣmabhū.
Tīkṣṇabhu 5; Yamāntakabhu 6; Pañcāntakabhu 7; Pañcaśikhabhu 8; Kapardibhu 9; Meghavāhanabhu 10. Thus in the wind [direction].
The Lord of Treasures, handsome and blessed, with a gentle body and wearing matted locks;
the bearer of Lakṣmī and jewels, full of desire, gracious, and radiant.
Having overcome the power of Soma and being endowed with sovereign might (*prabhu-śakti*), the great gods roam about, well-honored by King Soma. [The lords of the treasures are:
Nidhīśa-bhu (1), Rūpavat-bhu (2), Dhanya-bhu (3), and Saumyadeha-bhu (4).
Jaṭādhara-bhū 5; Lakṣmīdhara-bhū 6; Ratnadhara-bhū 7; Kāmin-bhū 8; Prasādaka-bhū 9; Prabhāsaka-bhū 10. Thus ends the northern [section].

The Lord of Knowledge, the Omniscient One, the consumer of wisdom, the one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas; the Corpse, the Lord of the Gods, the Eldest, the Protector of Beings, and the lover of offerings.
The gods, worshipped by the immortals, act with the permission of Īśāna; the great gods move about, presided over by the power of Īśa.
Vidyādhipatibhu 1; Sarvajñabhu 2; Jñānabhukbhu 3; Vedapāragabhu.
4. Śarvabhū, 5. Sureśvarabhū, 6. Jyeṣṭhabhū, 7. Bhūtapālabhū, 8. Balipriyabhū, 9. Īśānabhū—thus in the Śāna [section].
Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Antaḥ, Krodhana, Mārutāśaya, Grasara, Ḍambareśa, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭraka.
Having overcome the power of Viṣṇu, the great gods, endowed with sovereign might and well-honored by Ananta, move about:
1. Vṛṣabhu, 2. Vṛṣadharabhu, 3. Anantabhu, 4. Kradhanabhu.
Mārutāśibhu 5; Grasanabhu 6; Taḍambarabhu 7; Īśabhu 8;
Phaṭīndrabhu 9; Vajradaṃṣṭribhu 10—thus [are the worlds] below. Likewise are the worlds within the Brahmāṇḍa: Rudrabhuvana 1; Viṣṇubhu 2; Brahmabhu 3.
Śarvabhu 4; Hāṭakabhu 5; Kuṣmāṇḍabhu 6; Kālāgnirudrabhu 7;
and Anantabhuvana 8.
Within this interval, one hundred and forty principal hells are also to be understood.
This will be written on the occasion of its purification. Thus [ends the section on] the worlds according to the order of emanation. || 108 ||

La-pa, va-pa, ya-pa, oṃ-pada, and likewise caivaṃ-pada—these are twenty-eight. The phoneme *kṣa* alone is the single [final] letter.

The heart is the *sadyojāta* mantra; the subtle path is the obstructer of consciousness (*cidrodhin*). The two seeds are the *valas*; the two channels are *piṅgalā* and *iḍā*. The two winds are *prāṇa* and *apāna*. The two organs are the nose and the anus. The object is smell, which is the subtle element of odor (*gandhatanmātra*). These are the qualities (*guṇas*).
Smell, taste, form, touch, and sound; the state is waking; the two aspects of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) are sound and touch; the cause is Brahmā.

Having thus meditated upon and deposited the portion of the *nivṛtti*-kalā containing the womb of the path, one should immediately thereafter perform the deposition of the *kalās* with the faces and limbs of the purifier above the object to be purified.
Furthermore, at the beginning here, the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the five *kalās* must be performed by the disciple, as follows:
*oṃ haḥ kṣaṃ śāntyatītā-kalāyai namaḥ*.
In the Svatantra [tantra],
having meditated upon the All-pervading Lord in the hand of Śiva as a mass of mantras blazing with its own light,
and having brought forth the two abodes and joined them together, one should place the hand upon the head of the disciple.
With the hand of Śiva facing downwards, one should touch the heart and the back.
Having directed the pervasive Lord— who is self-effulgent— for the sake of burning away the fetters (pāśa),

as previously described, one should [perform the rite] through the sequence of the channels and mantras between the *brahmarandhra* and the heart; for even in the abode of the Blessed Lord, the state of being subject to the fetters exists in that fundamental ground.

O Supreme Lord, by the burning away of the fetters for the purpose of kindling one’s own nature, there is a touch by the venerable Hand of Śiva, which consists of the pervasion of the five powers— consciousness and the rest— as manifested through the five fingers.
In the light—
thereafter, one should worship the blazing wheel of mantras, which fills all paths, with the right hand,
while using the left hand to burn away the fetters.
Placing that [hand] on the head of the disciple, one should place it in sequence upon all his limbs; those [limbs] should not touch him [the teacher] in the same way.
Now, raising the objection, "But since this has been stated in the previous scripture regarding the present topic, from where has it been brought here? he says:
This has been stated in the *Dīkṣottara*: "By means of the Hand of Śiva bestowed by the One who shines with the descent of the flame, he is ordained as a *samayin*."
Sāyujya is the fitness for the absorption of the individual soul (jīva) into the reality of the Lord.

"Jvālāsampāta" [is so called] due to the presence of the splendor of the mantra. As it has been said: "Having meditated on the All-pervasive Lord within the Hand of Śiva, [one perceives] the collection of mantras blazing intensely. Here, "Īśvara" refers to that which exists above the level of the *vidyā-tattva*, and not to Kālāgnirudra, who resides below the level of the *pṛthvī-tattva*.
Because [the scripture] is not seen [otherwise]. "Adhīti" means study (*adhyayana*). As it has been said:

"One who is thus consecrated as a *samayin* indeed attains the right to recite; likewise in listening, studying, performing oblations, worship, and so forth, one whose self is purified through conduct and meditation attains the state of the Lord."
He states "But he who... and so forth, to show that by this [rite] not only the initiation of the pledge (*samayadīkṣā*) occurs, but even the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*).

Furthermore, for one who desires immediate departure (*sadya-utkrānti*), having worshipped him externally in a sacred field (*kṣetra*) or similar location appropriate for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [the teacher applies] that very same kind of Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*) to him.

The meaning is that one should cast [the mantra] onto the head of the one who separates [them] from their life-breaths; by the mere touch of that, immediate initiation into liberation (sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā) occurs for them.
[As stated] in the *Gurupustikā*:

One should worship the seat, the form, and the limbs of Śiva; having caused Śiva to descend into the heart of the disciple, one should worship Him along with His retinue. This has been performed primarily as the core of the union of mantras. [One should draw] a mandala in the middle of the hand with fragrant substances.
Having performed worship, once Śiva has been worshipped, one should indeed first give the hand that was worshipped by Śiva for the sake of purification;
and for the sake of stability, one should recite the mantra worshipped by Śiva's hand a hundred times. By that, one becomes a common initiate (sāmānya-samayin) regarding common rites.

Then, one should install Śiva, together with his limbs (aṅgas) and his vehicle (āsana), within that body of Somaśambhu; subsequently, having worshipped him with flowers and other offerings, one should [consecrate] his eyes with the Netra-mantra or the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having tied [the cloth] with a white garment that has fringes, one should enter by way of circumambulation,
starting from the right side of Śiva.
Having provided a seat with six meanings, he should cause [the disciple] to sit according to the prescribed turn; for the disciple facing east, [he should place it] on the head with the root mantra.
The Hand of Śiva (Śivahasta) should be bestowed, which grants the station of Rudreśa.
Having sprinkled it with the power of Rudra (Rudra-śakti), one should place it before the deity. Having gazed upon its arm, one should inflame it with the power of Rudra.
With that very [flower], he should place a flower upon his two hands smeared with fragrance; having placed those two [hands] so that they are without support, he should meditate upon them.
They were being drawn by the power of Rudra, which took the form of a blazing goad.
Then, having herself taken a cloth and tied it over her eyes so that she is blindfolded, she herself shall drop a flower; from its falling, one should discern her *kula*.

Then, having opened his mouth, one should cause him to prostrate at [the Guru's] feet; one should also worship the Goddess and the Cakra upon his hands and head. Above: Oṃ haiṃ yaṃ, salutation to Śāntākalā. To the East: Oṃ hūṃ raṃ.
Salutation to Vidyā-kalā in the south: Oṃ hīṃ vaṃ, salutation to Pratiṣṭhā-kalā.
In the north: Oṃ hāṃ laṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti-kalā. In the west.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the kalās upon the disciple.
Then, having worshipped the auspicious edict (śāsana) in the hands of the disciple and having caused it to descend into his heart,
one should perform the worship.

Then, one should mentally worship Śiva together with his retinue and the sacred seat (*āsana*) within the self of the disciple, according to the procedure for the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*). Thereafter, the Guru, having placed the hand of Śiva upon his own hands, places that hand of Śiva upon the head and the heart of the disciple.
One should give [it]. Again, in this very same way, having fully worshipped Śiva in the two hands of the disciple, [as stated] in the Tantrasāra.
Then, having worshipped the blazing wheel-deity in his own right hand,
he should place that hand upon the head, heart, and navel of the disciple, burning away the bonds.
Thus say the venerable Ācārya Abhinavaguptapāda:
one should perform the worship of the hand of Śiva as previously described and the transmission of the mantra.
Having washed the hands of the disciple and smeared them with fragrant substances, he should worship them with the five faces [of the mantra] using the root mantra.

Then one should perform the transmission of the mantra (*mantra-saṃkrānti*), the retention of the mantra (*mantra-sandhāna*), the retention of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), and the process of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*). As follows: while uttering the mantra in the central abode through exhalation (*recaka*), having pierced the *bindu* by way of the *suṣumnā*, [one should sever] all knots.
Having first performed the tearing apart and entered the supreme abode, one should contemplate the form of the mantra residing in the hand; this is the conjunction of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna).

Having led [the breath] from the heart to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *recaka* (exhalation), and having entered the heart from the *dvādaśānta*— which has the palm of the hand as its abode— by means of the *recaka*; then,
entering one's own heart again by that same path through *pūraka* (inhalation), one [utters] the *niṣkala-mantra*.
"One should meditate [on it] as pervading everywhere"—this is the "conjunction of mantras" (mantrasandhāna).
Thus, having visualized his hand as filled with a multitude of blazing mantras through the transference of the mantra,
he should place it upon his own head; that is, having performed the transference of the worship-mantra into the disciple’s hand,
he places it on the disciple’s head and heart.
"For one to whom the *sadguru* has bestowed the *caru* of the sacrificial remains in the belly and the hand of Śiva upon the head, the initiation is perfected as its constituent parts.
One should recite the mantra bestowed by the Hand of Śiva a hundred times. [The initiate should wear] white garments and bound *sarṣapa* seeds.

A bracelet made of gold or other materials, having been tied to the right hand of the disciple with three Āryā verses proclaimed in the *Viśvāsasaṃhitā*, the Guru should likewise tie a bracelet from that [disciple's] hand onto his own. Then, as for the triad of vessels: "May the Blessed Lord Civa be the remover of your sins."
May it take away misfortune; may they be diligent for the pacification of all hosts of spirits, and may Nārāyaṇa protect the heart.
May Lord Śiva protect the out-breath and in-breath, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the mind, the head, the hands, and even that which is innate, as well as whatever else is to be protected.
With a mind resolved to uproot the fear of worldly existence, I bind this bracelet upon you—
steadfast, stainless, and skilled in devotion— to attain the eternal state that is free from rebirth in this world.

Then, as previously described, having worshipped [the deity] in the path, in the jar, on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in one's own hand, on the sacrificial mound, in the liṅga, in the maṇḍala, in the sacrificial porridge (caru), as well as in the water and in the fire, one shall obtain the full fruit of initiation.

[The initiation] is performed in one's own hand, in the hand of Śiva, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), according to the Vāma tradition, in a linga, in the consciousness of the disciple, in the form of a Bāṇa [linga] and so forth, or in water contained within a ritual jar.

The fire should be contemplated with a sense of oneness among one's own disciples. For example: from the *brahmarandhra* of the disciple who is thus seated, [the fire proceeds] from the *samanā* situated within the *śivatattva*, which is contained within the *śāntyatītā-kalā* located at the forehead.
The pervasion of the half-moon and the bindu; the preparatory stage (*bhūmikā*); the sixteen worlds in the form of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*);

the single word, the single mantra, and the sixteen phonemes; the cause, Sadāśiva; the mind as a portion of the *puryaṣṭaka*; the two seed-syllables of the subtle path (*sūkṣmādhvan*), the two channels, and the sense organs.

I unite, as one, the two— the word, the object of the word, the subtle element of sound, and the quality of sound— with the Turyātīta (the state beyond the fourth), within the womb, the path, the jar, the sacrificial ground, the fire, and my own disciples; obeisance!

Likewise, [the subtle path] consists of the seventeen worlds, eleven stages, three phonemes, and two mantras located within the three principles known as Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā, which reside respectively at the end of the forehead and the end of the palate, within the Śāntākalā; it also includes the Lord of Causes (Kāraṇeśvara). This is the subtle path.
The path consists of the two seeds obstructing consciousness, the two channels, the two vital airs, the two sense organs, the two types of touch,
the subtle element of touch, the quality of sound, the quality of touch, the state of the Fourth (turyāvasthā),
the portion of the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka), and that which contains the intellect and ego within it.
Likewise, from the two palates down to the navel, there are the seven principles (tattva) included within the category of Vidyā-kalā,
twenty-seven worlds (bhuvana), twenty words (pada), seven phonemes (varṇa), two mantras,
the two seeds that obstruct consciousness on the subtle path (sūkṣmādhvan), two channels (nāḍī), two vital airs (vāyu), and two sense organs (indriya).

The path within the womb of Rudra, which has form as its object, consists of the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra), the three qualities (guṇatraya), the state of deep sleep (suṣupti-avasthā), a portion of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka-aṃśa), and has fragrance as its form; it is the causal [state].
Then, having released the disciple in that manner from the navel down to the ankles,

[one should contemplate] the subtle path (sūkṣmādhvan) consisting of the twenty-four principles (tattva), the fifty-six worlds (bhuvana), the twenty-one words (pada), the twenty-one phonemes (varṇa), and the three mantras, which are contained within the principle of Pratiṣṭhā.
The obstruction of consciousness consists of the two seeds, the two channels, the two vital airs, the four qualities, the five objects,
the five sense organs, the five objects of taste, the five subtle elements of taste,
the state of dream, the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), the cause of the arrow, and the path within the womb of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, from the ankle to the end of the foot, situated within the *nivṛtti-kalā*, are the one hundred and eight worlds belonging to the earth-element, the twenty-eight syllables, the two mantras,
the subtle path (*sūkṣmādhvan*) which obstructs consciousness, the two seed-syllables (*bīja*), and the two channels (*nāḍī*).
(Sc 58; p. 57) (In the *Svatantra*:
"Having caused [the disciple] to arise and having placed a flower in his joined palms (*añjali*), by means of Bhairava...")
Having entered, one should worship Śambhu;
the word "having raised" (*utthāpya*) is used here because the preceding verb *tiṣṭhati* has the sense of "activity.
The meaning is: having caused [the disciple] to undertake the effort of worshipping the Blessed Lord. This is the entry into the maṇḍala.

Having worshipped Śrī Śiva with knowledge, for one who is oriented toward devotion and faith, the accomplishment of intent is such that he has been introduced into grammar, and so forth. "One should worship" (*arcayet*) is from the root *arc* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Thus, the disciple, having been instructed in the mantra by the teacher, [offers] a flower...
Having uttered "Śrī Śiva," one should cast [the flower]. Then, having gone out, one should likewise prostrate like a staff before the Lord within the maṇḍala and perform three circumambulations.

One should salute the Śiva-pitcher situated in the midst of the fire and the one established upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Thus, three times— in each of the three types of temporal paths— the devotee, prostrating like a staff, with the desire "May you, O Blessed Lord, become intent on manifesting my own true nature," [salutes] the Blessed Lord who is indeed to his right.
While performing [the rites], he should wander about and offer praise. And likewise:

"In the worship of Śiva, the fire-ritual, and so forth, one whose body has been made manifest (sakalīkṛta-vigraha) is worthy of worship; otherwise, in his prior state, he would not be fit for worship."
The word "should be" (bhavet) is to be applied to both sentences; the word "etc. (ādi) refers to recitation, meditation, and so forth.
The witness of the sacrificial act of protection, the substratum of action, veiled by impurity, the liberator, the bestower of grace, and the all-pervading Lord possessing five offices.
"In the water-pot, the mandala, the fire, the disciple, and finally the guru— thus it is to be contemplated in sequence," so it is stated in the *Gurupustikā*.
In the light— thus, having grasped the pervasion through oneness within these five: the mandala, the jar, the fire, the disciple, and oneself, one should deposit the path residing in the disciple.
The two winds, the two organs, the object of smell, the subtle element of smell, the five qualities, the waking state,
the puryaṣṭaka (the eightfold city), sound and touch, the causal Brahman, the womb, the path, the jar, the sacrificial mound, the fire— all these are unified within one's own disciples.
"I unite [thee]; obeisance"—with this mantra, one should contemplate through meditative visualization.
And so says Somaśambhu:
He is the witness of the rites in the mandala, the protector of the sacrifice in the ritual jar, devoted to the fire-oblation and other rites in the sacrificial fire,
and the liberator from bonds in the disciple.
"Thus the all-pervading Lord stands in five ways as the benefactor within his own self:

in the *kalaśa* (vase) he is the protector of the sacrifice; on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) he is the witness of the ritual action; in the fire he is the substratum of the ritual action; in the disciple he is the liberator from bonds; and in the guru he is the benefactor. Thus it is said.
The all-pervading one, who has five bases, is to be contemplated.

Then the Guru, reciting the root mantra along with the mantras of the faces and limbs, causes the disciple to offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to each [deity] in the water-pot (*kalaśa*), on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), and so forth— [as well as to the Guru and the Fire]— with the mantra "Homage to all yogis" (*namo'stu sarvayogibhyaḥ*), and causes him to perform a prostration like a staff (*daṇḍapraṇati*).
Without separating the hands, one should lead [the breath] to the fire-ending point.
There, on a mandala marked with the *praṇava* (oṃ) situated to his own right near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
having seated that disciple and sprinkled him with water from the *vidhyargha* vessel,
[he should take] a blade of *darbha* grass root consecrated by the Bhairava mantra, measuring three and a half cubits in length.

Having wound a blade of *darbha* grass counter-clockwise and placed it between his two hands, he should rest the tips against the middle of his own waist and support them with his shins and lower legs, while [holding] that very root of the *darbha* grass.
In the *Svatantra*:

"By the splendor of the mantra deposited [within him], which consists of the expansion of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), with his own hand he draws forth the powers of knowledge and action of this [disciple] by means of the technique of pulling with the hand; thus, 'with the hand' (*hastāt*)."
The meaning of separation is as follows:
then, having offered salutation to the child within one's own self in the fire of the jar, which is the vessel of light;
One should cause [it] to be made. "The preceptor" (ācārya) is an elliptical designation.
Having placed the tip of a *darbha* grass blade in his right sprout-like hand,
there is another opinion that its root should be placed on his own shank and the tip elsewhere.
Thus says Somaśambhu.
Having seated him, one should offer a blade of darbha grass into his hand with the Bhairava mantra.
The root of the *darbha* grass, held in the hand of the disciple with its tip facing upward, stands between the two legs of the preceptor,
positioned in the middle of his outstretched hands which resemble the left and right branches [of a tree].

"In the hands" means [the mantra is] situated in the hands. "In the two shanks" (jaṅghayoḥ) means in the lower shanks and upper shanks; that is to say, at the joints of the thighs and knees. This describes the pervasion of the *darbha* grass.
The piṅgalā and madhyamā channels have emerged from the body of the disciple;
they have become the sacrificial grass (darbha) here and have merged into the channel of the guru.
Then, for the purpose of joining the channels, three oblations are offered by means of Bhairava; through that channel,
one should enter the disciple's heart once.

However, for the purpose of seizing and attracting: seizing and attracting are appropriate only after first establishing a connection between the channels (*nāḍī*) in the form of attaining oneness (*aikātmya*), as stated in the *Śrīspanda*:
"This alone is the seizing of the Self. For this very reason, he says: "Seizing and releasing again and again."
And because it is so at the time of initiation, for that reason there is a convergence of the channels (nāḍī-saṃhati).

"The teacher becomes the very self of the disciple"—this is the remainder from the end of the previous quarter-verse. Having uttered the root mantra, one should cast [the sacrificial substance] into the fire with "svāhā"; with "haḥ," there is the casting upon the head of the disciple, impelled by Śiva.
He explains for the sake of the summary.
Those mantras which reside within the body of the disciple, both externally and internally,
as well as those established in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and worshipped from the primary abode (dhāman) up to the final enclosure (āvaraṇa)— [all these are present].
The simultaneous satiation of these is proclaimed as *sampāta*; herein, for each individual mantra, there are three oblations.
The meaning is that *sampāta* is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the simultaneous manifestation of one's own nature as the essence of Agni and Soma everywhere. Furthermore:
"And then, having raised the disciple from there, [one should perform] the satiation of the mantra for that purpose."
The meaning is that one should perform it; therein:
Having offered one hundred oblations to Bhairava with the Heart-mantra, there should be ten additional oblations;
this is the meaning of "by a tenth part.
Then, having risen with the *dhāman* mantra, one should offer oblations and satisfy [the deity] with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

By the word "having risen," he recalls the procedure for the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation). Thus, having explained the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) pertaining to the general initiation into the *samaya*, he intends to set forth the rule for the *pāśasūtra* (the cord of bonds), which will serve as the specific means for [initiating] the *putraka* and others.
Or, having placed a blade of *darbha* grass upon his own calf and lower leg,
the Guru should contemplate the central channel, the *suṣumṇā*, as it emerges from the body of the disciple and dissolves into his own channel.
Oṃ hūṃ! May [the breath] of [Name], having dissolved into my central channel from his central channel, become absorbed;
svāhā! || 3 ||
Oṃ hūṃ! May the central channel of [Name] become endowed with play within my own central channel;
svāhā! (3 times)

Thus, for each disciple, the masters maintain that there is a connection of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) for the purpose of entering and exiting, abandoning and grasping, and drawing [the breath] therein.
Then, having placed the disciple’s head on the ground with the Bhairava [mantra],

one should perform the *sampāta* (the pouring of remnants) upon the disciple’s head with three oblations each from the *Saṃhitā* [mantra] using "svā" for the fire and "hā" for the disciple’s head, as follows:
(Thus, with the root mantra, one should cast an oblation of clarified butter in the form of supreme nectar onto the head of the disciple:

"Oṃ hūṃ, I perform the *sampāta*; svāhā"—thus into the fire. "Hā"—thus is the casting of the ghee-oblation onto the disciple's head. In the same manner, [one performs it] with the heart-mantra and others: "Oṃ hāṃ, I perform the *sampāta*."
"svā" in the fire, "hā" on the head of the disciple, and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra and ten parts (daśāṃśa) with the heart-mantra and the others, and having maintained the visualization (dhyāna), the full oblation (pūrṇā) should be given:
"Oṃ hūṃ, may there be the accomplishment of the entire wheel of mantras, svāhā vauṣaṭ. Thus is the full oblation.
Having given.
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each of the four attainments (*sampatti*), the mantra for this is as follows:
Oṃ hūṃ! May the prosperity of the land be accomplished; svāhā! || 108 ||
Oṃ hūṃ! May the perfection of time be accomplished, svāhā! || 108 ||
58) Regarding this, he speaks in order to perform the kindling of the mantra for the binding of the nooses:
One should perform the illumination (*dīpana*) of the mantras in sequence, beginning with the *dhāma* and ending with the weapon (*astra*).
To the question "How?", he says:
while reciting the root mantra between two *huṃ*s, preceded by the *praṇava*.
One should present the oblations with [the mantra] ending in *phaṭ*.
This very same [is the case].
Furthermore, the *jāti* (class/type) of all [mantras], beginning with the *hṛdaya*, is stated here in the context of their illumination (*dīpana*).
It is called *jāti* because by means of it, there arises a suitability for its respective effects; it is a specific application of mantra.

The Supreme Lord is a mass of consciousness and bliss, the independent Bhaṭṭāraka.
