The pervasiveness belongs to the *tattvas*, the pervadedness to the worlds (*bhuvanas*); the pervadedness belongs to the *mantras*, the pervasiveness to the phonemes (*varṇas*); the pervasiveness belongs to the *mantras*, the pervadedness to the words (*padās*); and the *kalās*, *tattvas*, and worlds are the denotables (*vācyas*).

The syllables and words of mantra are the denoters (*vācaka*). Thus, the world exists in two ways as the denoted (*vācya*) and the denoter (*vācaka*): the phonemes (*varṇa*) and the supreme energies (*kalā*) are subtle, while the principles (*tattva*), mantras, and the worlds (*bhuvana*) of words are gross; this is another classification. Alternatively, the phonemes are all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*).
The mantras are the pervaded; the mantras are the pervaders, and the words are the pervaded.

The *tattvas* are the pervaders; the *kalās* are the pervaded. The *tattvas* are the pervaders; the worlds (*bhuvanāni*) are the pervaded. Alternatively: the path of the signifier (*vācakādhvan*), consisting of phonemes and so forth, is the pervader; the signified (*vācya*), consisting of the *kalās* and so forth, is the pervaded.

61) Thus, the three bonds to be purified, which reside in the thread and constitute another body here, are fit for cutting, burning, and so forth; however, the conceptualization of the three bonds as residing in the physical body is not [the case].
In that regard, having begun from the state of being a seed, one should include all karma pertaining to the three times, without the bond of the body and its conventional constraints.

In this context, for those who follow the dharma of Śiva, [the result] is to be included as being devoid of the fruit of the mantra accomplished above; for those who follow worldly dharma, it is to be included as being devoid of auspicious fruit.
In the initiation for immediate liberation (sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā) for one whose death is imminent, everything is to be internalized.
For the seedless (nirbīja) disciple, everything is to be internalized except for that which has already begun to bear fruit (prārabdha).

Following that are the path of the powers (kalādhvan), the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of the words (padādhvan), the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan), and the path of the mantras (mantrādhvan).
Having meditated upon the path of purification as form within the body of the disciple,
one should take it up onto the thread by means of the mudrā of withdrawal, preceded by the striking [of the limbs] from their respective locations.
Extending the right hand, slowly drawing back the fingers in order starting from the little finger,
one should bind them and press the tip of the thumb against the moon.
"The *mudrā* is said to be the one that withdraws.
One should place [the mantras] in those very locations in sequence with their respective mantras.
(The reading "amukasthapāśa" is superior; that alone should be employed everywhere.)
Oṃ hūṃ haḥ, to the one who pervades the bonds of the self named [so-and-so], O Śāntyatītā, hūṃ phaṭ!
Having thus struck the head of the disciple with a flower:
Oṃ hūṃ haḥ, to the one who pervades the bonds of the self named [so-and-so], O Śāntyatītā, hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus, taking [the substance] from the head of the disciple with the *saṃhāramudrā*, [there is] the grasping.
Oṃ hūṃ haḥ Śāntyatītā.

Now, [the author] speaks, having raised the doubt: "In what way is there the pervasion of the fetters (*pāśa*) by the *kalās*, and how can the fetters exist in the state of Śāntā and Śāntyatītā, which reside above Māyā?"
The supreme power of the Lord, known as action (kriyā), pervades these three;
it is established under five names according to the divisions beginning with Śāntyatītā.

That eternal power of the Supreme Lord which is inseparable from Him is called *kriyā* (action). When it assumes the state of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), it attains a fivefold nature—beginning with *śāntyatītā*—through the carving out of various diversities. It pervades the three impurities (*mala*s), as it has been said:

This very power, whose nature is action, belonging to Śiva and residing within the bound soul (paśu), is the binder. Therefore, as long as the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā) persists, the fetters remain present according to its propriety; thus, even at the stage beyond peace (śāntyatītā), their purification is appropriate. [This applies] to the pervasive [power].
And when [the self] is purified, there occurs the complete purification of that vital breath (*prāṇa*) which pervades it.
The purification of the impurities (*mala*), which have become one with the self, through the pervasion of the *kalās* and by means of their designations,
is nothing other than the emergence of the nature of the Supreme Lord’s power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), which is eternally inseparable from Him.
As it has been stated: "She who abides on her own path is known to be superior as a means for attaining accomplishment.

It has been determined that the purification of these [energies], which—though appearing as if they have attained duality through being immersed in the nature of those mantras whose essence is the power and vigor of that [reality]—are in fact of that ultimate nature, is accomplished by means of those very mantras. And thus, everything is entirely logical. Furthermore:
One should cause the animal victim to contemplate that the vessel to be placed has been grasped by the receptacle.

"The digits (kalās) are to be placed within the stainless supports. Having joined [the thread] to the thread with the mantra, "I fashion the noose of the digits for the soul of [Name], obeisance," one should color the mark with saffron at the place of the crest-lock (śikhā). || 1 ||
Oṃ hūṃ haiṃ, [Name] residing within the self, to the peaceful *kalā* that pervades the bonds, hūṃ phaṭ! Having thus struck the disciple on the forehead with a flower:
Oṃ hūṃ haiṃ, [Name] self, to the peaceful *kalā* that pervades the bonds, hūṃ phaṭ!
Thus, having taken [the essence] from the disciple’s forehead by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should say:
"Oṃ hūṃ haiṃ! O Śāntā Kalāpāsa, I fashion [you] upon the thread of the one named so-and-so; homage! Having thus applied it to the forehead, one should mark it with saffron. || 2 ||
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, to the Vidyā-kalā who pervades the bonds of such-and-such a self, hūṃ phaṭ!
Having thus struck the disciple on the palate with a flower: Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, to the Vidyā-kalā who pervades the bonds residing in such-and-such a self, hūṃ phaṭ! Thus.

Having taken [the thread] from the palate with the *saṃhāramudrā*: "Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Vidyā, I join the noose of the parts [of the mantra] of [the disciple named] so-and-so to the thread of the noose; obeisance! Having thus joined it to the thread at the palate, one should mark it with saffron. || 3 ||
Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ, to the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā* that pervades the fetters residing within the self of [the disciple named] so-and-so, huṃ phaṭ!
Having thus struck the disciple on the navel with a flower— (sc 63;

Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ, to the *pratiṣṭhā* stage that pervades the bonds residing within [the self] of [Name], huṃ phaṭ! Having thus taken [the power] from the locus of the navel by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*: Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ, I fashion the bond of the *pratiṣṭhā* stage for the soul of [Name] upon the thread of bonds; homage!
Having thus joined it to the cord of the noose, one should mark it with saffron.

Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ, to the Nivṛttikalā who pervades the bonds residing in the self of [Name], hūṃ phaṭ! Having thus struck the disciple at the ankle with a flower: Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ, to the Nivṛttikalā who pervades the bonds of the self of [Name], hūṃ phaṭ! Thus [to] the disciple...

Taking [the thread] from the ankle with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*: "Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ, I join the noose of the *nivṛtti-kalā* of [the soul of] so-and-so to the thread of the noose; obeisance. Having thus attached it to the thread at the ankle, one should mark it with saffron. || 5 ||

In this way, one should, through meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*), join the consciousness of the disciple to the vital points (*marmans*) marked with saffron, primarily up to the end of the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Having meditated upon the persistence of the *āṇava* impurity, there follows the oblation:
*Oṃ hūṃ, may the presence of the *āṇava* impurity be established in the *pāśasūtra* of [Name]!*
Svāhā, three times.
Having meditated on the state of the impurity of Māyā—which is of the nature of Māyā, dependent upon Viṣṇu, and extending as far as the throat—one recites: Oṃ Hūṃ [Name]’s breath.
(In the light.)

Thus, having grasped the pervasion through identity within the five— the mandala, the jar, the fire, the disciple, and one's own self— and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should meditate upon [the deity] as residing in the disciple.
The Kumbha [triangle] is included here within the Artha and Arkartari [triangles], which is why it was stated that there are five.

The teacher should cast the three impurities— the kārma, māyīya, and āṇava— into the arm, the throat, and the crest-lock respectively, by means of the application of thread-knots; "by means of the application of thread-knots" means by way of their respective forms.
Anticipating the objection that these [verses] might be interpolated because they appear in the form of a knot (granthi), he says:
The appearance of that [object] as having such a form is called the "knot of impurity" (malagranthi); thus, the external postulation of a knot is for the purpose of strengthening this conviction.
The manifestation of that Supreme Brahman, whose nature is full light, as something other than its true form— that is, its appearance as a contracted self—
is precisely what is called *mala* (impurity), because it conceals one's own essential nature and yet acts as the means of awakening.
It is called a "knot. To confirm this very point, knots are fashioned externally on the binding thread and so forth in this manner.
Having raised the doubt as to why this was spoken by Bāhu, the son of Devaka, he says:

Viṣṇu, whose nature is *māyā*, resorted to the throat as the locus for the action of his arms; because the downward-flowing flame attained a subtle state (*aṇutva*), such a conceptualization was made by him.

"It has the nature of *māyā* because of its authority within that [womb]; it is called 'downward-flowing' (*adhovahā*) because the power of breath (*prāṇa-śakti*) flows from there as far as the heart.
(Having raised the objection: "Even so, what is the purpose of tripling the thread three times?", he says:)
Anticipating the objection that this is merely his own intention, he says:
To explain the many divisions of the triad known as Nara, Śakti, and Śiva,
one should fashion a cord of nine strands for the purpose of tying it together.
The intended meaning is that all this is indeed composed of the nature of Śiva, the individual soul (nara), and power (śakti).
In this very context, he speaks in order to demonstrate the pervasive presence [of this principle] even according to the methodology of other scriptures.
The triad of fire, water, and food is each threefold within itself; therefore, some in the Upanishads have understood them as white, black, and red.

Regarding what was stated as "the end of the Vedas," in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*’s instruction to Śvetaketu, it is said that from the one Supreme Brahman, fire (*tejas*) was produced; from that, water (*āpas*); and from those, food (*anna*).
Each of these became threefold. Among them, the red, white, and black aspects belong to fire.

Forms came into being: that which is red is fire, that which is white is water, and that which is black is food. Thus, "from this" [means] because the triad of fire, water, and food has such a nature.

In this context, since burning, drying, and other such effects might occur when the direct enjoyment of the body and the severing of its bonds are being performed, this is called a *sūtra* because it indicates the infinite bonds and so forth residing in the primary body through the application of those [aforementioned] actions, and because it provides protection by serving as the means for their destruction.
"In this which is expressed by the word [Śiva], there is the task of severing the bonds (pāśa) and so forth"—this is the meaning of the *pāśasūtra*.
May the proximity of the impurity of Māyā (*māyīya-mala*) exist within the *pāśasūtra*, svāhā! 3.
Having meditated upon the duration of the impurity of karma (karmamala), extending to the limit of its causal activity:
*Oṃ hūṃ, may the presence of the impurity of karma (kārmamala) reside in the cord of bonds (pāśasūtra) of [Name], svāhā*—three times.

Oṃ hūṃ haḥ, homage to the noose of the Śāntyatītā kalā. Thus is the worship. Oṃ hūṃ haiṃ, homage to the noose of the Śāntā kalā. Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, homage to the noose of the Vidyā kalā. Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ, homage to the noose of the Pratiṣṭhā kalā. Oṃ...
HŪṂ HĀṂ, obeisance to the noose of the nivṛtti-kalā. Thus is the worship.
Oṃ hūṃ haḥ! May the presence of the power (kalā) Śāntyatītā be established within the binding-thread (pāśasūtra) of such-and-such a person; svāhā! || 3 ||
Oṃ hūṃ haiṃ! May the peaceful *kalā* reside in the noose-thread of [the soul of] such-and-such; svāhā! (3) Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ! May the *vidyā-kalā* reside in the noose-thread of [the soul of] such-and-such.
Svāhā! 3.
Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ! May the presence of the power of installation (pratiṣṭhā-kalā) within the noose-thread of such-and-such a person be established; svāhā! 3.
Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ, may the bond of the *nivṛtti-kalā* be present within the noose-thread of [the soul of] so-and-so; svāhā!
(3) Oṃ hūṃ haḥ, [may] the bond of the *śāntyatīta-kalā* [be present] within the noose-thread of [the soul of] so-and-so.
I illuminate: *huṃ phaṭ hūṃ svāhā* (3).
*Oṃ hūṃ haiṃ*, [for] such-and-such a person, in the noose-thread, may the peaceful *kalā*-noose [be pacified].
*dīpayāmi huṃ phaṭ hūṃ svāhā* (3).
(Indeed, for the purpose of causing separation, there should be the kindling of the nooses.
*oṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, I kindle the noose of the *vidyā-kalā* within the noose-thread of [the soul of] such-and-such a person.
HŪM PHAṬ HŪM SVĀHĀ (3).
OṂ HŪM HĪṂ, I illuminate the bond of the kalās within the noose-thread of such-and-such a person; HŪM PHAṬ HŪM SVĀHĀ (3).
Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ, I illuminate the bond of the kalā of cessation within the binding-thread of such-and-such a person;
hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ svāhā. (Recite three times.)

Then, according to the method of division previously described for the nyāsa, one should contemplate the distinct pervasion of each kalā. For instance, from the aperture of the heart to the end of the forehead is the Śāntyatītā kalā;
within it is a circular maṇḍala, marked with a bindu and having the luster of crystal.
Having visualized [the deity] as single-faced in meditation, with hands granting boons and fearlessness. || 1 ||

Then, from the forehead to the palate, one should meditate upon the Śāntā-kalā; within it, one should visualize a black hexagonal mandala marked with six dots, having one face, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 2 ||

Now, as for the pervasion of the Vidyā from the palate down to the navel: one should meditate upon its mandala as triangular, red, and marked with a svastika; having visualized it, one should contemplate [the deity] as having one face and hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 3 ||
The *Pratiṣṭhā* [kalā] is situated pervading from the navel to the ankles;

having meditated upon its mandala as being half-moon shaped, white, marked with a lotus, single-faced, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), one should contemplate it. (4)
Now, the pervasion of the Nivṛtti-kalā extends from the ankles to the ends of the feet.
Within that, one should meditate upon a yellow square mandala marked with a vajra,
visualizing [the deity] with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

By such statements as "the measure of the bondage, of the karma, and of the object," it is shown that there is not only the knotting [of the soul], but also at the time of bondage, the measure of the *karma*—
which consists of the auspicious, inauspicious, and so forth— and of the *viṣaya* (object), which consists of the worlds (*bhuvana*) and the like, as well as the nature of the *māyīya-mala*.
From sound, one should calculate the fixed magnitude of the impurity of individuality (āṇavamala) and its pervasion through the paths (adhvan).
It is as follows:

The pervasion of the object—which consists of the *māyīya* impurity—extends up to the level of the *tattvas* and *bhuvanas*, ending at *vidyā*. The pervasion of action—which consists of the *kārmamala*—extends up to the same limit. The pervasion of the impurity itself—which consists of the *āṇavamala*—extends up to the end of *śāntyatītā* in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Having then resolved that it exists in a subtle form, there will be the striking [of the breath] one hundred and eight times for the cessation of the earthly element (*pārthiva-tattva*) and for the cessation of the worlds beginning with Kālāgni; such shall be the measure of the object. This is the cessation of karma.

Pratiṣṭhā extends as far as the end of Vidyā due to the pervasion of impurity; however, Śāntā exists even up to the end of Śāntyatītā in the form of latent impressions (saṃskāra), as a subtle form that persists— let all this be understood in this way.

The fetters (*pāśas*) are then ignited; they are to be bound by means of striking, seizing, and so forth—the word "and so forth" including the tying of knots—for the purpose of ensuring they do not sprout again.
The binding of these very fetters, which have been inflamed, serves to veil the consciousness of the disciple.
The removal of independence.
First, one should place knots of fine thread attached to the marks of the lines, as follows:
Oṃ hūṃ haḥ! O Sāntyatītā, who resides within the essence of [the disciple's] name, who pervades the thread of bonds—here I bind you!
Haḥ hūṃ oṃ namaḥ! With these words, one should place a knot upon a flower fixed at the location of the crest-lock (śikhā). || 1 ||
Oṃ hūṃ haiṃ, I bind the binding-thread that pervades the self-abiding Śāntākalā, O Amukā;
haiṃ hūṃ oṃ namaḥ. With this, one should place a knot of a flower attached to the forehead. (2)
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, I bind the thread of the noose that pervades the self situated within the digit of knowledge (vidyākalā) of [Name];
hūṃ hūṃ oṃ namaḥ. Thus, one should place a knot with flowers upon the *lālunī*. (3)

Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ! I bind you, who reside within the self of [Name], the digit of consecration (pratiṣṭhākalā), pervading the thread of bonds—hīṃ hūṃ oṃ namaḥ! Thus, one should place a knot upon a flower fixed at the navel. (4)
"Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ! O you who reside in the self of the syllable *ma* of the *nivṛtti-kalā*, I bind you, who pervade the thread of bonds!
Hāṃ hūṃ oṃ namaḥ! With these words, one should apply a knot to the flower placed at the location of the ankles. (5)
Thus, with their respective mantras, one performs the tying of knots at their respective locations: at the crown of the head, the forehead, the palate, the navel, and the ankles.
Then one should display the Niṣṭhura-mudrā. Thus, by means of the Niṣṭhura-mudrā, there is the sound:
"O fair-limbed lady, the two fists are clenched, and the two thumbs are positioned in the middle of the palms."
This mudrā of the Lord is known as Niṣṭhurī, which obstructs [the senses].
p. 64) Having placed the nooses in the vessel, one should offer the *sampāta* oblation once.

"Pāśān" means "having established the *pāśa*-cord," which implies "having released it from the body of the disciple. The *sampāta-homa* (the oblation of the collected residue) has been determined in the passage beginning with "the *sampāta* by all mantras," etc. Now, these *pāśas*...
One should offer [the offerings] situated within the pair of vessels onto the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
This is with the intention that these [offerings], which reside within the vessels, are situated between the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*);
and also because of the pervasion of the armor (*kavaca*) and the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*). "On the sacrificial mound" means on the Blessed One worshipped therein.

"Vinivedayet" means that one should make this representation: "The bonds of this sacrificial animal (paśu) were bound by you alone after entering this body. And in the same manner, having led [the disciple], one should offer him into the Kumbha.
Standing there, one should inform the Blessed One as follows: "O Lord, protect the bonds!

And protect the future sons and others who are to be initiated; for them, perform now the consecration of *adhivāsa*, which consists of binding their own capacity for action. Then, [the teacher takes] a blade of *darbha* grass...

He should liberate the disciple. Then, for the purpose of joining the channels (*nāḍī*), he should cause him to place a flower previously prepared in his hand. With that [flower], he should worship the Blessed One together with the mantra, as well as on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), the *śivakuṇḍa*, and the *śivāgni*.
By the use of the word "ca" (and), [the rite] is also performed before the form of the Guru. Then, having circumambulated [the deity], one should prostrate on the ground like a staff.
Having restrained and then released the cord of bonds: *oṃ hāṃ haḥ pāśasūtrāya haḥ hāṃ*.
Thus, having joined the pair of vessels together like a casket.
Having prepared the weapon against women as follows: "Oṃ haḥ hāṃ, for the cord of the noose, hāṃ haḥ," one should enclose [the offering] within a pair of vessels.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the cord of the noose. Having thus worshipped it, [proceed].
(From the *Girupustaka*: "One should perform the *sampāta* [pouring] of the fire for both the teacher and the disciple with the three [mantras] in *saṃhitā* order;
having set aside the remainder of the clarified butter from the *śruva* ladle, one should [offer] drops here into the fire.
One should perform the *sampāta* with the mantras of the faces and limbs in *saṃhitā* order, as before.

"Oṃ hāṃ, I perform the *sampāta*; svāhā," and so forth. Having placed the cord of the noose (*pāśasūtra*) in the hand of the disciple, he should lead that disciple to the vicinity of the sacrificial altar (*yāgavedi*). There, upon the sacrificial altar, he should worship the All-pervading Lord (*vibhu*) with the root mantra (*mūla*).
"The bonds of this sacrificial animal have been bound by you alone, having entered this body consisting of the sacrificial portions.

Thus the Guru should speak. Having caused that disciple to perform a prostration like a staff, he should likewise lead the disciple—who holds the cord of bonds and the vessel in his hands—into the presence of the water-jar (kumbha).

In the water-pot (*kumbha*), having worshipped the Blessed One with the *mūla-mantra*, one should perform the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*) with "Oṃ haiṃ, I veil [you], obeisance," and then cause the disciple to make this petition: "Oṃ, O All-pervading Lord, protect me from the bonds. Thus, for the sake of protection, [one applies] the cord of bonds (*pāśasūtra*).
One should place it in the presence of the Blessed One.

Having untied the root of a *darbha* grass or a *darbha* stalk that has been prepared for the purpose of connecting the channels (*nāḍī*), one should worship it with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the *darbha* stalk. Then: "Oṃ, O Blessed One, protect my channel; for the sake of protection, [I offer] this *darbha* stalk as well."
One should place it upon the leaf of the noose that has been joined together.
(Regarding "before and after"...)
On a clean spot, one should prepare three mandalas with cow dung; in one of these mandalas, the child, having been seated, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having sat down in the second [maṇḍala], the wise one should consume the *caru* offering; having sipped water and standing in the third maṇḍala, he should use the tooth-stick.

O Goddess of the gods, having consumed it, one should then cast it away. A widow should be seated facing that [direction], while a woman who is not a widow, as well as a man, should be seated facing the east. One should also prepare the *pañcagavya* and a portion of the sacrificial rice (*caru*).
For the sake of fitness for eating: one should consume the *caru* from this point forward to determine the state of being the enjoyer of that which is to be enjoyed as consisting of Śiva;
and one should eat the tooth-stick to manifest supreme purity. The term "having sipped water" (*ācamya*) is to be supplied here as well as in the preceding [injunction].

Then, having caused the disciple to perform a circumambulation three times around the omnipresent Lord situated in the three places, one should have him offer a handful of flowers with the mantra beginning "Oṃ namo'stu sarva... and so forth.
And one should worship in the Śiva-fire with: "Oṃ, obeisance to all."

Even before the form of the Guru: "I bow my head to the peaceful True Guru, who is manifest as Śiva himself, seated upon the Yoga-pīṭha, for the sake of attaining the goal of liberation and desire. Thus, with devotion, one should touch the lotus-feet of the Guru.
Now follows the procedure for the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (caru).
In the eastern, western, and middle sections, one should cause three circular mandalas to be made.

Therein, first, when the western mandala has been stepped upon with the feet, the disciple should first drink three handfuls of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), all consecrated with mantras.

In the center of the second mandala, having swallowed eight mouthfuls of sacrificial porridge (caru) the size of a hen's egg, without touching them with the teeth and having caused them to pass down the throat; |||
(The meaning is: "the size of a peacock's cheek").

Following the purification of the face and the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), [one should place] in the third mandala to the east [a branch] from a *cirabilva*, *arjuna*, or *āmra* tree—or in their absence, one from a milk-tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*). (In this regard...)

The *cirabilva* is a tree known as *karañja* in foreign lands; thus says Amara: "The *cirabilva*, the *naktamāla*, the *karaja*, and the *karañjaka* [are synonyms]. Furthermore, regarding the procedure for cleaning the teeth, it is stated in the *Sārasaṅgraha*: "With *cirabilva* and *karañjas*..."

"By *khadira*, mango, and likewise by *arjuna* trees"—this refers to the *karañja* tree, intending it as *pūtīkarañja* or *karañja*. Thus Amara [Kośa] states: "The *pūtīka*, *pūtikarañja*, *pratīka*, and *kalimāraka* [are synonyms]."
Having cleaned the teeth with a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths long and round,
he should face east for the purpose of eating and north for the purpose of drinking,
with his two hands joined in *añjali* between them.
Having taken up the tooth-stick, one should cast it upward; by throwing it toward the tip of the nose with the face turned upwards, one should let it fall slowly upon the ground.
(Śrīsomaśambhu):
Having prepared the three mandalas, he should seat the disciples there, with those seeking liberation facing north and those seeking worldly enjoyment facing east.
First, one should consume three mouthfuls of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the hand joined by kuśa grass, and then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the inner self.
That *caruka*, however, in the second [offering], should be measured by three mouthfuls or eight mouthfuls in size,
and it must be free from contact with the teeth.

For the sake of liberation, one should feed [the deity] from a vessel made of *palāśa* leaves; for the sake of worldly enjoyment, from a vessel made of *pippala* leaves. Having offered [the food] while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should cause [the deity] to eat, and once purified, one should have [him] rinse with water.
Having taken the tooth-stick with the heart-mantra, having rubbed its tip against his teeth, and having rinsed it,
he should cast it upward toward the ground with his face turned upwards and raise the vessel.
In the Guru’s manual:
one should first form three mandalas of three squares each, joined together from front to back.
Therein, upon the central square of one [mandala], [the deity] is seated while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.

One should cause [the disciple] to drink three handfuls of the consecrated five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Having sipped water three times in between, he should eat eight morsels on a Palāśa leaf, untouched by his teeth, for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation; and at the end, he should sip water three times with the mantra of the eastern abode (carudhāman).
The third type of tooth-stick, made from *cirabilva*, *arjuna*, or *āpāmārga*, is said to be twelve finger-breadths in length and as thick as the little finger.
One should purify the teeth from the left side up to the right canine with the Astra-mantra; having chewed [the tooth-stick], one should discard it.
As it has been said:
"When [the breath] remains with the face upward, one attains sovereignty or liberation; but when it is downward-facing, death occurs; one should offer a hundred oblations into the heart."
One should predict the attainment of yoga in the east, disease in the southeast,
death in the south, and strife in the southwest.

In the western direction there is the increase of wealth; in the northwestern direction, there shall be the subjugation of others. In the northern direction one attains success, and in the northeastern quarter, liberation.
Above, Indra, water, and Yakṣas; [the result is] the attainment of beauty. Below, there is heat, death, great disease, wandering, and falling elsewhere.
One should observe the characteristics of the auspicious and inauspicious. The fruit therein: when the tip is directed upwards...

In the east, sovereignty; in the southeast, fortune; in the south, death by weapons; in the southwest, strife; in the west, gain of land; in the northwest, incantations; in the north, success; and in the northeast, liberation.

In this case, if the brushing of teeth is observed in an inauspicious direction or vessel, one hundred and eight oblations should be performed with the *mūlamantra*. For example: *oṃ hūṃ dantadhāvana-vyañjitā śubha-śuddhir astu svāhā* (108).
Alternatively: Oṃ haḥ phaṭ! May there be auspicious purity manifested by the cleansing of the teeth; haḥ phaṭ! || 108 ||
Thus concludes the purification rite of the tooth-stick and the fire-oblation.
(Sesame, rice, clarified butter, milk, and sugar—these constitute the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) for the fire-oblation (*homa*), which wards off untimely death.
Oṃ hūṃ! May there be atonement (*prāyaścitta*) for the removal of whatever faults have been committed through deficiency or excess.
May it be so; svāhā! || 108 ||

Thus, having performed one hundred and eight expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-homa*) with the root mantra to ward off the evil deeds committed through [the errors of] inversion, transposition, deficiency, or excess, he recites: "O sword-bearer on the left! (*vāme kheṭaka*).

Oṃ hūṃ! May the expiation that wards off all deficiencies and excesses, as well as all misdeeds committed, be complete, svāhā vauṣaṭ! Having thus offered the full oblation (pūrṇā), [one performs] the special worship at the sacrificial altar (yāgavedi).

Having performed the satiation of the mantra with a thousand or a hundred [recitations], one should offer the three full oblations as before. The meditation: Oṃ hūṃ, may there be nourishment for Bhairava, svāhā vauṣaṭ. 1.

Meditation: Oṃ hūṃ, may there be satisfaction for the wheel of all mantras; svāhā vauṣaṭ. 2. Meditation: Oṃ hūṃ, may there be the fulfillment of deficient or excessive rites; svāhā vauṣaṭ. (Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one is purified from transgressions.)

Then, one should subsequently satisfy him who has pursued rest in the Root [mantra] with a thousand or a hundred oblations; the meaning is that this continues until his rest is accomplished. This applies to the mantras denoting the limbs and faces, and immediately thereafter to these very same [mantras] by means of a portion of the Śiva-mantra.

O fair-faced one, having performed the offering of food (naivedya) into the fire, the special worship, the water-offering (argha), the binding of the mudrās, the hymn of praise (stotra), and the instrumental music, one should then offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) and dismiss the venerable Supreme Lord— this is the implied meaning— after having offered the argha with the "sealing" (nirodha) argha.

O fair-faced one! Having gathered that Bhairava by means of exhalation (recaka) while recollecting him, and having brought him along as he is filled [with breath] by means of a fist, O fair-faced one, one should worship him as Agniṣṭa. Regarding "Agniṣṭaṃ tam," this refers to what was previously mentioned; "filled" means having gathered him from the mandala by means of inhalation (pūraka).

Having caused the fire to abide by means of *recaka* (exhalation), and having worshipped it there in the same manner, one should take it up with *pūraka* (inhalation) and place it back again; then, having worshipped that which resides therein with flowers and other offerings, one should deposit Bhairava into the *kalaśa* (vase).

Having thus offered the three *pūrṇāhuti*s, and having offered the *nirodhārgha*, one should take the mass of light from the vessels and meditate upon it as dissolved into the All-pervasive Lord (*Vibhu*) situated in the center of the sacrificial altar. Having removed the grass mats (*viṣṭara*) from the vessels, and having cast the water and other substances contained in the vessels onto the *nirmālya* (the discarded floral offerings).

Then, preceded by the recitation of the mantra from the sacrificial altar, one should take with the *pūraka* breath the Lord, together with his retinue, in the form of a mass of light, place him within the *kumbha*, and worship him there in the *kumbha*.
(The worship in the *kumbha* is performed with the intention that the sacrificial hall (*yāgagṛha*) should not remain unoccupied.)

Having performed the *vyāhṛti-homa* for the fire as well with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), [and] having brought fire from another source, one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites as before, worship the Guru and the Brahmins, and offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). The meditation is: "Oṃ Hāra Manoharā. Oṃ Hūṃ.

"May there be the cessation of whatever was done deficiently, excessively, or otherwise incorrectly; may there be the fulfillment of the ritual injunctions, svāhā! vauṣaṭ! Having thus offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and applied the ash-mark (bhasmatilaka), one should then perform the offerings to the quarters (digbali), the libations for the spirits (bhūtatarpaṇa), and so forth, with the sacred thread over both the left and right shoulders.
Having offered water for the cessation [of suffering], one should lead [the deceased] with the exclamation, "Aho!"
On this very night, the sacrifice should be performed in writing, strictly out of the sight of the disciple.
One should also station the disciples individually in that very same sacrificial hall.
"Even the Guru should sleep separately in that very place," so say our teachers.
Now follows the procedure for the disciple’s bed:
having removed the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) from the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), one should smear the *sthaṇḍila* with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Immediately thereafter, upon a bed of *darbha* grass sprinkled with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), [one should place the disciple] who has had a *tilaka* made with musk, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and other substances, while reciting the mantra: "Oṃ juṃ saḥ, protect [Amuka] from all calamities, protect! Saḥ juṃ oṃ vauṣaṭ."
66) Having prepared a rampart of sesame, mustard seeds, and so forth, and having donned the armor, one should [consecrate it] with the *śikhā* mantra together with *darbha* grass:
"Oṃ hūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crown-lock of primordial awakening. Thus, with the *śikhā* mantra.

Having performed the binding of the topknot, he should lay the disciple down—facing east on a bed of *darbha* grass for the sake of enjoyment (*bhukti*), but facing south on the ashes of the *Śaiva*-fire for the sake of liberation (*mukti*). Then, [he should recite]:
"Oṃ haiṃ, I cast this covering over the disciple, huṃ namaḥ," and thus [place it] above.
Having shaken off the covering, he then enters within through the left channel (nāḍī) of the disciple; having ascended to the *dvādaśānta*,
he experiences there the state in which the web of the lunar digits (*kalā*) has been exhausted, and then, ascending again from that full-bodied state, he returns to the heart.
"One should rest. Thus, the teachers maintain that the transition of auspicious and inauspicious dreams occurs for this [individual] through the sequence of entry and exit.
Then one should worship the Night-pitcher (niśākalaśa). Having recited "Oṃ haḥ phaṭ hiṃśakebhyaḥ phaṭ namaḥ" one hundred times, it should be worshipped and placed at the head of the bed.

Oṃ, salutations to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul; salutations to the Auspicious One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams. Speak, O Lord of the Gods of gods; I have come into your presence for refuge. [Tell me] all matters regarding dreams.
Whatever desires reside in my heart, and whatever auspicious things are yet to come—tell them all to me;

salutations to you! Oṃ hili hili! O Mātaṅginī, to the wielder of the trident! Take away my bad dreams, show me what is auspicious! O Lord of All, [reveal] to me that which has been, that which is to be, and that which will be.
Show [it], show it! Oṃ svāhā! (Then the Guru should recite:
Oṃ lihini hilini haṃsini hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, show me my dream, show it! Saḥ saḥ! Destroy the bad dream of [Name]! Hūṃ phaṭ!

Oṃ kāṃ kālike, O destroyer of time, O three-watch goddess, O deity of Yama, hūṃ hūṃ! At the time of initiation for [the person named] so-and-so, grant him his own dream; destroy evil dreams! Svaḥ svaḥ!
Having recited this *svapnamānavaka*, one should cause the *svapnamānavaka* to be recited. Oṃ namo...

To the Blessed One, Vāmana, the deformed one, the three-eyed one, who holds a golden staff and a hand-drum; come, come! O Lord in the form of a child, naked, tell me my dream—past, future, and present—Oṃ Hrīṃ Hrāṃ Phaṭ Svāhā. (Thus.)
"Having caused [him] to recite"—this is the mantra of the dream-boy.

Or [one may offer] with the Vedic mantra: *Oṃ! To those beings who roam by day and night, who desire an offering and are dear to Vidura—to them I, desiring prosperity, present this offering; may the Lord of Prosperity grant me prosperity.*
(Here, in the middle, the phrase "beginning with Dhruva" refers to the world of Dhruva; furthermore, taking Dhruva as the Praṇava, this mantra should be recited:
Oṃ! Those beings of various forms who dwell upon the earth and in the intermediate space...
Those residing in the depths of Pātāla, those belonging to Indra, and those situated with Yama— all beings from Dhruva down to the end of the worlds— are naturally absorbed in the sacrifice of Śiva.

"May they accept the offering; being satisfied, may they bestow auspiciousness upon me. Having given the *bhūtabali* with this mantra, having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and having consumed the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and so forth, one should proceed with the sacrifice itself, accompanied by assistants and armored with mantras.
The preceptor should sleep or remain intent on meditation; this is the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).

O fair-faced one, he should thereafter sleep on the sacrificial ground together with the disciples in the sacrificial hall presided over by the Blessed Lord, so that the Guru and others may observe dreams appropriate to the objects of their initiation.
Either through the yoga of meditation on Bhairava, or while remaining awake in samādhi.
The remainder is that the teacher exists for the sake of the disciple's welfare.

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of the destruction of bonds and the bestowing of the state of Śiva. It is the ritual of dwelling (*vāsakarma*) for the Ācārya, the Sādhaka, the Samayin, and the Putraka during the performance of the great sacrifice (*mahādhvara*). The illustrious Manodaguru is non-dual.
Having extracted the essence of the scriptures, he composed this [work] for the sake of quelling the doubts of those who possess self-control.
And this is written regarding the rite of impregnation (*adhi-vāsakarma*), including the preparation of the milk-oblation (*kṣīra-caru*) and so forth, which is appropriate. Day 2:

Oṃ. Now, on the third day, having performed one's own duties such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyā-vandana*) and so forth, one should perform the examination of dreams (*svapna-parīkṣā*). And that [dream] of one's own is more powerful; nor...
Belonging to the disciples.

In the *Śrīmataṅga*, the teacher should also inquire about dreams with affectionate words; among those, a dream occurring during the final watch of the night quickly indicates what is auspicious or inauspicious.
He states that very point in the *Svacchanda*: "Oṃ, having performed [the rites] at the clear dawn..."

Having performed the rites of purification (*śauca*) and so forth in the same sequence as before—(the word "and so forth" including *prāṇāyāma* and other rites)—and having performed the ritual of total identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should enter the house as before. (Regarding the phrase "as before": this means having performed the worship of the deities of the door.)
Then the disciple, pure and having sipped water, with flowers in hand, should bow his head to the Guru and report his dreams to the delighted Guru.
O fair-faced one, I shall describe auspicious and inauspicious dreams; regarding dreams:
The drinking of intoxicants and the eating of raw meat;
(Āloka:
"That which generally leads to pleasure is usually declared to be auspicious.")
One should proclaim that [result] for the increase of satisfaction, for joy is indeed the supreme fruit;
anything other than this is inauspicious, and in that case, one hundred and eight oblations are prescribed from the Astra-mantra.
The guru should tell his disciples that there is neither pure nor impure;
for he must sever their firmly rooted doubts, which requires great effort.
But for those whose minds are agitated by doubt, nothing— whether auspicious or inauspicious— would arise from the power of dreams.

The word "prāyaḥ" (mostly) implies that there is no capacity for pleasure resulting from the cutting off of the head and so forth. "Tat" refers to that auspicious dream; "ataḥ" means from the aforementioned dream. "Anyat" refers to the opposite category, such as eating the flesh of a side [of the body] and so on. Regarding "astraṃ tataḥ," this refers to the recitation of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) when describing an inauspicious [dream].
The second half [of the verse] provides the reason. "Of them" refers to those whose doubts have dissolved;
the sense is that for one who is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), there could not possibly be a distinction between the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Furthermore, because they consist of the three *guṇas*, these [dreams] possess variety even in the state of sleep; thus he says:

Thus, by virtue of their diversity, they may be as follows: the *rājasa* being clearly perceives the self through the mere signs (*liṅga-mātra*); the *tāmasa* being perceives nothing at all for him—neither pleasure nor pain, neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious.
Now, if the *tāmasa* being perceives nothing whatsoever, from where [could his experience arise]?

Anticipating the doubt as to how there can be a determination of the auspicious and inauspicious, it is said: "Its auspiciousness and inauspiciousness consist in pleasure and pain. Now, having raised the objection—"But how can one who is dominated by tamas have any qualification for the rite of initiation (dīkṣā)?"—the author demonstrates and refutes that doubt.
"Surely, in this context, one called 'tāmasa' would be fit for mention in the rule? Not so; no one anywhere possesses a deficiency in any respect whatsoever."
The word *vai* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), and it should be connected with every [term]; "quality" (*guṇa*) is [the term] implied as being predominant. He demonstrates this very point.
If one who possesses all sāttvika conduct is tāmasa in his eating, does he thereby become base,
or is there some great reversal of excellence?
"Therefore" means that because tamas is present even in mere eating; "its opposite" means that when tamas is entirely absent, sattva is present even in mere eating.
He applies this very point to the subject at hand.

O Lord, even one who has received the descent of power (śaktipāta) and has been initiated may, due to the persistence of his latent dispositions (guṇasthiti), possess a manifold nature; therefore, one should remain concentrated on the primary goal.
"Of the state of the qualities" (*guṇasthiteḥ*) means because the natural body persists for some time. "Principal" (*mukhya*) refers to that characterized by initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth.
[The rites include] smearing with excrement and worms, consecration with blood, and eating...
For one who has eaten curd-rice, there shall be the smearing of white garments.
A white parasol held above the head, white garlands, garments, and ornaments; travel by means of lion-thrones and chariots, a banner, and the consecration of sovereignty.
Jewels, limbs, ornaments, and the like; betel-leaf and fruit as well; the sight of Śrī and Sarasvatī; and the embrace of auspicious noble women.
Having held a discourse with kings, sages, gods, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Gaṇas, and teachers, one attains success in a dream.
Crossing rivers and the ocean, traveling through the sky, as well as the rising of the sun and the blazing of the sacrificial fire.
The sight of the orbs of the moon, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars;
and likewise, ascending a palace tower or even its pinnacle.
Climbing upon men, horses, bulls, young elephants, trees, and mountain peaks; traveling by celestial chariot;
and beholding those who have perfected mantras.
For one by whom the mantra has been mastered through successive stages,
there is the attainment of the movement of the *siddhas*, as well as visions of gods and other beings; furthermore, there are the pill,
the tooth-stick, the sword, the foot-ointment, and the gorocanā pigment.
The sacred thread, collyrium, nectar, the pārautauṣadhī plant,
a spear, a water-pot, a lotus, a rosary, and realgar.

"The term 'within the dream' does not refer to the beginning or the middle of the dream. As it was stated before: the omen perceived during the day is to be grasped at the end [of the night], whereas that perceived at night is to be grasped at the beginning [of the day].
Having seen blazing substances of accomplishment, such as red ochre and others, one attains success."
At the end of the dream, the acquisition of land will certainly occur.
"A wound" refers to one produced on one's own body by a weapon; there is also a reading: "A wound [arising] from the acquisition of land. (Sc 69;
A battle that was a crossing through a sea of blood, a victory in combat, a blazing cremation ground,
yet beautiful, and filled with heroes and lords of heroes.
Together with heroes, vītalas, and siddhas, [he] partook of the eating of great flesh (the reading "selling" also exists),
having respectfully offered a portion of the Great Animal (the Great Animal being the human victim) to the gods.
Worshipping the deity by himself, muttering prayers, meditating, and even offering praise, he beholds the blazing fire as if it were worshipped with his own oblations.
[He saw] a vehicle for mounting, resonant with the sweet cries of swans, cranes, and ruddy geese, [attended] by the Pitṛs,
the Mātṛs, and the Bhairavas, together with the hosts of Mātṛrudras (the Mātṛrudras being specific classes of deities).
Having beheld Bhairava and Bhairavī, one attains perfection here; of this there is no doubt.
(Siddhyati means that one attains the supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) corresponding to that dream; this is the meaning.
Seen, heard, experienced, desired, imagined, and likewise meditated upon— [The text continues: *bhāvito*... [is attained].
And that born of the humors (doṣa); thus, dream is said to be of seven kinds.

(Thus, although dream is a separate causal factor, nevertheless, here— in this abode of sacrifice presided over by the venerable Lord and the Guru— it is seen to correspond exactly to the future fruit, due to the majesty of the mantras and so forth, during the period of residence.)
Auspicious dreams have thus been described; now learn from me those that are inauspicious:
anointing with oil, drinking oil, and entering into the netherworld (rasātala).
Falling into a blind well, or sinking into mud; falling from trees, vehicles, or elephants, or from a palace or a mountain.
The cutting off of ears, the nose, or the hands and feet; the falling out of teeth and hair; and the sight of yakṣas and monkeys.
Likewise, for those of cruel nature such as vetālas (where "cruel beings" refers to tigers and the like), one should likewise [visualize] the Kālapuruṣa,
with black, upright hair, and a soiled appearance, clothed in black garlands and garments.
If a red-eyed woman embraces a man in a dream, he will die;
there is no doubt about this, unless one performs a propitiatory rite.
The destruction of houses and palaces, as well as [the loss] of beds, clothes, and seats; one's own defeat in battle, in combat, and the seizure of one's wealth.
[The practitioner undergoes] rebirth and activity among donkeys, camels, dogs, jackals, herons, vultures, and crows, as well as among buffaloes,
owls, and ravens.
A person of distorted mind perceives the eating of cooked meat, red garlands and ointments, and black and red garments, as well as his own marriage and other such events while laughing.
Leaping is the state of being a man.
Laughing, leaping, wearing a withered garland and fine garments in a dream,
cutting off one's own flesh, being bound, and being devoured by a black serpent— [these are the signs].

One whose mind is agitated by obstacles or who has a terrifying appearance, as well as one who sees a marriage in a dream— such a person perishes. Indeed, these are declared to be inauspicious signs that must be understood by the most excellent of instructors.
(The meaning is that the consideration of the relative strength or weakness of these [dreams]— such as their timing, nature, and so forth— should be carried out in accordance with their effects.
Thus ends the examination of dreams.

Upon seeing an inauspicious dream, having performed worship to the Lord residing in the water-pot (kalaśa) and having offered oblations into the fire for the sake of expiation; if an inauspicious dream occurs at the end of the night, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times;
if it occurs during the first watch of the night, a hundred times; and if at midnight, three hundred times.
Having performed the oblation, one should spend the day with special worship, recitation, *dūrvā*, and *śamī* offerings;
however, if an auspicious dream is seen, one may commence the ritual (*tantra*) on that very day.
And therein, the procedure for the layout of the nine-naved [mandala], which is the subject at hand, is now written down.

There, having constructed a sacrificial altar (*yāgavedī*) fifty-six *aṅgulas* wide and four *aṅgulas* high, one should smear the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting: "Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to the heart of Aghora. Then, at the station of Brahmā, one should recite: "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance."
One should perform the worship.
(This means in the central region, at the place of Brahmā.

At the root of the *karaṇa-khaṭṭika*, having meditated upon the powders (*rajas*) that pervade the digits (*kalā*) after consecrating them with mantras, one should bring those powders; he speaks of them as follows:
One should prepare white powder from crystal, pearl, and conch shell;
and red powder from ruby and coral, as well as yellow powder from *pīlu*.
That which is born from gold is yellow; that from sapphire is black; rice powder is to be known as white;
and the king [of powders] is born from black color.
This is declared to be the middling [method], which grants success through the middling [practice];
that powder is said to be white ash and stone-dust, perfumed with fragrances.
Likewise, one should carefully cause a baked brick [image] to be made red, yellow with turmeric powder,
or black with oily pigments.

Sindūra should be red, as it destroys all calamities; in its absence, red ochre, yellow ochre, or that derived from water-weeds may be used. Alternatively, the five-colored powders (*pañcaraṅga*) should be prepared in whatever way is most beautiful, such as with *piśikisorā* and the like; for without these powders, [the rite cannot be performed].
For the disciple, there is indeed the performance of the rite of subjugation at the proper time.

Having reflected thus, one should apply effort toward the *rajas* (energies). One should contemplate the *rajas* as pervading the *kalās*. To explain how this is so, he says: therein, in the cool (*suśīta*) *rajas*, one contemplates Śāntyatītā;
in the black (*kṛṣṇa*), Śāntā; in the red (*rakta*), Vidyā; in the white (*śukla*), Pratiṣṭhā; and in the yellow (*pīta*)...
Having meditated upon the cessation [of worldly activity],

one should perform the subsequent scattering of the consecrated powders (*rajas*) by means of the hand— which, through its fingers, pervades the form of the digits (*kalā*) of Bhairava’s big toe— while the invoker himself remains present.
Otherwise, the mention of future defects would be untenable.

Having prescribed the descent of dust and so forth through the recollection of the Abode (*dhāman*), the sacrificial mandala— which is called "nine-navelled" (*navanābha*) and consists of the *Svatantra* and other [tantras]— is [performed] while the disciple is out of sight, according to authoritative tradition.
One should cause [it] to be made.
As it is said in the Śrī Svacchanda:
Oṃ! A wise man should draw a nine-cubit house for Vadyārāja, whose syllables are characterized by the number nine, beginning with eight joints and so forth.
Indeed, this world, consisting of two hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths,
reflects the various paths within itself.
That [mandala] is divided into seven parts and further partitioned from south to north; herein, the conceptualization is that each part consists of thirty-two finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Having first divided the square and marked it with fish-figures, the east-west alignment shall be established by means of the fourfold fish-bond.
The field, square on all sides, should be divided into seven parts; one should draw forty-nine squares using a cord.
O Great Goddess, having drawn a lotus measuring thirty-two finger-breadths within the middle enclosure, which has been divided into four parts, one should omit the fourth part.
One should fashion the pericarp in the first [circle], the filaments in the second, the joints of the petals in the third,
and the tips of the petals in the fourth.
Having drawn eight lines in each of the cardinal directions as well as the intermediate directions,
one should then rotate four circles, each measuring four finger-breadths in diameter.
One should lay out a thread between the two lines of each pair of directions;
then, from the tip of that thread, one should rotate [the compass] according to the procedure for the half-moon.
The wise one should place [the syllable] situated upon the filaments in the middle sūtra; having thus prepared the eastern petal, [one proceeds].
